In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven requirements for every input, compared with three under parallel Oracle@8. Together, our benchmark, analysis, and data pipeline establish a foundation for models to reflect on 3D content through reliable verification feedback.

title: Band-Resolved Superconducting Gaps via the Thermal Hall Effect in CeRu2
abstract: Standard bulk probes of multiband superconductors cannot assign pairing gaps to specific electron or hole Fermi surfaces. Here we show that thermal Hall transport ($κ_{xy}$), constrained by specific heat and normal-state magnetotransport, resolves this ambiguity in the compensated heavy-fermion superconductor CeRu$_2$. Fixing the gap magnitudes ($Δ_e/k_B\approx 13$K, $Δ_h/k_B\approx 8$K) and band mobilities completely determines the electronic degrees of freedom in $κ_{xx}$ and $κ_{xy}$. A low-field sign reversal in $κ_{xy}$ places the larger gap on the heavy Ce $4f$ electron sheets and the smaller on the hole sheets.

title: CoDA: Co-Evolution of Data Engines and Action Policies
abstract: Generative simulation can automate robot environment construction, but physically valid environments are not necessarily useful for training. The challenge is to identify environments that address a policy's failures and supervision that helps it overcome them. We introduce CoDA, a framework in which a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve through a shared heterogeneous memory of environment construction, policy failures, and learning progress. The memory compiles validated diagnoses from a vision-language critic into generation programs that recreate difficulties and training programs that help the policy overcome them. We further propose Text2potential to convert these diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, providing dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard shaping assumptions. Measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. Across four manipulation task families, CoDA improves out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, exceeding the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points with the same generation budget. On LIBERO-Pro, 15 rounds of generation and training raise success from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations.

title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual-action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision-language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. Project Page: https://p3-wam.pages.dev/

title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.

title: $^6$He structure from semiclassical 3D models based on $\textit{ab initio}$ spatial correlations
abstract: We construct semiclassical 3D models based on $\textit{ab initio}$ no-core shell model calculated two-body spatial correlations, which represent the preferred spatial configuration of nucleons for the ground state of $^6$He. We demonstrate that the presence of the two valence neutrons distorts and flattens the $α$ core in $^6$He, marking a clear departure from the tetrahedral configuration of free $^4$He, and that the two valence neutrons and the center of mass of the $α$ cluster ($α$-CM) are roughly located at the three distinct vertices of an equilateral triangle. We compute the geometric parameters that commonly characterize $^6$He structure, 1) $θ_{nn}$, the opening angle of the two valence neutrons with respect to $α$-CM, and 2) $r_{nn}$, the root-mean-square separation between the two valence neutrons. Refining the model with uncertainty estimation, we obtain $θ_{nn}= 58.5^{+5.4}_{-6.2}$ degrees and $r_{nn}= 4.12^{+0.37}_{-0.43}$ fm, agreeing with those calculated via a phenomenologically modified continuum-discretized coupled-channels method, while an interferometry experiment obtained a marginally higher $r_{nn}$.

title: Uniform estimates for elliptic systems with critical Sobolev coefficients
abstract: The $W^{1,p}$ estimate for uniformly elliptic operators of divergence form with VMO coefficients is classical. In particular, this provides $W^{1,p}$ estimates for elliptic operators with coefficients in $W^{1,n}$. However, this theory does not yield constants in the estimates controlled by the $W^{1,n}$ norm of the coefficients, since the total $W^{1,n}$ norm does not control the rate of decay for the mean oscillation. In this work, we establish uniform estimates for divergence-form elliptic systems whose coefficients lie in the critical Sobolev--Lorentz spaces $W^{1,(n,s)}$ with $1\le s<\infty$, have an $L^\infty$-bounded spatially symmetric part, and satisfy an integral ellipticity condition. The constant in the estimate is controlled by the corresponding norms of coefficients and the ellipticity constant.

title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

title: Value as Memory: Online Value-Guided Post-training for General Robot Policies
abstract: Real-world post-training of generalist robot policies faces two challenges: partial observability makes action selection ambiguous, while offline post-training methods delay feedback from deployment experience. We present Value as Memory (VaM), a framework that addresses these challenges through value caching and online real-world reinforcement learning (RL). Value caching conditions actions on recent value predictions as task-progress memory, while online updates enable timely policy improvement by combining offline demonstrations, off-policy interventions, and on-policy rollouts for sample-efficient adaptation. As a result, VaM transitions from offline RL warmup to online autonomous learning with sparse rewards. Across long-horizon tasks involving deformable objects and contact-rich manipulation, VaM yields a mean absolute success-rate gain of $29.4\%$ with value caching, while achieving a $32.8\%$ gain with online autonomous learning over matched offline training. The evaluated online schedule performs $8\times$ as many policy iterations under the same gradient-step budget, with more than $2\times$ lower recorded time per gradient step with concurrent data collection and training.

title: SoftCache: Adaptive Step Size Caching for Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Diffusion and flow models generate a sample over iterative steps, each a full pass through a large network, and that pass dominates generation cost. Training-free caching accelerates them by reusing activations from recent evaluations instead of recomputing them. Dynamic caching methods decide when to refresh by accumulating a cheap probe of the network input into a staleness signal and spending a fresh evaluation once it crosses a threshold. They perform hard caching: the signal is a binary switch between refresh and reuse, and every step, fresh or cached, advances by the prescribed step size. We observe that the signal carries much more than this switch. How far it sits below the threshold, its headroom, predicts the error induced by reuse. We propose SoftCache, which performs soft caching: instead of a binary switch, the headroom sets how far each cached step goes. Where the headroom is large, the sampler jumps past several scheduled nodes, and as a refresh nears, its steps shrink back toward the original step. These adaptive jumps may land between the scheduled nodes, taking the sampler off its fixed grid. SoftCache requires no training and adds no per-backbone settings: on FLUX for images and on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1 for video, at speedups from $3.5\times$ to $6.9\times$, it is ahead of every baseline on all four fidelity metrics.

title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation
abstract: Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence. In this work, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the underlying diffusion dynamics. Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information. To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics- aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised estimate. The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details. Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates. Experiments on PixArt-a and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungJuCha/DaTMe.

title: Gen4P: Video Generators are 4D Perceivers
abstract: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p.github.io for more visual results.

title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.

title: Structured Authority Injection: Persistent Human Control for LLM Agents via Typed MCP Overrides
abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used as autonomous orchestrators in distributed and multi-agent systems, yet a control gap remains: no protocol-level mechanism allows human operators to inject binding directives that persist across planning cycles. Free-text overrides suffer from ambiguous interpretation due to lack of schema validation and from authority erosion as operator instructions lose influence within accumulating context. We propose Structured Authority Injection (SAI), a protocol that addresses these issues by routing operator corrections through typed, schema-validated Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool calls and maintaining a ranked authority context prepended to each LLM prompt. SAI defines three override classes (Constraint, Priority, and Strategy) with distinct persistence semantics and an explicit precedence order enforced via a directed authority channel inaccessible to the planning process. The method requires no model fine-tuning or access to model weights and applies to instruction-tuned LLMs supporting MCP tool use. Evaluation across nine LLMs and eight scenarios targeting agent failure modes shows reduced ambiguous directive interpretation and mitigated authority decay across planning iterations, with lower prompt overhead in the strongest models (up to 38% depending on model and scenario), though benefit varies substantially across models. SAI provides a general design pattern for agent systems requiring explicit and persistent human control.

title: Quadratic mixing for the Lee--Sidford Dikin walk
abstract: Let $K=\{x\in\R^d:Ax\ge b\}$ be a bounded full-dimensional polytope with $m$ inequalities. For targets on $K$ with density proportional to $\exp(-\vartheta^\transpose x)$, we prove a $\widetilde O(d^2)$ bound, measured in Markov chain iterations, for the chi-square mixing of the $1/2$-lazy Metropolis Dikin walk based on a polylogarithmically rescaled Lee--Sidford metric. The estimate holds for every initial law with finite chi-square divergence. The proof controls the reverse Gaussian proposal through a quantitative average self-concordance estimate at the required $O(1/d)$ scale. We establish this estimate from uniform analytic derivative bounds for the Lewis-weight subspace and an all-order projection-weighted contraction inequality for Gaussian chaoses. For order $j$, the latter bounds each base-point polynomial at scale $d^{j/2}$, up to $j$-dependent and logarithmic factors. Truncating at logarithmic order then absorbs the remaining pathwise loss. This resolves, in the affirmative, the open problem of whether the Gaussian Lee--Sidford Dikin walk mixes in $\widetilde O(d^2)$ iterations: the previously stated quadratic bounds \cite[Theorem~1.4]{LLV20}, \cite[Theorem~1.2]{GKM24} rest on reverse-proposal steps identified as unresolved in \cite[Section~1]{Kook26}, whose $\widetilde O(d^{9/4})$ bound was the best rigorously established rate prior to this work. The proof is found by ChatGPT 5.6 Pro.

title: A Physics-based and Geometry-aware Reduced-order Framework for Accelerated Part-Scale Thermomechanical Simulation of Additive Friction Stir Deposition Process
abstract: Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) is attractive for naval and aerospace sustainment because it enables high rate, solid state near net shape fabrication and repair of large metallic components. However, full part scale thermomechanical simulations remain computationally demanding because of the moving heat source, progressive material deposition, and evolving geometry. This work presents a physics-based and geometry-aware reduced order framework for rapid prediction of temperature and residual stress fields in part scale AFSD builds. The transient temperature field is represented using a tensor product quadratic B spline basis on a fixed Cartesian background grid, while arbitrary part geometries are embedded using a signed distance function (SDF) and a smooth material indicator. Residual stresses are recovered through an inherent strain formulation in which an offline thermo elasto plastic representative volume element (RVE) simulation supplies a calibrated eigenstrain field that is spatially scaled using the part scale peak temperature history. The thermal formulation is evaluated against published numerical and experimental AFSD data and two sample multilayer builds are simulated as demonstrations. For a four layer thin-wall build, the thermal solution requires approximately 22 s compared to 806 s for the finite element model, while the complete thermo-mechanical framework requires approximately 86.4 s compared to 2,406 s. For a larger 20 layer hollow cylindrical build, the reduced order thermal simulations requires 0.148 to 0.152 h compared with 1.8 h for the finite element model, corresponding to thermal speed-ups of approximately 11.8 to 12.2 times. The complete thermomechanical framework requires 0.346 h compared to 5.4 h for the full finite element analysis, providing an overall speed-up of approximately 15.6 times.

title: Physics-Transfer Learning: A Physics-Constrained Theory for Zero-Shot Generalization Along the Ladder of Complexity
abstract: Reliable out-of-distribution generalization remains a central challenge in machine learning, particularly when models are deployed in data-scarce high-fidelity domains. Existing approaches often rely on statistical distribution alignment, or invariance assumptions that can fail when domain shifts reflect changes in underlying mechanisms. Inspired by a longstanding paradigm in physics that understands complex systems by starting from tractable idealizations and progressively incorporating additional mechanisms and levels of fidelity, we propose physics-transfer (PT) learning, a physics-constrained learning theory for zero-shot generalization along a ladder of complexity. PT constructs chains of anchor domains (CADs) that connect low-cost source domains to complex targets and introduces computable feasibility and reliability indicators for assessing transfer before target-domain labels are observed. Under physical-consistency and stable-representation assumptions, we derive an operational upper bound on target risk in terms of source empirical risk, the PT indicators, and finite-sample errors, and establish convergence as adjacent complexity gaps shrink and data coverage improves. We evaluate PT on excited-state energy prediction in quantum systems and dynamical-transition prediction in classical systems using neural networks trained without target-domain labels. Across substantial distribution shifts, PT yields accurate high-fidelity predictions, while the indicators identify incorrect physical mappings before target-domain prediction fails. These results provide a model-agnostic framework for designing, diagnosing, and controlling generalization in data-scarce learning problems.

title: Memory Bandwidth, Not FLOPs: Profiling and Accelerating Query-Based Segmentation Decoders on Edge GPUs
abstract: Query-based segmentation models achieve strong performance even under real-time inference on workstation GPUs. On edge devices, however, we show their transformer decoders are deeply memory-bandwidth-bound, a bottleneck invisible to standard FLOP analysis that worsens with input resolution and limited DRAM bandwidth. An FP16 roofline analysis with tensor-core GEMMs active and hardware DRAM counters shows that the non-tensor-core aggregates of FastInst and Mask2Former reach only $2.5\%$ to $6\%$ of the CUDA-core ridge yet account for $53\%$ to $70\%$ of decoder time and $61\%$ to $71\%$ of decoder bytes. The largest individual kernels sustain up to $90\%$ of nominal peak DRAM bandwidth, effectively saturating the memory bus. The bottleneck is therefore not primarily low GEMM intensity, but cross-kernel activation traffic. CompactInst addresses this bottleneck using parameter-free spatial pooling at $4{\times}$, which reduces the bytes moved within the transformer decoder, while a two-convolution refinement head recovers spatial detail. Under TensorRT FP16 on Jetson Orin Nano, CompactInst delivers decoder speedups from $2.35{\times}$ to $4.74{\times}$ and model speedups from $1.57{\times}$ to $2.62{\times}$ as input resolution grows, while closely matching accuracy ($-0.4$ AP on COCO val2017, $+0.2$ AP on Cityscapes test). A heavier variant with $2.57{\times}$ more decoder FLOPs still runs its decoder $1.74{\times}$ faster on the most bandwidth-constrained device, confirming at the deployment level that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, govern latency.

title: Regime-Aware Coupled Orchestration of Neural Operator Specialists for Multiphysics Dynamics
abstract: Real-world physics often unfolds over a variety of characteristic lengths and time scales. These non-uniformities are among the main reasons numerical simulations remain expensive when used predictively on practical systems: the same computational domain can contain smooth transport, vortical structures, thin interfaces, reaction fronts, and rapidly relaxing regions. Neural operators are attractive surrogates for such problems. However, a single architecture is still expected to represent all these local behaviours with a single set of weights and a single inductive bias. In this work, we introduce the regime-aware coupled neural orchestrator (RCNO), a framework that learns to distribute and connect a library of local operator specialists in space and time. For every patch, an orchestrator builds a causal query from the current fields, neighbouring halo values, local regime features, patch identity, activity level, and case parameters. The nine expert embeddings exchange two rounds of query-conditioned message passing before an edge-biased cross-attention stage produces a dispatch distribution that can be evaluated sparsely. Local predictions are assembled into a global field and projected onto system-specific physical constraints. A seam-aware extension additionally learns residual corrections across internal patch interfaces. We apply the same orchestration architecture to two qualitatively different systems: reacting flow and Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes (CHNS) dynamics. The results show that useful operator specialisation exists across local regimes, that the advantage of conditional composition increases as the spatial decomposition becomes finer, and, on reacting flow, that explicitly treating patch interfaces improves continuity, PDE consistency, and rollout accuracy.

title: When is a large language model a good calibration agent? Physics-labeled prompting for budgeted engineering simulator calibration
abstract: Calibrating expensive engineering simulators requires tuning model parameters to match reference data, a process heavily constrained by computational costs. This study investigates whether Large Language Models (LLMs), conditioned on physical diagnostic descriptions of simulation errors, can propose informative parameter updates more efficiently than conventional derivative-free optimizers. We test this on a cylinder-wake Large-Eddy Simulation and a damped-oscillator inverse problem. Physics-labeled prompts are evaluated against four text ablations (removed, anonymized, padded, misdirected) and standard optimizers (Nelder-Mead, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and random search). Results demonstrate a strong early semantic advantage: the first physics-informed LLM proposal improves the initial design in 23 of 25 trials. After five evaluations, the median calibration error is 21.9 times lower than physics-free controls. However, this advantage is transient - disappearing by fifteen evaluations - and inherent LLM decoder variability yields a 9.8-fold performance spread. To address this, we introduce a hybrid workflow that uses the LLM as a warm-start, passing accumulated evaluations to a conventional optimizer. This two-stage numerical continuation policy reaches target accuracy in just 9 simulator runs, outperforming the LLM alone (12 runs), Nelder-Mead (17 runs), and Bayesian optimization (>60 runs). Supported by sensitivity analysis validating the test cases, this hybrid physics-labeled LLM scheme proves highly effective as a calibration agent under strict evaluation budgets.

title: Trust but Verify: Designing Region-Inhomogeneous Forward Dynamics for Discrete Diffusion
abstract: Continuous diffusion treats the forward process as a design space; discrete language diffusion often uses absorbing corruption, leaving context fully trusted throughout generation. This makes trust binary: corrupted context is copied as ground truth, propagating errors into generated spans. We reopen this design space by combining absorbing and uniform-mixing kernels with region-dependent rates. Missing positions follow absorbing dynamics, while context undergoes low-rate random substitution, exposing the model to observed but uncertain tokens during training. At inference, a heuristic sampler re-injects noise into suspicious context under an annealed intensity and freezes context updates late in the trajectory. An 8,000-step finetune of a pretrained 170M-parameter masked diffusion model takes under five hours on a 6 GB laptop GPU. The base model assigns roughly 50% probability to observed tokens even when they are uniform-random garbage. For uniform-random corruption, finetuning detects corrupted context with 0.96 recall and 0.91 precision, improves infill token-F1 by 3.8 points at 10% corruption and 6.4 points at 20%, and removes the accuracy dip next to corruptions. Clean conditioning shows no measurable regression, with a false-edit rate below 0.4%. Gains for plausible corruptions are weaker: about 0.5 F1 points at 10% corruption, without statistical significance. Our results suggest that detectability and damage depend jointly on departure from the data conditional: nearby noise is hard to detect and semantically mild, while distant noise is conspicuous and destructive. We interpret absorbing diffusion as the infinite-contrast limit of a trust axis, analogous to the signal-to-noise gap between known and unknown regions in diffusion inpainting. In our setting of a 170M model and a single text domain, intermediate trust is reached by changing forward dynamics rather than architecture.

title: Binding-Specific Relearning Savings for Test-Time Continual Learning
abstract: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? Parameter-updating test-time continual learning agents are usually evaluated by current output accuracy; we ask whether that measurement captures how prior experience shapes later updates. We test whether learning a specific factual binding produces a later relearning advantage beyond familiarity with its entity, answer vocabulary, format, or query slot. In Qwen2.5-1.5B, we compare three matched, counterbalanced histories: LEARNED receives the correct binding, CONTROL receives matched exposure without it, and WRONG receives a competing relation-valid answer in the same slot. After an identical rehearsal-free continual fine-tuning stream, LEARNED reacquires the target faster than CONTROL at a prespecified checkpoint of partial forgetting. WRONG shows no positive advantage over CONTROL, while its comparison with LEARNED provides slot-matched corroboration, subject to possible competitor interference. The advantage remains positive after adjustment for measured pre-relearning behavior. In a secondary descriptive conversion using an unpaired never-seen pool, prior learning reduces the optimizer updates required for restoration by about 18%. Current behavioral accuracy can therefore underestimate the lasting effect of previously acquired experience. Code is available at https://github.com/zhezhou1106/relearning-savings

title: Eliciting Specifications: When Does Interactive Clarification Help?
abstract: LLMs can generate Lean specifications from task descriptions, but those descriptions are often underspecified or ambiguous and may omit verifier-relevant edge cases, yielding imperfect formal specifications. We study whether an elicitation agent (EA) can improve verifier-checked Lean specifications by seeking clarification from a reference-grounded simulated developer before formalization. The agent decomposes the task, identifies unresolved decisions, asks bounded clarification questions, and uses the answers to write a refined natural-language specification that an LLM formalizer then translates into Lean. On 189 Verina Lean 4 specification-generation tasks, we compare single-shot generation with elicitation under question budgets of k=3 and k=10, allowing at most three or ten EA questions per task, across same-model and cross-model configurations. The same-model Claude Sonnet 4.6 pipeline has negative strict pass@1 estimates at both budgets, showing elicitation is not a uniform accuracy booster. In contrast, the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 and Sonnet 4.6-to-Gemini 3.8 Flash pipelines have positive strict estimates. The largest strict result reaches 65.6%, a +6.3-point change (+12 tasks), in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 pipeline. Six of eight conditions have positive compile-conditional estimates, with a maximum cross-model difference of +4.9 points among compiling outputs. Treatment estimates also differ across the basic and advanced splits; the largest advanced-task change occurs in the Sonnet 4.6-to-GPT-5.6 configuration at k=10, from 42.0% to 50.6%. Failure analysis identifies postconditions as the largest source of degradation. These findings suggest future autoformalization systems should treat elicited natural-language specifications as intermediate artifacts and optimize jointly for semantic correctness among compiling outputs and reliable translation of clarified information into Lean.

title: Sorted Mutability as an Entropic Functional: Theory and Two Applications
abstract: We investigate sorted mutability, $ζ_S$, as an information-based quantity with an explicit entropic character. We show that $ζ_S$ is directly proportional to the diversity of a data sequence and can therefore be expressed in terms of Shannon entropies, establishing a connection between compression-based measures and conventional information theory. In contrast to regular mutability, which preserves the sequential ordering of the data, sorted mutability removes this ordering and provides a static characterization of the distribution of observed values. We illustrate these properties in two complementary settings: the two-dimensional ferromagnetic Q-clock model and wind-power production data. For the Q-clock model, sorted mutability and diversity display the same temperature dependence, consistent with their analytical relation, while conventional thermodynamic observables provide an independent reference. In the case of wind power, we report monthly results for sorted mutability and diversity, showing proportional time evolutions. These results support sorted mutability as a useful, easy-to-calculate entropic functional for analyzing both equilibrium and non-equilibrium data sets.

title: Automated end-station at the soft X-ray beamline featuring robotic air-to-ultrahigh-vacuum sample transfer, scanning probe spectroscopy, and machine learning analysis
abstract: Driven by the growing integration of artificial intelligence and robotics in experimental science, we redefine the execution of user experiments at synchrotron soft X-ray beamlines by developing a highly automated end-station that can be operated without on-site staff. Installed at beamline BL08U of NanoTerasu, the system comprises four chamber units and two robots that automatically transfer samples from ambient air to an ultrahigh vacuum measurement stage for spectroscopic evaluations, before returning them to their original locations post-measurement. Soft X-ray absorption spectra are automatically acquired once programmed by scanning the micro-focused beam over the designated sample area, followed by automated evaluation using machine learning techniques such as principal-component analysis, multidimensional scaling, t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding, and uniform manifold approximation and projection. The high-throughput data are systematically accumulated in the database for remote user examination. This unstaffed end-station provides efficient beamtime for users and allows beamline scientists/technicians to pursue more human and creative endeavors.

title: Universal link between structural relaxation and self-diffusion in simple supercooled liquids
abstract: Despite a vigorous effort, a comprehensive and satisfactory understanding of the dynamics underlying the glass transition in finite-dimensional systems has not yet emerged. One key hallmark of supercooled liquids approaching the glass transition is the breakdown of the classical Stokes-Einstein (SE) relation, manifested as the decoupling between the self-diffusion coefficient and structural relaxation time, commonly described by a fractional SE relation. Whether and how the fractional SE exponents vary remains an ongoing debate, even for the simplest supercooled liquids. In this work, we numerically establish a universal relation between the self-diffusion coefficient and structural relaxation time by introducing characteristic scales that are revealed under the condition of constant dynamical heterogeneity. Moreover, this universal relation could also capture literature data for supercooled water and silica. Remarkably, we find that the fractional SE exponent is invariant across various supercooled liquids studied spanning a wide range of fragility, thereby challenging the prevailing view that the fractional SE exponent is correlated with fragility. Our study demonstrates that investigating dynamical heterogeneity yields more valuable insights into understanding glassy dynamics than expected.

title: Noise-Induced Restoration of Entropy Concavity Near Gaussian Equilibrium
abstract: We study a quantitative form of noise-induced restoration of entropy concavity for one-dimensional nonequilibrium states relaxing toward a Gaussian thermal equilibrium. A partially thermalized state is modeled by $X_q=\sqrt q\,X+\sqrt{1-q}\,G$, where $G$ is Gaussian equilibrium noise and $q$ is the retained signal fraction. For two independently prepared copies we ask when the entropy of the mixed state $h(\sqrt{1-t}\,X_q+\sqrt t\,Y_q)$ is concave in the mixing parameter. The problem is motivated by entropy geometry along Ornstein--Uhlenbeck/Fokker--Planck relaxation, where the relative score is the nonequilibrium thermodynamic force and relative Fisher information is entropy-production rate. We derive an exact symmetric endpoint-curvature formula, separating a nonnegative Ornstein--Uhlenbeck restoring term from a fourth-cumulant correction, and extend it to nonsmooth generalized-Gaussian states $e^{-a|x|^p}$ for $p>3/2$. For half thermalization of a symmetric log-concave input, posterior-variance identities give a quantitative outer-region theorem confining any endpoint obstruction to two explicitly bounded near-equilibrium sectors. We also give spectral and MMSE reformulations of the auxiliary inequality $A\ge2δ$, prove it in an explicit nonlinear neighborhood of Gaussian equilibrium, and show how it sharpens the endpoint bounds. The main all-mixing result concerns the leading symmetric non-Gaussian Hermite mode: for $p_a=\phiG(1+a\He_4)$, $0<a\le10^{-2}$, we prove strict entropy concavity for every $0<t<1$ and every $0<q\le5/8$, hence throughout the currently unresolved symmetric range $0<q\le4/7$ for this explicit nonequilibrium family. Numerical searches over broader log-concave families are reported only as supporting evidence.

title: QMBL: the Quantum Many-Body Leaderboard. A live record of published ground-state energies for lattice Hamiltonians and the electron gas
abstract: In condensed matter physics, scientists explore phase diagrams of matter through various methods (analysis, numerics, experiment) and achieve consensus when enough methods agree. The quality of variational results for quantum many-body ground states is mainly judged by energy values and respective errors. Here, we present QMBL, the Quantum Many-Body Leaderboard (https://www.qmbl.org), serving as the energy layer of the scientific consensus. It is a maintained, interactive record of published ground-state energies for lattice Hamiltonians and the homogeneous electron gas. The latest release v0.5.0 holds 2511 energies on 532 instances and collects all of the community's efforts into one view. Of those instances 285 have no exact solution (164 lattice and all 121 electron-gas instances) and any new record serves as a direct improvement to an open science problem. They are the targets of a companion benchmark, QMBL: Open Problems.

title: Eventual Exactness and Rigidity for Abelian Covers of Groups
abstract: For a group $G$, let $a(G)$ denote the minimum number of abelian subgroups covering $G$, and let $ω(G)$ be the maximum size of a pairwise noncommuting set. We prove the exact formula $\sup_{ω(G)\leq n}a(G)=2^{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}+1$ for every $n\geq 63$. Equality holds precisely for groups with derived subgroup of order two and binary symplectic central quotient of dimension $2\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor$. The proof combines centralizer descent with a structural separation of nonscalar alternating commutator maps.

title: Development of a Particle Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook Method for Rarefied Monatomic Gas Mixtures
abstract: The Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method has long served as a reliable numerical approach for simulating rarefied and non-equilibrium gas flows. Its computational cost, however, increases rapidly as the flow approaches the near-continuum regime. This limitation has motivated the development of kinetic model equations that replace binary collisions with simplified relaxation processes. This paper presents a particle multi-relaxation unified BGK (UBGK) model for monatomic gas mixtures. The model retains pairwise species relaxation and determines the target velocity, temperature, shear stress, and heat flux by matching the corresponding production terms to those of the Boltzmann equation. A stochastic particle algorithm is developed. The model is implemented in SPARTA, and two validation problems are considered: homogeneous relaxation and a Mach 3 flow over a cylinder. In both cases, the UBGK solution reproduces the DSMC reference behavior, including species-dependent relaxation and non-equilibrium shock structure.

title: Physics-informed Neural Networks Based on the Fokker-Planck Model for Rarefied Gas Flows
abstract: Rarefied nonequilibrium flows are described by the Boltzmann equation, which can be solved using stochastic particle or deterministic methods. With advances in computing, data-assisted physics-informed neural networks have been widely used for flow prediction by combining governing equations with measured or computed data. Data-free PINNs do not require such training data and have been widely studied for continuum flows, but their application to rarefied flows remains limited. This study develops a data-free Fokker-Planck physics-informed neural network (FP-PINN) to describe rarefied nonequilibrium flows. The physics loss is constructed from the ellipsoidal statistical Fokker-Planck (ES-FP) equation using a velocity distribution function (VDF) closure and moment projection. The FP-PINN is evaluated for a steady one-dimensional Mach 10 normal shock. The FP-PINN results agree with the numerical ES-FP results, with errors below $1\%$. Compared with the particle ES-FP results, the FP-PINN predicts a sharper shock structure with errors up to $17\%$. This difference is attributed to the VDF closure and moment projection.

title: Thermodynamics of coupled electromagnetic and mass fields
abstract: We formulate a unified thermodynamic framework for chemical, mechanical, and electromagnetic transport by extending the Gibbs--Duhem relation to include kinetic free-energy contributions associated with material and field motion. The resulting kinetic Gibbs--Duhem relation establishes a thermodynamic connection between free-energy variations, generalized chemical potentials, pressure, and transport momentum, while preserving the invariance of the system free energy under changes of reference frame. Within a Lagrangian formulation of free-energy evolution, the relation provides a common structure for diffusion, momentum transport, and electromagnetic dynamics. For nonuniform chemical systems, the framework recovers the coupling between Cahn--Hilliard dynamics and the Korteweg stress arising from composition gradients. Its extension to electromagnetic systems incorporates electric, magnetic, charge, and mechanical contributions into the same thermodynamic formulation, yielding a unified description of electromagnetic and momentum evolution. The framework further separates dissipative from nondissipative transport and establishes a common thermodynamic form for mechanical and electromagnetic propagation. In the isentropic limit, the characteristic propagation velocity is determined by the derivative of the thermodynamic pressure with respect to density, yielding the speed of sound for mechanical systems and the speed of light for electromagnetic systems. These results show that kinetic contributions can be incorporated consistently into the Gibbs--Duhem framework, providing a common thermodynamic basis for coupled chemical, mechanical, and electromagnetic transport without introducing separate thermodynamic principles for each mechanism.

title: Noise Correlation Spectroscopy: A Review
abstract: The frequency noise of an ordinary diode laser, often a nuisance in spectroscopy, can be used to measure atomic coherence. When atoms are prepared in a coherent superposition of two ground states, each random shift in laser frequency changes how much light they absorb, so the transmitted light carries a record of that coherence. Correlating the intensity fluctuations of two fields, each linking one ground state to a shared excited state, reads this record out, a technique known as noise correlation spectroscopy. The correlation signal is narrower than the transparency window the same fields create and switches sign as their frequency difference is tuned. Its width is set by the rate at which the atoms lose coherence and, over a wide range, does not grow with laser power. Over two decades the method has spread from warm vapors to cold atoms, to multi-field schemes, and to diamond and rare-earth-doped crystals. This review, to the author's knowledge the first, brings together its theory, experiments and applications, and examines its limits, the challenges that remain, and the opportunities that could make it a standard spectroscopic tool.

title: Advanced computational methods for simulating the classical hydrogen atom in stochastic electrodynamics
abstract: Stochastic electrodynamics (SED) is a theory of nature that seeks to derive key aspects of quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics from a purely classical physics perspective. While SED has been successful in many areas, it has largely failed to stably simulate the 3D classical hydrogen atom. The computational methodology presented here overcomes these foundational challenges. We develop a pseudo-wave formulation that integrates the solid angle in k-space utilizing symmetry, resulting in a significantly reduced memory footprint and lower computational overhead for generating the zero-point radiation spectrum. This optimization is paired with a logarithmic frequency grid, a sliding window tracking the instantaneous Keplerian frequency, and a Tukey smoothing function to eliminate discrete force discontinuities. Integrated via an adaptive RKF45 solver across highly dense grids of up to 100-million bins, these techniques demonstrate the asymptotic convergence of ensemble stability. We show that increasing the grid resolution in the high-frequency domain systematically mitigates artificial electron decay, yielding a simulated probability density function that closely aligns with the quantum mechanical ground state P(r).

title: Visualizing surface-reaction-driven chloride migration and cascading failure in sulfide solid electrolytes
abstract: Moisture instability of sulfide solid electrolytes limits practical use in all-solid-state batteries. Spatially resolving gas--solid reactions during moisture exposure remains challenging. Here, cryogenic four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (cryo-4D-STEM) maps nanoscale degradation in low- and high-Cl argyrodite electrolytes, Li\(_6\)PS\(_5\)Cl and Li\(_{5.5}\)PS\(_{4.5}\)Cl\(_{1.5}\). Li\(_6\)PS\(_5\)Cl undergoes predominantly surface-localized degradation that progressively extends inward, whereas Li\(_{5.5}\)PS\(_{4.5}\)Cl\(_{1.5}\) exhibits rapid interior amorphization accompanied by outward chloride redistribution. Density functional theory calculations indicate a lower chloride-migration barrier along the modeled pathway in the higher-Cl composition, while chloride removal and vacancy formation distort the PS\(_4^{3-}\) framework and may destabilize the lattice. Surface treatment suppresses detectable large-scale chloride segregation and improves moisture tolerance, retaining 99.9% of the capacity measured at the start of 0.33 C cycling after 150 cycles. These results identify chloride redistribution as a key process in degradation propagation and suggest a route toward moisture-tolerant solid-state batteries.

title: Not All Frames Are Equal:Difference-Aware Quantization for Ultra-Low-Bit ASR
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods such as GPTQ and AWQ compress large language models effectively, but applying them to automatic speech recognition (ASR) at ultra-low bit-widths (2-3 bits) causes severe transcription degradation. Unlike discrete text tokens, speech activations are highly correlated in steady-state and zero-padded regions yet change rapidly at phonetic boundaries; when all frames contribute equally to the Hessian, static frames dominate calibration and obscure informative transitions. We propose DiffAQ, which computes frame-to-frame activation differences to measure the rate of acoustic change and assigns Hessian importance proportionally, concentrating quantization precision on phonetically critical frames. As a training-free modification to GPTQ, DiffAQ consistently reduces WER across various Whisper sizes and standard benchmarks, with the largest gains at 2-bit precision where baseline methods frequently produce degenerate outputs.

title: General Relativity in Three Lines
abstract: We show that complex general relativity can be formulated directly in terms of three affine lines assigned to each spacetime point. The lines are represented by Plücker bivectors, and Urbantke's construction applied to the associated two-forms reconstructs the conformal spacetime metric. Starting from the chiral Plebański action, the simplicity constraints turn the three two-forms into a null internal basis of simple bivectors and thereby into three projective lines. A $3+1$ decomposition then yields a first-order canonical theory whose configuration variable is the weighted triple of lines and whose conjugate variable is a line momentum. The resulting constraint system consists of three internal Gauss constraints, three vector constraints, and one Hamiltonian constraint. A notable feature of the line formulation is that the equation obtained by varying the line momentum is pointwise algebraic after the spatial integrations by parts. Consequently the momentum can be eliminated explicitly wherever the corresponding Legendre map is invertible, giving a second-order action whose only dynamical configuration variable is the weighted triple of lines. The line curvature separates naturally into a cosmological trace and the Weyl matrix of the selected chiral sector. The Legendre map becomes singular on a distinguished null-evolution locus where the spacetime metric remains nondegenerate. There its rank drops from nine to six, giving three algebraic compatibility conditions. We construct a finite invariant partial Legendre transform and a smooth constrained second-order continuation through this locus. This analysis provides a regular framework for regimes in which the evolution direction becomes null and may be useful in the study of near-horizon geometries and related gravitational phenomena.

title: When the implementation matters more than the algorithm: NSGA-II and other multi-objective optimizers in engineering design tools
abstract: Engineering design tools increasingly embed optimizers as ready-made components that users select by algorithm name, while operator settings and bound, integer and duplicate handling stay fixed inside each tool. This study tests whether the name predicts the result. A tool-agnostic harness exposes one deterministic black box, an emulator of a published 22-variable mixed-integer building-performance problem, to the native optimizers of three Grasshopper plug-ins, to canonical NSGA-II, SMS-EMOA and GDE3 from Python libraries, and to the model-based RBFMOpt. Eighteen configurations were run at 5,000 evaluations under three population allocations, with statistics fixed in advance. Four NSGA-II implementations differed by up to 5% in hypervolume, more than three canonical algorithms of different families differed from one another, and their response to population size differed by up to 10 percentage points; for two MOEA/D implementations, by 28. On ZDT test functions the same NSGA-II implementations differed up to 470-fold in IGD. An ablation in one open-source NSGA-II reproduced the behaviour of one tool from its documented settings but not the gaps of the other two, so documented parameters do not identify an implementation. Counting the budget in wall-clock time reversed the ranking of the model-based optimizer, and reporting the final population instead of the archive understated some configurations by up to a third; most differences fell below the surrogate's error. For optimizers embedded in design-support systems, the implementation is part of the method; a reporting checklist is derived: implementation and version, effective settings, budget in time and evaluations, and archive-based indicators.

title: Dynamical entropy and thermodynamics of causal diamonds
abstract: We study the dynamical entropy of causal diamonds using Wald-Zoupas charges and fluxes on their null boundaries. For a chosen boundary symplectic potential, the boost charge defines an entropy made of an area term plus an expansion correction, which reduces to one quarter of the area at the edge on the diamond. In Einstein gravity, we find an exact balance law relating the entropy on any two cuts of the null boundary to a signed flux, so the entropy decreases only when this flux is non-negative. We obtain a linearised physical process first law without assuming a background Killing symmetry, both in the presence and absence of external matter; and extend it for semiclassical gravity based on the improved quantum null energy condition. We also examine causal diamonds in maximally symmetric spacetimes and in Einstein-scalar gravity.

title: Geodesics in Black-Hole Spacetimes: A Qualitative Classification Using Vieta's Formulae
abstract: This monograph classifies the geodesics of the Schwarzschild, Kerr and Schwarzschild-de Sitter black holes without solving for their turning points. In all three spacetimes, the radial and polar motions are governed by polynomials whose coefficients depend only on the constants of motion, and the qualitative behavior of a geodesic is fixed by the pattern of their roots. We read this pattern directly off the coefficients, using Vieta's formulae together with the discriminant, Descartes' rule of signs, and the values of the polynomials at the horizons and at infinity. In Schwarzschild spacetime, the reciprocals of the radial roots of every non-radial geodesic add up to $1/(2M)$, which gives the third root of a bound orbit in closed form and the separatrix $p=6+2e$. In Kerr spacetime, the signs of the coefficients show that no radially bound orbit has $\varepsilon^2\geq1$ and that vortical geodesics, timelike or null, have no radial turning point; a positive discriminant is necessary but not sufficient for bound motion, and Descartes' rule applied at the event horizon gives the exact criterion. Spherical orbits and their stability, the equatorial ISCO and light rings, and the photon shell follow from the same relations. In Schwarzschild-de Sitter spacetime, the timelike radial polynomial is a quintic with exactly one negative root, a bound branch requires $\varepsilon^2+ΛL^2/3<1$, and both marginally stable circular orbits lie beyond $6M$. Most of these results are known; the aim is to show that a single, elementary algebraic route leads to all of them. The text is meant for graduate students who have taken a first course in general relativity, and each chapter ends with worked examples.

title: Rethinking User Encoders: Routing Diffusion States for Scenario-Adaptive User Representation
abstract: Existing large language model (LLM)-based user encoders serialize heterogeneous behavioral logs and compress them into static representations through autoregressive (AR) prediction. However, their unidirectional constraint limits bidirectional information flow, hindering cross-modal interactions and the joint preservation of multi-source signals. Consequently, the learned static representations struggle to accommodate the distinct evidence requirements of diverse downstream scenarios. We address these limitations by unlocking the iterative denoising process of diffusion language models (dLLMs) as a multi-granularity reconstruction space. Based on this insight, we propose FINDERS (FactorIzatioN of Diffusion statEs for Routing across Scenarios), a router-equipped dLLM framework comprising four operations: denoise, factorize, route, and compress. Learnable meta-slots organize complementary denoising states into transferable cross-modal semantics and modality-specific behavioral factors. To provide grounded supervision, we construct BehaviorQA, a large-scale corpus containing explicit behavioral rationales. Guided by scenario queries, a lightweight router dynamically emphasizes relevant slot directions via an input-level residual pathway before cross-source fusion and final compression. Extensive experiments and online A/B tests across ten industrial scenarios demonstrate that FINDERS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both unified and scenario-adaptive settings. This work effectively pushes the boundaries of dLLMs beyond language generation, demonstrating their immense potential as powerful user representation learners.

title: Audio System One Model: Typed Probabilistic Perception of Emotion in Speech
abstract: Speech applications ask many questions about the same voice: which emotion a listener perceives, how aroused the speaker sounds, whether they sound frustrated. Classifiers answer fast, over one fixed label set; audio language models (ALMs) take any question in text, but answer by generation, one pass per question, with poorly calibrated probabilities. We present ASOM (Audio System One Model), a System One model for speech: choice, score and yes/no questions written at request time are answered in one pass, without generation, each with a probability distribution. Frozen speech and text encoders feed a 6.2M-parameter reader with no per-class parameters, trained on listener vote distributions. On MSP-Podcast, ASOM matches a classifier on the same features and data, leads the best of 6 zero-shot ALMs by 0.072 and an ALM fine-tuned on the same data by 0.026, and answers 20 questions in 13.1 ms, 17-41 times faster than the ALMs. It also answers reworded, reduced and new label sets, scales and gender, and on 21 unseen corpora in 13 languages it leads the best zero-shot ALM by 0.138 where the words carry no emotion; where they do, the ALMs mostly read.

title: Synergistic Self-Driven Nanoconfinement and Dynamical Heterogeneity in Deeply Supercooled "No Man's Land" Water
abstract: The 150--235 K ``no man's land'' (NML) of deeply supercooled water is a highly debated regime where rapid crystallization hinders experimental observation of the hypothesized liquid-liquid phase transition. Using TIP4P/2005 molecular dynamics simulations, we uncover a structurally and dynamically heterogeneous state at ambient pressure that exhibits novel physical features. Our results demonstrate that this low-density state ($ρ\approx 0.925$ g/cm$^3$) is a unique supercooled liquid, distinct from both glassy and spinodal states. Specifically, it emerges as a stable, structurally arrested phase driven by a self-generated ``soft skeleton'' of nanoclusters. This network forms an intrinsic nanoporous structure that imposes nanoconfinement on the remaining fluid, proving that NML confinement can be an entirely self-driven phenomenon. Finally, we resolve the temperature-dependent, nonlinear behavior of density and compressibility, highlighting a structurally driven anomaly that clarifies the thermodynamics of deep supercooling. Collectively, this work provides a transformative structural framework for understanding the anomalous nature of water within the NML.

title: From Events to Reasoning: Hierarchical Rule Composition over Explicit States
abstract: What a reasoning system emits is a conclusion; what it owes is a justification. Producing one requires every operation to be admissible on the facts actually available, the dependencies of intermediate results to survive to the end of the path, and the path to be revised when a premise changes. We present the Event Reasoning System (ERS), in which the reasoning state is an explicit event graph. Semantic features nominate candidate objects and rule bindings, and declared rule and task conditions decide which may execute, so candidates that violate the represented period, unit, or evidence constraints cannot enter an accepted reasoning path. Low-level rules provide reusable local transformations, and recursively composable high-level control rules organize subgoals and legal paths under the current goal, information gaps, and budget; a finite library is thereby rebound into paths never stored as complete solutions. We formalize admissible transitions, task-dependent control, compositional expressivity, dependency-preserving revision, and the gap between reachable solutions and those a budgeted controller finds. On structured-event graphs, ERS builds dependency chains of up to twelve steps, cuts irrelevant executed domain operations from 32 to 0 as lookahead grows to 16, and produces no unsupported target output across 24 negative cases; with rules frozen, it passes 12/12 focused checks comprising nine accepted derivations involving unseen input/path combinations and three justified refusals, as well as 6/6 fact-change cases. On fourteen jointly solved development tasks, the recorded dynamic subgoal configuration uses 51.6% less inference wall-clock time than single-level global control under their respective frozen settings.

title: Aligning Information Theory and Formal Verification: A Lean Formalization of Rate-Distortion Theory
abstract: Large language models have recently demonstrated an ability to generate substantial mathematical proofs and formalizations, including machine-checked arguments for major open problems and classical theorems. These developments highlight a growing workflow in which AI systems search for proofs while proof assistants certify their correctness. Within information theory, however, formalized libraries remain limited, and existing formalized theorems focus almost exclusively on Shannon's foundational lossless theorems. This paper presents the first Lean formalization of core components of rate-distortion theory, a central framework for lossy compression and modern machine-learning analysis. We identify the alignment challenges that arise when translating information-theoretic definitions, such as distortion measures, typicality and achievability, into a proof-assistant setting, and we develop a reusable library of definitions and lemmas faithful to textbook conventions. Our formalization provides a foundation for future AI-assisted proofs in information theory and enables subsequent mechanized developments to build on a coherent, verified infrastructure rather than generating long proofs from scratch.

title: MedSonor: Learning to Use Clinical Audio in Medical LLMs
abstract: Clinical audio conveys medical information that transcripts may not preserve, but using it in medical responses requires interpreting it alongside clinical requests and dialogue context. Existing medical audio supervision largely targets classification or recognition, while general audio-language models lack specialized medical knowledge and direct feedback for open-ended responses. We present MedSonor, a medical dialogue model integrating medical knowledge, spoken dialogue, and clinical audio understanding. We pair authentic medical audio with clinical requests and combine these audio-integrated dialogues with collected medical audio and synthesized spoken dialogues for supervised fine-tuning, followed by two stages of rubric-guided reinforcement learning. We introduce MedVoice-Dial and MedVoice?AID to evaluate responses within supplied multi-turn medical contexts and to requests involving clinical audio, respectively. Across seven medical benchmarks, MedSonor outperforms the evaluated general-purpose open-weight audio-language baselines and ranks highest in aggregate physician preference evaluation, while broadly retaining general speech capabilities.

title: Resolving the heart of the Wolf-Rayet binary Apep with ALMA
abstract: The Wolf-Rayet (WR) phase is a critical stage in the evolution of massive stars. During this phase, the stars experience a large mass loss in the form of fast winds that are enriched with heavy elements. There are only a few WR binaries in the galaxy, with Apep being a truly exceptional system exhibiting a bright colliding-wind region at radio wavelengths and an impressive dust plume in the infrared. Although the angular separation between the two (WN and WC) components has been indirectly inferred to be about 47 mas, it has yet to be confirmed through direct measurements. We aim to image the Apep system at millimetre wavelengths to determine the position of the WR stars and their mass-loss rates. We observed Apep with ALMA in Bands 6 and 7 in a large baseline configuration, achieving an angular resolution of approximately 20 mas. We used a canonical spherical wind model to convert the measured flux densities into wind mass-loss rates. Towards Apep, we detect point-like emission coming from the WN star and elongated emission most likely from the colliding-wind region; the WC star is not detected. We also detect the O star at 0.7'' that has been associated with the system. Our analysis favours mass-loss rates for the WN and WC components of $\dot{M}_\mathrm{WN}\sim 2\times10^{-5}\,M_\odot \,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$ and $\dot{M}_\mathrm{WC}\sim10^{-5}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, respectively. The mass-loss rates of the WR stars are significantly lower than previously reported, and we examine several factors that may account for this discrepancy. The diffuse emission from the colliding-wind region cannot be accounted for by the synchrotron flux, and thus additional free-free or dust emission is present.

title: Towards Adaptive and Real-Survey-Aligned Simulated Urban Mobility Behaviour of Generative Agents
abstract: In existing agent-based simulations of multimodal urban mobility, agents, representing humans, choose their travel modes either using discrete choice or machine learning models fitted on structured travel survey data, or with rules explicitly written by the domain experts. Such approaches fix a priori the agents' possible behaviour space. Hence, a factor absent from variables or rules cannot affect agents' decisions. In reality, choosing a transport mode is a multidimensional decision in which objective and subjective factors intertwine and change over time. Integrating such complexity into a city-scale multimodal mobility simulation remains a challenge. Generative agents (GAs) built on large language models promise to respond to this challenge because they carry decision heuristics that travel surveys do not record. However, to the best of our knowledge, aligning their decisions with real household travel surveys remains an open question. In this paper, we build an agent-based model of daily multimodal mobility for Toulouse (France). We compare the performance of fifteen decision-makers (simple baselines, models fitted on the survey, GAs with minimal and tuned prompts, and a typed classifier) on the real household travel survey. Our results show that GAs with tuned prompts come close to the fitted models on the modal split of a simulated day without transport disruptions, but not trip by trip. GAs also react when unforeseen events occur. The recently released Jev-1.13 TypeSafe classifier gives surprisingly great results, showing that generating output text is not necessary. The results presented in this paper would be of interest to transport policy makers and service providers looking to apply generative agent-based modelling for improving urban mobility services.

title: ECHOES: Seeing Beyond the Current Image via Recursive History Compression and Privileged On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Long-horizon GUI agents rely on visual history to maintain task states, but retaining historical screenshots increases visual-token usage and inference costs, while textual summaries can discard critical state information, undermining long-horizon reliability. We propose ECHOES, which leverages training-time privileged information to guide textual history compression and strengthen long-horizon reasoning. Specifically, ECHOES adopts a Compression-Think-Action (CTA) format to recursively update a textual history state and reason. The same model, given privileged multi-image inputs, serves as a teacher that provides dense token-level on-policy distillation on student-generated CTA rollouts. Our Perception-Memory Fidelity (PMF) Gap-guided OPD-RL framework dynamically balances privileged distillation and task-reward optimization, with periodic teacher updates supporting continued improvement. We further introduce ECHOESBMK, a fine-grained diagnostic benchmark derived from real GUI agent failure trajectories to jointly evaluate visual perception and cross-modal state retention. Experiments on four GUI benchmarks and ECHOESBMK demonstrate substantial gains in task performance and memory fidelity. Without retaining historical screenshots at deployment, ECHOES achieves competitive performance with a favorable performance-inference-cost trade-off and exhibits positive zero-shot transfer to unseen visual planning tasks.

title: Social Bias or Social Desirability? Comparing Factorial Survey Experiments for Humans and Large Language Models
abstract: Factorial survey experiments are a survey method from the social sciences that uses descriptions of socially complex situation (``vignettes'') to elicit judgments such as social bias. They provide two major benefits: (a), they reduce the effect of social desirability inherent in self-reported social biases, and (b), they make it possible to separate the effects of multiple sociodemographic attributes. These aspects are also desiderata for the evaluation of social bias in LLMs, but are often ignored in social bias evaluations. In our study, we evaluate social bias in humans and eleven LLMs on the basis of four different English and German factorial survey experiments. Our results show that the LLMs mirror the human biases only partially and sometimes even invert them. We provide evidence that this is due to a fundamental difference in how humans and LLMs react to socially complex situations. While such vignettes reduce social desirability bias in humans, this is not the case for LLMs, where the alignment-induced tendency towards socially desirable responses carries over directly. We therefore caution against applying bias measurement techniques from the social sciences that were developed for human to measure attitudes and bias in LLMs.

title: The square achievement game on $n \times n$ boards
abstract: Two players alternately claim cells of an $n \times n$ grid; the first to hold all four corners of an axis-parallel square wins, and a full board without one is a draw. The first player has a winning strategy if and only if $n \ge 5$, which answers a question of Erickson. For $n \ge 6$ one strategy serves every board: a rule with no lookup table whose moves after the second reply are all forcing, built around the plus, a stone with the four cells at a common distance from it along the axes, a shape proposed for this game by Sirgedas in 2010. The rule is checked on the boards of size $6$ to $17$, and a simulation theorem carries one checked run on the $23 \times 23$ board to every larger board. The proofs are formalized in Lean 4, and the theorem for the rule states that the tree of its own moves is winning.

title: Decomposing URLLC Deadline Failures in Beam-Managed 6G Networks: Implications for Mission-Critical Wireless Systems
abstract: Mission-critical wireless systems require ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC), which sixth-generation (6G) millimeter-wave (mmWave) beam-managed networks are designed to provide. However, the reported URLLC deadline miss rate often masks the specific causes of packet failures. This paper introduces a framework that categorizes missed URLLC packets into three causes: queueing-limited (Q), transmission-limited (T), and beam-tracking-limited (B). Our analysis across ten scenarios with antenna counts from $\mathbf{64}$ to $\mathbf{4096}$ reveals three key findings. First, the dominant cause of missed packets shifts from Q to B when the antenna count exceeds roughly $\mathbf{1825}$. Therefore, operators of hyper-massive arrays should focus on improving beam-tracking accuracy to reduce the miss rate. Second, the beam-sweep period ($T_{\mathrm{sw}}$) significantly affects B-misses, while Q and T remain relatively unchanged. Reducing $T_{\mathrm{sw}}$ from $\mathbf{20}$ms to $\mathbf{10}$ms can cut the B-misses by more than half, without requiring a redesign of the scheduler. Third, Q-misses reach a cumulative distribution function (CDF) of approximately $\mathbf{0.98}$ by $\mathbf{0.8}\,$ms, so modest latency-budget relaxation can accommodate most overruns. In contrast, B-misses remain unsaturated at $\mathbf{12}\,$ms, making them difficult to accommodate within practical application-layer latency limits. Overall, this framework transforms an ambiguous aggregate miss-rate metric into a clear three-way diagnostic tool that directly informs remedial actions for network operators.

title: EnterpriseSynth: Zero-Execution SFT and Evaluation Data from OpenAPI Specs
abstract: Tool-using large language model agents require substantial training and evaluation data, yet collecting execution traces from enterprise APIs is often unsafe, expensive, or infeasible because of access controls, compliance constraints, rate limits, and the risk of modifying production data. We present EnterpriseSynth, a zero-execution framework that converts OpenAPI specifications into supervised fine-tuning trajectories and paired evaluation instances without invoking the underlying APIs. The framework uses a four-stage pipeline for specification parsing, intent generation, trajectory synthesis, and static validation. Each generated trajectory is checked against the source specification for endpoint, parameter, type, and schema consistency before being admitted to the dataset. We evaluate EnterpriseSynth on 17 real and synthetic APIs. Adversarial refinement increases the validator's detection rate for planted schema violations from 57-80% to 98% (43/44). Across five random seeds, a compact open-weight model fine-tuned on EnterpriseSynth data outperforms both an untuned model and a Self-Instruct baseline on held-out APIs. Performance remains consistent on five private, hand-authored API specifications that were not available during training, with tool-selection accuracy of 40.0% on the private set and 39.6% on the public held-out set. However, an independent LLM-based evaluation shows that endpoint-selection accuracy substantially overestimates end-to-end correctness: accuracy falls from 48.9% under the endpoint-level metric to 21.3% when argument selection and values are also evaluated. These results demonstrate that OpenAPI specifications can support scalable, execution-free data generation, while highlighting the need for argument-level evaluation when assessing the deployment readiness of tool-using agents.

title: napari-TurboBox: Interactive Multi-Viewer Bounding Box Annotation for AI-Guided Volumetric Bioimaging
abstract: Promptable segmentation models turn one 3D bounding box into an instance mask. Box placement therefore limits how fast microscopy volumes with thousands of objects are annotated. Each box must be checked in several synchronized viewers, but napari-bbox shares no state between viewers. An edit must update every viewer and slows down with more boxes. napari-TurboBox instead holds one shared copy of the boxes for all viewers. In a four-viewer layout, napari-TurboBox needs a few milliseconds per mouse move to update the three slice viewers up to $10^4$ boxes. The same update in napari-bbox leaves the 33 ms budget beyond about $10^3$ boxes and takes 159 ms at $10^4$. Boxes stay axis-aligned and export to COCO and YOLO as per-slice 2D boxes. napari-TurboBox is a pure-Python plugin for napari 0.6.6 to 0.9. The code is available at https://github.com/N-Friederich/napari-turbobox under the Apache 2.0 licence, and version 0.1.0 is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23090828 on Zenodo.

title: Semiclassical Analysis of Wave Dynamics via Wigner Transforms: Applications to the Quantum Harmonic, Anharmonic, and Dirac Oscillator
abstract: In this Master's thesis, we give a pedagogical introduction to the semiclassical analysis of wave dynamics in single-band and multi-band systems. We show how the semiclassical evolutions of Wigner functions can approximate the dynamics of wave packet centers and wave packet deformations.
