Spatially-varying DLNMs can capture this heterogeneity, but their computational demands limit their application to fine-scale nationwide datasets with thousands of small areas. In this paper, we adapt a 'divide-and-conquer' approach to spatially varying DLNMs. The method partitions the spatial domain into smaller regions, expands each region with a k-order neighbourhood to reduce boundary effects, fits separate models within each partition using Laplacian P-splines, and combines the resulting estimates using conditional predictive ordinate-based mixture weights. We evaluated the approach in a simulation study based on municipalities in Sicily and applied it to daily summer temperature and mortality data from 7122 municipalities in mainland Italy between 2011 and 2021. Simulation studies show good performance, with relative-risk estimates comparable to those from a global model and relatively robust to the choice and number of partitioning units. Computational efficiency can be substantially improved by using parallel computations. The Italian application reveals significant spatial heterogeneity in the temperature-mortality relationship, with clear regional differences. The proposed framework makes spatially varying DLNMs feasible for large, fine-scale spatiotemporal datasets while retaining location-specific exposure-lag-response estimation.

title: Weak$^*$-weak points of continuity and very smooth points in Bochner function spaces $L^{p}(μ, X)$
abstract: Suppose that $([0,1],\mathcal{A},μ)$ is the Lebesgue measure space and $1< p<\infty$ with $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1$. We prove that an unit vector $h\in L^{p}(μ, X)^*$ is a weak$^*$-weak point of continuity of $S(L^{p}(μ, X)^*)$ if and only if $\frac{h(t)}{\|h(t)\|}$ is a weak$^*$-weak point of continuity of $S(X^*)$ for almost every $t\in [0, 1]$ with $h(t)\neq 0$, where $X$ is a Banach space such that $X^*$ is separable. As an application of this result, under the same hypothesis on $X$, we prove that a point $f\in L^p(μ, X)_{1}$ is a very smooth point if and only if $\frac{f(t)}{\|f(t)\|}\in S(X)$ is a very smooth point for almost every $t\in [0, 1]$ with $f(t)\neq 0$. We give several examples to show that these results does not hold for $p=1$.

title: HBFSim: A Simulator for Exploring HBF in Memory Hierarchies for LLMs
abstract: High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) has recently emerged as a promising technology that provides terabyte-scale accelerator-local capacity at bandwidths approaching HBM, with a potential cost-per-bit advantage over HBM. However, its NAND foundation brings long latency, out-of-place updates, and finite write endurance directly into the accelerator memory hierarchy, making its effects on performance and lifetime difficult to predict. To study this emerging design space, we present HBFSim, an LLM-aware event-driven simulator for heterogeneous HBM+HBF memory systems that preserves application-level memory semantics while modeling flash-internal behavior. HBFSim models HBM, HBF with host-managed flash translation, and conventional capacity tiers in one simulation driven by a calibrated serving frontend. Using HBFSim, we study decoding of Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-235B-A22B under three workloads that differ in their input and output lengths. HBF serves data that does not fit in HBM 11.0--19.0$\times$ faster than host DRAM; HBM is better used to hold the running sequences' KV cache than as a cache for HBF; and at a published peak load of Llama-3.1-70B, HBF lasts 2.0 to 6.9 years, in proportion to the stacks that share the KV writes. The artifact is available at https://github.com/FlashLabAE/HBFSim and will track public HBF device data as it becomes available.

title: Weighted spatial averages with missing observations: Convergence and accuracy of delta-method variance approximations
abstract: Weighted spatial averages from incomplete networks are ratios whose variance is approximated by truncating a Taylor series (the delta method). Three questions remain open: whether the series converges, how large a truncation's error is, and how it behaves as the network grows. We address these for observations missing completely at random, independently with a common probability $α$. First, the truncations, which count corrections for the denominator (the total reported weight) and for its coupling with the numerator, converge for a given network only if $α>\tfrac12$ and both corrections increase together. Second, whether or not the series converges, the error of truncations correcting only for the denominator is controlled at any network size by its coefficient of variation $ρ$, with $ρ^2=\tfrac{1-α}α\sum_iβ_i^2$ for weights $β_i$, and by the probability of rare reporting patterns. Third, for uniform weights and bounded fields, these errors vanish as the network grows, at any fixed availability. If correlations also decay with distance, the first-order approximation of earlier work has error of order $ρ^4$, against $ρ^2$ for the simplest approximation. Only truncations of equal order in numerator and denominator, beginning with the first-order truncation, avoid spurious dependence on the mean level; higher ones need not be more accurate. The exact variance for uniform weights, a single sum, shows that for correlated fields the first-order approximation overstates the contribution of missing data but is conservative overall. Concentrated weights degrade it more than $ρ$ indicates. Rainfall simulations over India illustrates results, several of which extend to self-normalized estimators.

title: mixed Hodge structures on the strictly upper triangular Lie algebras
abstract: We show that, for $k\geq 3$, a lattice in the unitriangular Lie group $U_k(\mathbb{R})$ is the fundamental group of a smooth quasi-projective complex algebraic variety if and only if $k=3$. The proof uses the conjugation symmetry and weight conditions of mixed Hodge structure on the Malcev Lie algebra proven by Morgan. This result identifies a family of groups that must be excluded in the search for smooth quasi-projective varieties with torsion-free nilpotent fundamental groups of high nilpotency class.

title: MLOps-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Production ML Engineering in Real Repositories
abstract: AI agents are increasingly expected to modify and maintain machine-learning systems in production, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate either competition-style ML experimentation or generic repository issue resolution. We introduce MLOps-Bench, a repository-grounded benchmark for production ML engineering. Unlike prior ML-agent benchmarks, MLOps-Bench evaluates executable lifecycle changes inside real ML repositories, spanning data pipelines, feature engineering, model training, model serving, monitoring, CI/CD and governance, and end-to-end integration. Each task is grounded in repository evidence and includes a natural-language requirement, oracle patch, plausible buggy baseline, fail-to-pass tests, pass-to-pass tests, and provenance metadata. The benchmark contains 212 validated tasks from 31 public ML repositories, with 636 fail-to-pass tests and 856 pass-to-pass tests. We evaluate six agents and find that the best system solves 31.2% of tasks while passing 68.7% of tests, showing that current agents often make partial progress but still fail production-relevant behavioral requirements. MLOps-Bench shifts agent evaluation beyond model building and issue fixing toward repository-native MLOps work where correctness depends on lifecycle reasoning, behavioral robustness, and preservation of existing system behavior.

title: Solving Large-Scale Parameter Inference in Controllable Nuclear Fusion via Coherent Ising Machines and Block Coordinate Descent
abstract: Bayesian inference enables self-consistent plasma parameter inversion in tokamak integrated data analysis by fusing multi-source diagnostics. However, under nonlinear Gaussian likelihoods, finding the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate typically relies on sampling methods whose high computational overhead precludes real-time plasma control. To address this bottleneck, we propose a Bayesian inversion framework using a Coherent Ising Machine (CIM)-a quantum computing architecture based on coupled degenerate optical parametric oscillators (DOPOs). With native all-to-all connectivity, the CIM directly maps the negative log-posterior potential onto a spin Hamiltonian and leverages quantum vacuum fluctuations for rapid state-space search during pitchfork bifurcation. Validated on plasma current profile inversion for the EAST tokamak, this method achieves a single-run solution time of approximately 1 ms. Although current qubit limits necessitate a block-wise iterative scheme that prevents full real-time execution today, rapidly scaling quantum hardware offers a clear pathway toward real-time tokamak control.

title: Adaptive conformal prediction on the Grassmannian
abstract: We introduce a conformal prediction framework for regression with Grassmann-valued responses. The proposed method constructs prediction regions in the form of metric balls directly on the Grassmann manifold, using basis-invariant geometric distances as non-conformity measures and scaling the corresponding non-conformity scores through a learned prediction difficulty estimator. This yields locally adaptive, input-dependent prediction regions that respect the underlying manifold geometry, while retaining the finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction under exchangeability. We evaluate several Grassmannian distance metrics and compare their prediction-region efficiency on synthetic benchmarks and an airfoil inverse shape-design problem. The results highlight the advantages of geometry-aware non-conformity scores, while local adaptation improves empirical coverage uniformity across prediction difficulty levels and, in strongly heteroscedastic settings, can substantially reduce prediction-region size while maintaining the target coverage.

title: When Conformal Interfaces Become Logarithmic
abstract: We construct conformal interfaces having defect conformal manifolds between two-dimensional rational CFTs, at least one of which is non-unitary. In a continuous family, interfaces with real and complex spectra can be marginally deformed to each other via their defect moduli parameters. An exceptional point then arises along the trajectory in the conformal manifold, where two interface operators with complex conjugate weights coalesce into a logarithmic pair. We reconstruct the entire trajectory of this novel spectral collision, independently, from self-annulus partition functions and bulk two point correlators in the presence of the interfaces.

title: LSNR: Learned Sparse News Recommendations with Attentive User Modeling
abstract: Current learned sparse approaches for recommender systems, such as STAR, represent a user by concatenating their interaction history into a single query string. For news, this creates two bottlenecks: concatenation collapses a user's distinct reading interests into one flat query, and, because news articles are long-form text, concatenating several news articles quickly overruns the context window of the language model used as backbone and forces quality-degrading truncation. To address both bottlenecks, we introduce learned sparse news recommendations (LSNR). LSNR encodes each article independently and constructs a sparse user vector by combining learned, attention-based weighting of the per-article sparse representations with a dense-projected expansion at the user level. Experiments on the MIND and EBNeRD datasets show that LSNR significantly outperforms STAR, with these gains holding even in short-history settings where truncation is not a factor. Compared to state-of-the-art dense recommenders, LSNR is competitive in standard settings and it outperforms them when the user history is short. An ablation of the user encoder confirms that learned attention-based aggregation outperforms simpler pooling alternatives. Beyond effectiveness, an additional advantage of LSNR is that it serves from an index an order of magnitude smaller than an uncompressed dense baseline.

title: LocalIntent: Outcome-Specific Structured Generation for Backend-Compatible Smart Building Automation with Local LLMs
abstract: Locally deployed large language models (LLMs) can reduce reliance on remote cloud services for natural language smart building automation, but backend-facing processing requires correct outcome selection, alignment with local capabilities, and valid structured outputs. We investigate whether a complete outcome-specific prompting design improves compact-model outputs beyond generic route-then-generate prompting. The proposed LocalIntent approach routes requests to ordinary or persistent-rule branches: the former produces commands, clarifications, or rejections, while the latter generates trigger-action rules, followed by deterministic validation. We evaluate four locally executed Gemma and Qwen models spanning 2B-9B parameters on 101 non-persistent and 54 persistent-rule records, comparing Monolithic prompting, generic two-stage prompting, LocalIntent, and validation-guided repair. Across the evaluated datasets, LocalIntent achieves higher intent understanding, device identification, and action/parameter correctness than generic two-stage prompting, while clarification/mode correctness remains model-dependent. The largest gains occur for rules, where LocalIntent improves intent understanding from 26.4% to 80.6%, device identification from 59.3% to 84.7%, rule-mode correctness from 49.1% to 98.6%, and action/parameter correctness from 5.6% to 44.9%. For non-persistent requests, pooled gains are smaller: intent understanding increases from 39.6% to 53.2%, and action/parameter correctness from 30.7% to 42.8%.

title: topas-editor and TOPilot: tools for AI-driven analysis of diffraction and total scattering data
abstract: This paper describes topas-editor and TOPilot, which provide a powerful interface to the TOPAS software suite and allow generative AI-driven automation of complex crystallographic tasks. topas-editor is a TOPAS-aware VS Code extension designed for the rapid creation and editing of TOPAS input files and for interacting with the software. It knows TOPAS syntax, has crystallographic-aware editing features and provides in-line user guidance via hover tips and automated links to reference manuals. TOPilot is a collection of Python routines and machine-accessible reference documents that allow AI-driven automated analysis in TOPAS. It uses a transferable topas-inp-writer skill that can be applied in all TOPAS application areas. We demonstrate the power and reliability of the approach using examples including: a complex Rietveld refinement with sample- and data-related complications; automatic analysis of multiple data sets; a pipeline from indexing through structure solution to refinement; automatic identification of the phases present in a sample; single crystal and powder diffraction analysis of incommensurate structures; and fitting PDF data. TOPilot can be used directly alongside topas-editor, via a stand-alone topilot-wizard, or via command line interfaces or desktop apps from major AI providers. TOPilot was developed and tested using Claude large language models, but can be configured to use other cloud or local models. topas-editor and TOPilot are freely available.

title: Classification of boundary blow-ups for the Mumford-Shah functional with Dirichlet boundary conditions
abstract: We classify boundary blow-ups of minimizers of the Mumford-Shah functional on bounded planar domains with Dirichlet boundary conditions. At every point where the discontinuity set meets the boundary of the domain, we prove that the discontinuity set of each blow-up is the tangent line to the boundary at that point. This settles the conjecture formulated by the author in 2024.

title: Timelike entanglement entropy with gravitational anomaly from complexified geometry
abstract: We investigate the timelike entanglement entropy (TEE) in a two-dimensional conformal field theory with a gravitational anomaly, $c_L\neq c_R$, dual to topologically massive gravity in AdS$_3$. Holographically, the TEE is determined by the on-shell action of a massive spinning particle on a single complex geodesic anchored at the endpoints of the timelike interval. This action consists of the complex geodesic length and the twist of a parallel-transported normal frame. We carry out the computation in Poincaré AdS$_3$, non-extremal and extremal rotating BTZ backgrounds, and provide an equivalent Chern-Simons derivation in which the bulk connection stays real while only the saddle of the Wilson-line probe becomes complex. In each case, the holographic result matches the corresponding TEE in dual field theory. The real part of the TEE is fixed unambiguously whereas its imaginary part depends on the boundary $iε$ prescription and the orientation of the interval. In the bulk, the dependence on orientation reflects an ambiguity in the choice of framing. Along the complex geodesic, the residual frame group becomes $SO(2,\mathbb C)\simeq\mathbb C^*$, so the endpoint conditions determine the frame twist only up to integer multiples of $2πi$. The difference between the two orientations, $\frac{c_L-c_R}{6}\,iπ$, is fixed entirely by the gravitational anomaly and persists for the Rényi pseudo-entropies.

title: Uncertainty-aware AI-enabled framework for predicting hydrogen dispersion in confined spaces to enhance operator situational awareness
abstract: We present a two-stage AI-enabled framework for enhancing operator situational awareness during compressed hydrogen bunkering in maritime confined spaces. In the event of a leak, the framework first estimates the unknown leakage rate from early sensor readings and then forecasts how the hydrogen cloud will disperse over the next time steps, providing operators with a predicted concentration map together with confidence bounds. The framework is based on two independent AI models building one AI system. The AI system is designed as a decision-support tool. It augments sensor readings, and thus enhances operator situational awareness and supports decision-making. This enables preventive safety barriers to be deployed before hazardous concentrations are reached, while an independent emergency shutdown system remains the ultimate safety layer. The system design incorporates safeguards to ensure the AI system operates within its competence envelope. Trained and tested on an open dataset of confined-space hydrogen releases, the framework achieves a mean absolute error of $0.052$~g/s in leakage-rate estimation and $\approx0.018$ in hydrogen-concentration prediction, approaching the sensor precision bound of $\pm0.01$. The hydrogen-concentration prediction provides well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that allow operators to judge the reliability of each forecast. These results suggest that the framework may provide early information about hazardous concentration build-up, potentially supporting preventive actions by operators.

title: On the crystalline Artin--Mumford invariant
abstract: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $W=W(k)$. We prove that the torsion subgroup of $H^3_{\mathrm{cris}}(X/W)$ is a birational invariant of smooth projective varieties over $k$. The proof combines the action of correspondences on Hodge--Witt cohomology and on the first Nygaard piece of the de Rham--Witt complex.

title: Combinatorial Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
abstract: We develop a framework to identify and quantify arbitrage across logically related prediction-market contracts. We prove that prices outside the convex hull of admissible payoff vectors admit arbitrage and identify optimal arbitrage portfolios through integer programming. Using venue metadata and semantic analysis of resolution criteria, we recover 1.9 million logical relations and compile them into constraint systems covering more than 255,000 contracts. We replay full-depth Polymarket order books to simulate an arbitrageur executing these portfolios against resting orders. Among settled portfolios, an ideal arbitrageur that takes the full displayed depth of every opportunity and reuses its capital at resolution earns a risk-free return of 3.5% a week after spreads and fees. We find that arbitrage opportunities persist longer and attract less observed participation where relation discovery and execution are more costly.

title: Primal-dual forward-reflected splitting with linesearch for distributed min-max problems under local Lipschitz smoothness
abstract: We consider a network of finitely many agents aiming to cooperatively solve a convex-concave min-max problem combining nonsmooth terms with a smooth saddle function whose partial gradients are only locally Lipschitz continuous. Without requiring prior knowledge of the local Lipschitz moduli of the partial gradients, we propose a distributed proximal-reflected-gradient algorithm which incorporates a distributed backtracking procedure to adjust the stepsizes at each iteration. The algorithm is derived by reformulating the min-max problem as a composite monotone inclusion involving the sum of a maximally monotone operator, a linearly composed maximally monotone operator, and a single-valued locally Lipschitz continuous monotone operator. To solve this inclusion, we introduce a novel primal-dual forward-reflected splitting method with linesearch and establish its convergence using a Lyapunov-based analysis. In addition, when specialised to the min-max formulation, we derive an $\mathcal{O}(1/N)$ ergodic convergence rate for a consensus-penalised gap function. Finally, applying this splitting framework with mixing matrices yields our distributed method for consensus min-max optimisation.

title: Diversifying Moving Target Defense Against Adaptive Attacks Through Factorized Diffusion
abstract: Proactive defense offers a means to enhance power-system cybersecurity through controlled modifications of system configurations. One example is moving target defense (MTD), which uses distributed flexible AC transmission system (D-FACTS) devices to perturb transmission-line reactances against stealthy false data injection attacks. Existing MTD methods primarily rely on deterministic optimization, producing a single perturbation plan for each operating condition. However, repeated or highly correlated plans may expose predictable system configurations that attackers can learn and exploit. To address this limitation, this paper reformulates MTD as a conditional generative problem that produces diverse, secure, and physically feasible perturbation candidates. Learning such a distribution is challenging because MTD decisions jointly involve selecting branches, determining perturbation magnitudes, and coordinating adjustments across the network. To make this problem tractable, we factorize the decision distribution into three sequential conditional stages: branch selection, magnitude allocation, and continuous refinement. Graph-conditioned diffusion models are employed to capture the discrete and continuous decisions while accounting for network dependencies. Furthermore, a - objective is incorporated into diffusion training to favor candidates with desirable defense effectiveness and operational costs. Numerical studies on the IEEE 118- and 300-bus systems show that the proposed framework achieves AC feasibility comparable to that of optimization-based MTD baselines and higher - values, while reducing online computation time by an order of magnitude. The generated candidate pool remains effective under changing operating conditions and device availability, providing diverse high-value alternatives for flexible online cyber defense.

title: Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling Models: Taxonomy, Classification and Open Challenges
abstract: Over the past three decades, a large number of optimization models have been proposed for Earth observation satellite (EOS) scheduling. The main goal of this paper is to provide an overview of these models and to relate them to the characteristics of the problems they address. To do so, we first identify the main features of EOS scheduling problems and those with the most impact on the computational complexity of the model. Based on these features, we propose a new taxonomy of satellite agility and a classification of EOS scheduling problems that allows the problem under study to be clearly identified. We then propose a classification of the optimization models into five categories, based on their time and event representations, and describe representative formulations of each category in a unified notation, together with their extensions, discussing the respective advantages and limitations. The trade-offs between the alternative representations are analyzed, showing that discrete-time formulations allow time-dependent parameters, such as transition times and image quality, to be pre-computed, which preserves the linearity of the model but makes its size depend on the adopted discretization, whereas continuous-time formulations treat these parameters as functions of the start times, which introduces nonlinearities unless simplifying assumptions are adopted. Finally, we identify the main open challenges, including the exact modeling of time-dependent transition times and the integrated scheduling of active imaging satellites.

title: Perceive, Solve, Reason: Progressive Capability Formation in Time Series-LLMs
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now perceive, describe, and reason about images and audio, yet time series understanding remains underestimated: most work uses LLMs as forecasters and classifiers, reasoning studies are few and narrow, and no suite trains and evaluates the full range of capabilities. In this paper, we build the first such suite, with 337K training and 44K evaluation samples across three progressive capabilities, Perceive, Solve, and Reason, and use it to ask how time series should enter an LLM that must master all three, and in what order. We find that a dedicated encoder is essential: with one, a 4B model surpasses GPT-4o on every perception attribute we test, whereas textualizing the series costs 8--10 points in reasoning accuracy. The capabilities then build on one another: learning them in order beats mixing the same data and rivals reasoning-only training with over three times the reasoning data, but only when an encoder is used. Analyses further reveal that capabilities are transferred through distinct network depths rather than simply stacked, and that a stage converged on its own benchmark is not necessarily ready for the next. Distilled into a simple recipe, these findings yield 4B TS-LLMs that, without any target-domain data, outperform four recent 7B TS-LLMs on seven of eight out-of-domain metrics, by up to 11 points. We therefore advocate treating time series as a first-class modality for LLMs, read through dedicated encoders and taught to perceive before they reason.

title: The metric-affine $\mathring{R}^2$ scalaron: parameter-free inflation
abstract: We present a model of slow-roll inflation in metric-affine gravity, where the connection is independent of the metric. We require that the Einstein-Hilbert term is the only operator that breaks three out of four shift-symmetries of the connection, and impose them on the metric-affine Starobinsky term $αR(Γ)^2$. This replaces it by $α\mathring{R}^2$, the square of the invariant part of the scalar curvature. The theory propagates only the graviton and one healthy scalar, the metric-affine $\mathring{R}^2$ scalaron. Its potential approaches a plateau polynomially, $U\simeq U_0(1-μ^2/χ^2)$, with $μ=\sqrt{6}\,M_P$ fixed by the curvature of the connection. Once $α\simeq2\times10^{8}$ is set by the scalar amplitude, the model has no free parameters. It predicts $n_s\simeq1-3/(2N_*)$ and $r\simeq2\sqrt3\,N_*^{-3/2}$ at leading order in $N_*$, and $n_s=0.968$--$0.974$ and $r=0.011$-$0.008$ with exact slow-roll for $N_*=50$-$60$ $e$-folds. These values agree with current data, and $r$ is within reach of the next generation of $B$-mode measurements.

title: Complexity of liveness in ring Petri nets and of halting in chip-firing on simple digraphs
abstract: A ring Petri net (weighted circuit, cyclic weighted T-system) consists of a single directed circuit with arbitrary positive arc weights. We show that deciding liveness of ring Petri nets is coNP-complete, and that coNP-hardness holds in the strong sense already for token-conserving rings, in which every transition consumes and produces the same number of tokens. The proof is a short reduction from the covering problem for systems of residue classes (the complement of Simultaneous Incongruences). Together with a known reduction to circuits, it follows that liveness of weighted T-systems (weighted marked graphs, synchronous dataflow graphs) is coNP-complete, and coNP-hard in the strong sense. As a further consequence, the halting problem for chip-firing on simple directed graphs is NP-complete, which answers a question of Farrell and Levine. On 7 October 2026, the problem of liveness was posed to the AI model Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), which found the reduction, also suggesting the application to the chip-firing problem, and wrote a first version of this paper; the human authors checked it and, together with the model, revised it iteratively into the present form.

title: QIEN: Quantum-Inspired Energy-Neutral UAV Trajectory for WPT-Enabled Industrial HRLLC
abstract: This paper introduces Quantum-Inspired Energy-Neutral (QIEN) UAV Trajectory for WPT-Enabled Industrial HRLLC, a novel framework for mobility-integrated trajectory and resource optimization in solar-powered uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) relay systems supporting autonomous mining robots in post-disaster environments. We formulate a mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP) that jointly optimizes UAV trajectory, finite blocklength allocation, transmit power, and wireless power transfer (WPT) over discrete time horizons to maximize aggregate data throughput. The system operates under strict extreme hyper-reliable low-latency communication (HRLLC) constraints, energy sustainability requirements via solar harvesting, and continuous robot power delivery. To solve this large-scale optimization problem, QIEN employs a hybrid Cooperative Quantum-behaved Particle Swarm Optimization (Co-QPSO) algorithm using quantum tunneling mechanisms and a heterogeneous swarm architecture. Our simulation results demonstrate that the proposed QIEN framework significantly outperforms benchmark algorithms, achieving successful convergence while maintaining energy-neutral operation and satisfying all reliability, power, and mobility constraints.

title: Trapped in Your Story: Evaluating Narrative-Induced Sycophancy in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to exhibit sycophancy by adjusting their responses toward users' expressed views. However, real users often justify their opinions through reasons, personal experiences, causal explanations, and broader narratives, raising the question of whether such narratives can further steer model judgments. We construct a controlled benchmark of 500 debatable questions across ten domains, where the user stance is held fixed while its justification is systematically varied without introducing new task-relevant evidence. Each question is instantiated under 11 matched conditions: one neutral baseline and five mirrored narrative levels for each of two opposing positions, yielding 5,500 evaluation instances. We evaluate seven LLMs and observe substantial differences in narrative-induced agreement. The effect is not monotonic with narrative elaboration: personal experience can reduce agreement, whereas causal framing and worldview-based synthesis increase it. Controlled GPT-5.1 ablations further show that causal framing produces the strongest positive effect, while claim-preserving bullet presentation also increases agreement over paragraph form. These findings suggest that sycophancy is shaped not only by user stance, but also by how supporting explanations are structured and presented.

title: Interpreting SSL Representations for Spoof Detection: a WavLM Study
abstract: Self-supervised speech models such as WavLM achieve strong spoofing detection performance, yet which layers encode the most spoof-relevant information and what acoustic properties they capture remain opaque. We present a layer-wise interpretability study of WavLM using the ASVspoof 5 database, combining three complementary analyses: (i) per-layer linear probing with attack-level evaluation across speech synthesis, voice conversion, and adversarial attacks; (ii) a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) linking layer representations to spoofing-relevant acoustic features; (iii) an exhaustive grid search over layer subsets showing that use of five layers outperforms full thirteen-layer pooling. CCA analysis reveals that, while most acoustic features peak in alignment with mid-layers and then decay, voice quality measures jitter, shimmer, and the harmonics-to-noise ratio show the opposite trend, with correlation increasing toward later layers. Embedding visualisations reveal that deeper layers capture a continuous acoustic similarity among attacks rather than discrete categories, suggesting these layers encode fundamental synthesis artifacts rather than attack-specific signatures.

title: Truth in Contrast: Calibrated Factual Evidence from Language Model Likelihoods
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode substantial factual knowledge. Yet, estimating confidence in factual claims reliably remains challenging. We study likelihood-based factual confidence from the complementary perspectives of discrimination and calibration across multilingual factual statements. Specifically, we instantiate contrastive generative likelihoods as Contrastive Factual Evidence (CFE), which compares the likelihood of the same claim under competing factual and non-factual conditions, and derive its probabilistic counterpart, the Contrastive Factual Posterior (CFP). We show analytically that CFP calibration depends on the differential error between the two surrogate conditionals, allowing errors shared across them to cancel and yield tighter calibration bounds. Empirically, CFP substantially improves calibration while maintaining factual discrimination comparable to its strongest competitor. Nonetheless, discrimination is uniformly weak across methods in lower-resource languages, which simultaneously undermines the utility of the measured calibration. To this end, we interpret a likelihood geometry, within which an evidence-bearing direction is induced, along with an orthogonal evidence-invariant direction. In our investigation, we selectively align target-language claims with stronger English evidence only along the factual-evidence direction, improving discrimination and open-ended factual generation without target-language labels.

title: Out of Support, Not Out of Reach: In-Context Learning with Unsupported Instructions and Composed Tasks
abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) enables pretrained LLMs to adapt to downstream tasks from a small set of input-output demonstrations, without parameter updates. Yet existing theory primarily explains ICL as identifying a latent task already represented in pretraining, leaving unclear whether ICL can succeed when either the instruction or the target task falls outside the pretraining support. We develop a theoretical framework under mild assumptions that separates these two forms of distribution shift. For target tasks represented in pretraining, we show that demonstrations can identify the task and reduce sensitivity to pretrain-supported prompt templates as their number increases. For an unsupported instruction, we show that under a fixed model-induced reference extension, demonstration evidence can dominate an $N$-independent instruction shift while preserving the exponential identification rate. We then use the same ICL framework as an interpretive lens for long-horizon target tasks that are not represented in pretraining but admit a plan that decomposes them into pretraining-supported subtasks. Applying the supported-task analysis step by step yields a standard accumulated-error bound and clarifies how invoking familiar subtasks along an intermediate-state trajectory can avoid directly selecting the unsupported complete task. Together, our results characterize when demonstrations, instructions, and task decomposition can support ICL beyond the corresponding pretraining supports.

title: Renormalization Group Domain Walls from Phantom Symmetries
abstract: We develop a systematic construction of renormalization group (RG) domain walls between two-dimensional rational conformal field theories. Using phantom currents, we consider an auxiliary chiral extension linked to the folded ultraviolet--infrared theory by a topological interface. The construction of RG walls then reduces to identifying suitable automorphism-twisted Cardy states in the auxiliary theory. We find two such types of automorphisms: outer automorphisms exchanging identical current algebra factors, as in Gaiotto's construction, and continuous inner automorphisms generated by the zero modes of spin-one phantom currents. In the latter case, the RG domain walls generically admit a continuous defect conformal manifold. We further show that, when an RG flow can be orbifolded to another one, the orbifold may lift defect conformal moduli of the RG brane constructed using inner automorphisms. The two types of RG branes can then be mapped to each other via a topological interface defined by the orbifold. We demonstrate the two types of RG brane construction via various examples of flows between non-unitary minimal models, from parafermions to minimal models, and between generalized parafermions. Many physical observables of the RG walls are computed non-perturbatively, including boundary entropies and spectra, and UV--IR operator mixings. We also find interesting nontrivial boundary monodromy: a closed cycle in the defect conformal moduli space can carry an RG domain wall into other distinct non-trivial conformal interfaces.

title: EduWild: How Teacher-Configured Chatbots Fail in Real-World Use and How to Fix Them
abstract: Teachers increasingly configure educational chatbots through natural-language instructions, but how these bots fail in real-world use remains poorly understood. We introduce EduWild, a dataset of 1,726 conversations with 217 teacher-configured chatbots, each paired with the instructions and configuration behind it, including 900 conversations from the intended end users of 35 deployed chatbots. We develop a 29-code taxonomy covering factual, workflow, diagnostic, and pedagogical failures and apply it using a human-calibrated LLM judge. The most frequent failures are lapses in following teacher intent --- bots skip required workflow steps (53.8% of end-user conversations), omit expectation setup (33.4%), and overload learners with information or questions (37.1%). Guided by these findings, we design a prompt-based harness targeting the six most frequent failure modes. In a study with 200 college students across ten bots, the harness reduces the mean number of target failure codes per conversation from 1.406 to 0.489, a 65.2% relative reduction with bots weighted equally. These findings show how real-world failure analysis can guide practical improvements to educational chatbots.

title: PONDER: Learning to Generate in the Right Order
abstract: We introduce PONDER, a method that learns in which order an image generator should fill in content and which of its earlier predictions to revise. Masked generative models construct a sample by repeatedly filling in subsets of missing variables. The order of these partial predictions determines the context available in subsequent steps and therefore affects the quality of the final sample. Common strategies are to choose the order randomly or based on local confidence estimates. Conditioned on the partially generated sample and the generator's features, our policy chooses which positions to fill next and/or which previously filled positions to mask for later regeneration, a mechanism we call rethinking. In this way, the generation process is able to adapt to the evolving context and also to revise earlier predictions. We optimize the policy using group-relative policy gradients, with rewards that measure constraint satisfaction, human preference, or distribution quality. For the latter, we introduce FIDgrad, an image-level reward derived from the (first-order) change in Fréchet Inception Distance caused by adding a generated sample to the current feature distribution. With the generators frozen, learned ordering reduces MAR-B ImageNet FID from 4.09 to 2.78 and raises the accuracy on hard visual Sudokus from 3.9\% to 56.6\%, surpassing uncertainty-based greedy ordering (38.7\%). Rethinking further improves these results to 2.70 FID and 96.7\% accuracy, while increasing the rethinking budget of a fixed policy yields continued improvements at inference time.

title: Exploiting the Flexibility of LLM Inference for Frequency Regulation Service
abstract: While the widespread deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly driven up power demands in computing clusters, the unique execution characteristics of LLM inference offer a novel opportunity to utilize these clusters as controllable loads. In this paper, we investigate the potential of LLM inference cluster to provide frequency regulation services through inference request scheduling. First, we model the problem as a hierarchical Markov decision process that includes request-to-replica dispatching and token-level resource allocation. Then, we introduce a reward redistribution network to address the temporal asynchrony between millisecond-level scheduling decisions and second-level frequency regulation signals. Furthermore, we develop an optimization framework based on a mean-field approximation to enable coordination among a large number of replicas under high request concurrency. Simulations using real-world data demonstrate that the proposed approach accurately tracks frequency regulation signals without compromising service-level objectives.

title: ReVision: Reprogramming Image Generators for Dense Visual Perception
abstract: Recent image generators exhibit rich visual priors that can support dense visual perception. However, existing approaches typically encode multiple perception tasks into a shared parameterization, making joint training sensitive to the mixture and weighting of heterogeneous data and prone to cross-task interference. To address this issue, we introduce ReVision, an instruction-conditioned parameter generation framework built on a frozen multimodal understanding model and a frozen image generator. Given an image and a free-form instruction, the understanding model jointly encodes them into a multimodal image--instruction representation, which a trainable parameter generator maps to transient low-rank updates for the generator. Each image--instruction pair induces a distinct set of transient prediction parameters, enabling instance-specific adaptation while both pretrained backbones remain unchanged. ReVision requires no task-specific heads, explicit task identifiers, or stored adapters. A shared RGB output interface unifies segmentation, depth estimation, and surface-normal prediction. Across diverse dense prediction benchmarks, ReVision achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods while supporting flexible task specification through natural-language instructions. Our analysis further reveals substantial gradient disagreement across tasks, highlighting the conflict introduced when heterogeneous objectives share a single parameterization. Meanwhile, the generated updates exhibit structured task- and input-dependent organization in weight space, further validating instance-level parameter generation for multi-task perception.

title: From Billion-Scale to Million-Scale Language Models: Operational Capabilities for Embedded Post-Exploitation
abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for resource-constrained environments due to their low computational footprint. These characteristics also make them candidates for future autonomous malware, where connectivity, latency, privacy, or operational constraints may preclude cloud-based inference. Yet the ability of ultra-compact models to support malware during post-exploitation remains poorly understood. We systematically evaluate seven open-source SLMs (20M-1.5B parameters) on two post-exploitation code-generation tasks: Directory Enumeration and Backdoor Generation. We compare Python (high-resource) and Lua (low-resource) across prompting strategies, task formulations, iterative reasoning, grammar-constrained decoding, and execution-feedback loops. Results show that offensive code-generation capabilities do not increase linearly with model size. Successful execution depends on the interaction of model capacity, task formulation, and prompting strategy, with task formulation exerting a greater influence than prompt engineering alone. Algorithmic formulation combined with few-shot prompting enables Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B to reach Pass@5 of 100% in both Python and Lua for Directory Enumeration, 100% in Python for Backdoor Generation, and 99.2% in Lua. Although the evaluated models remain too computationally demanding for widespread deployment in contemporary malware, rapid progress in compact models may reduce this barrier. These findings help anticipate AI-assisted malware and inform future countermeasures.

title: PreciseEdit: Strong Yet Stable Semantic Transport for One-Step Image Editing
abstract: Recent one-step text-to-image (T2I) models enable efficient image synthesis, opening up new possibilities for interactive Web-based image editing. However, existing one-step editing methods often construct a global transport field through simple vector operations between conditional predictions. While such strong transport can effectively drive the image toward the target semantics, it may be released along unreliable directions or over non-edited regions, leading to structural distortions within the editing region and background drift elsewhere. More importantly, stabilizing the editing process through global smoothing or uniformly weakening the transport field often makes large semantic changes overly conservative. In this work, we revisit one-step image editing from the perspective of the tension between semantic strength and transport stability, and identify a key insight: strong semantic transport is not inherently unstable. What matters is whether it is applied along reliable directions and at reliable spatial locations. Motivated by this insight, we introduce PreciseEdit, a model-agnostic, training-free and inversion-free one-step editing framework that strengthens target-semantic alignment while preserving background fidelity and structural consistency. We further propose a dual-noise-scale role decomposition strategy: a higher-noise scale produces the strong target-directed transport used for actual editing, whereas a lower-noise scale jointly serves as a probe for directional agreement and spatial structure. Extensive experiments on PIE-Bench demonstrate that PreciseEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance and effectiveness on various editing tasks.

title: Temperature dependence of a warm ensemble based memory on quantum communication rates
abstract: The success of long-distance quantum communication will hinge on quantum repeater nodes equipped with robust and scalable quantum memories. Such memories must possess specific operating characteristics to make these nodes practical. An attractive option for these memory devices is an atomic warm vapor system operating under the conditions of electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT). These systems are easy to implement and require relatively low equipment overhead. A key metric in atomic-based quantum memory performance is optical depth, as it is closely tied to the strength of light-matter coupling. Here, we simulate and measure the optical depth-based performance of an EIT quantum memory using a warm atomic vapor cell. We then translate the simulated and measured optical depth and efficiency metrics into expected entanglement distribution rates. Our analysis evaluates the feasibility of these memories in optical quantum repeater nodes, which are essential for robust long-distance quantum communication.

title: PanoBench: A Panoptic Occupancy Prediction Benchmark for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Panoptic occupancy unifies 3D geometry, semantics, and instance identities, but its development is limited by scarce instance-aware annotations. Existing benchmarks mainly provide semantic labels reconstructed from incomplete sensor observations, while panoptic datasets have limited domain coverage or annotation completeness. We introduce PanoBench, a camera-centric panoptic occupancy prediction benchmark spanning synthetic and real-world driving scenes. It combines PanoBench-CarlaOcc, PanoBench-nuScenes, and PanoBench-KITTI360 through canonical data interfaces and unified evaluation protocols, providing multi-resolution annotations with persistent instance identities. The synthetic branch derives complete panoptic geometry from simulated meshes. For real-world data, a new pipeline reconstructs backgrounds using geometric priors and topology constraints, generates foreground mesh assets from multi-frame multi-view images, and fuses them into sparse panoptic voxels. A unified valid-mask protocol evaluates complete thing instances supported by temporal observations while scoring stuff regions at the voxel level. Analyses of observation fidelity, geometric completeness, spatial continuity, and temporal consistency demonstrate the benefits of the resulting annotations over existing occupancy benchmarks. We benchmark representative methods on semantic occupancy prediction, panoptic occupancy prediction, and 4D occupancy forecasting, and study voxel resolution, synthetic-to-real transfer, and storage efficiency. These results reveal complementary strengths of volumetric and ray-based metrics and persistent challenges in real-world instance-aware prediction. PanoBench is available at https://mias.group/PanoBench.

title: pymatgen: 15 years of community growth, new functionality, and future prospects
abstract: We present a retrospective on the Python Materials Genomics (pymatgen) library, reflecting on 15 years of community growth and established best practices. The current version of pymatgen builds on its robust, open-source foundation, emphasising its collaborative nature. Over the past decade, pymatgen has thrived as one of the largest open-source materials science codebases. We detail how pymatgen supports advanced computational materials science workflows, how it adapts to changing demands, and the lessons learned from its growing community, providing guidance beyond pymatgen's open-source community. Pymatgen will continue to evolve in response to the current rapidly changing landscape of computational materials science and materials informatics. We discuss the challenges and potential solutions to managing the community-driven evolution of pymatgen and provide an outlook on its future development.

title: ConvexLLM: Scaling Convex-Hull Speech Interfaces to General-Purpose Audio Intelligence
abstract: Speech and audio language models connect continuous acoustic representations to decoders pretrained primarily on text data. Most such models use MLP or Q-Former interfaces to map acoustic features into the decoder's input space, requiring the decoder to learn how to interpret the resulting representations. We investigate whether grounding these representations in the decoder's existing text embeddings can help it use acoustic information while better preserving its pretrained text capabilities. We present ConvexLLM, a general-purpose speech and audio language model whose C-Gate interface represents audio as continuous convex combinations of frozen text embeddings. ConvexLLM achieves an eleven-task VoiceBench aggregate of 75.36, the highest among the open-weight models we compare, and an MMAU Test-mini accuracy of 62.50%. Its largest margins over the baselines are on spoken knowledge and reasoning tasks, while the strongest baselines are more accurate on audio understanding and transcription. In a comparison with a 2B-parameter decoder, C-Gate achieves higher aggregate spoken-language performance than MLP and Q-Former interfaces, with text-task performance close to MLP and task-dependent tradeoffs in transcription and audio understanding. These results support convex combinations of text embeddings as a viable interface for general-purpose speech and audio language models.

title: Net-Zero Power UAVs: Facilitating Quantum HRLLC in Multi-Hop UAV Repeaters
abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel joint optimization framework for autonomous, quantum-enabled UAV repeater networks designed to support hyper-reliable low-latency communications (HRLLC) in challenging environments such as post-explosion chemical plant operations. The proposed system uses a symmetric dual-UAV architecture with three sequential quantum channels operating under strict energy harvesting (EH) constraints. We formulate a highly challenging non-convex mixed-integer non-linear programming (MINLP) problem. This model jointly determines qubit allocation, 2-D uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) spatial positioning (distance and altitude), and transmit powers to minimize the total decoding error. Crucially, our framework explicitly models real-world quantum physics, including decoherence, gate imperfections, and entanglement degradation. Since the objective function is demonstrably non-convex, to efficiently solve the MINLP, we propose a quantum-resource-optimized GA (QRO-GA). The results of our numerical simulations show that the QRO-GA yields better results than benchmark methods and it is highly efficient, with the convergence speed significantly increasing with the total qubit allocation. Convergence is achieved in as few as 5 iterations for higher qubit allocation. Moreover, the results reveal a critical U-shaped tradeoff, proving that an optimal latency distribution within a strict $80\ μ$s transmission window is strictly required to maintain HRLLC reliability. In addition, we find that the QRO-GA successfully optimizes the 2-D UAV positioning to minimize total decoding error. Finally, it balances consumed and harvested power to achieve net-zero power UAVs system.

title: Humanity's Last Choice: A Common Evaluation Standard for Generative Engine Optimization
abstract: Humanity's Last Choice describes the idea that the last choice people need to make is which AI system they entrust with the decisions that follow. These systems rely on external sources that content providers can edit through generative engine optimization (GEO) to increase source visibility and influence recommendations. Choosing among these systems therefore requires comparable evidence of how well they carry out user requests when exposed to GEO. Benchmarks have made progress in standardizing tasks, models, and metrics, but they often define their own spaces of GEO strategies and use different editing constraints. These differences can conflate gains from better optimization algorithms with those from greater freedom to edit sources, while making evaluation coverage difficult to compare across benchmarks. We therefore call for a common evaluation standard and propose a meta-taxonomy that describes where sources are edited, how they are edited, and what signals those edits target. Drawing on representative literature, we map existing strategies into a searchable space and outline a protocol for controlled comparisons with explicit coverage reporting. This provides a foundation for common leaderboards that can inform which systems people choose to rely on.

title: Execution Before Memory: Diagnosing Memory Failures in Video World Models
abstract: A memory test for a video world model should say whether the scene was set, whether the asked change was carried out, and whether the last frame shows the result. Current tests fold these into one number, so a low score is easy to read as forgetting. When the change is not carried out, the hidden state transition cannot appear, so the test is not really a test of memory. We introduce MIST, an evaluation that separates the change from the memory it should leave behind. The model first sets the scene while the change stays hidden, and only later is asked to show it, with leakage before that point kept under control. This separation locates the bottleneck: the model sets the scene but does not carry out the instructed change. The same gap appears in general memory evaluations. On that basis we propose M3-Agent (Make the Missing Move), which recursively revises the details of the input instruction so that the model successfully carries out the requested instruction. Relative to the baseline, it more than triples the MIST reveal score. On the benchmarks, WRBench's score T rises by 26.1% and MBench-T's score U by 52.7%. The method meets the problem from the execution side: it shows what the frozen model can do once the move is stated, and it sets a stricter baseline.

title: Causal Discovery beyond Conditional Independence: Identifiability, Algorithms, and Statistical Inference for Directed Acyclic and Cyclic Graphs
abstract: Learning causal structure from data requires assumptions about mechanisms, noises, observation schemes, and interventions. Historically, causal discovery has relied primarily on conditional independence. This review focuses on modern causal discovery methods that exploit properties of distributions beyond conditional independence. Our organizing principle separates the source of identification from the statistical estimator and its computational implementation. This perspective connects conditional-independence methods with distributional asymmetries, conditional-moment restrictions, and variation across environments or individuals. We examine discovery under latent confounding and feedback, distinguishing causal information about observed variables from reconstruction of latent structure and emphasizing the additional semantics required by cyclic models. We also distinguish population identification, frequentist and Bayesian consistency, uncertainty quantification, and algorithmic guarantees. Throughout, examples show why the same observational distribution can support different conclusions under different model classes. We conclude with guidance for comparing methods at their identifiable targets and a research agenda for uncertainty, heterogeneous populations, non-scalar variables, and the intersection of discrete data, feedback, and hidden confounding.

title: A Mixed Elliptic--Hyperbolic Monge--Ampère Problem: Modeling and a Least-Squares Solver
authors: J. H. M. ten Thije Boonkkamp
abstract: We consider a transport problem motivated by freeform optical design of a parallel-to-far-field reflector. Classical formulations rely on either elliptic or hyperbolic Monge--Ampère equations, leading to globally convex/concave or saddle-shape reflector geometries, respectively. However, the design of smooth reflector arrays may require optical surfaces combining both types of curvature. To address this, we introduce a mixed elliptic--hyperbolic Monge--Ampère system obtained by partitioning the source domain into one elliptic and one hyperbolic subregion, and we develop a least-squares method for its numerical approximation. Numerical examples demonstrate the ability of the proposed framework to compute both isolated and periodic mixed-type transport solutions, yielding smooth reflector configurations.

title: Linear response for machine-learned interatomic potentials: phonons at arbitrary wave vectors from the primitive cell
abstract: Phonon calculations with machine-learned interatomic potentials are almost exclusively performed with finite displacements in supercells, an approach that is exact only at wave vectors commensurate with the supercell and whose error depends on the range of the force constants. In message-passing networks this range grows with the number of layers, and reaches 140 angstrom for the deepest universal models. Here we show that the dynamical matrix of a message-passing potential can be obtained exactly in the primitive cell, at any wave vector, as the linear response of the forces to a displacement modulated by a Bloch phase, in the spirit of density-functional perturbation theory. The phase enters only where the features of neighboring atoms are gathered, and the trained model is used without modification. One further derivative yields group velocities and mode Grüneisen parameters analytically. We apply the method to NequIP and Prophet, and reproduce the Hessians of supercells to machine precision. Using these results as a reference, we find that the supercells commonly employed in high-throughput calculations lead to errors of several tenths of a THz in the phonon frequencies, and that these errors decrease slowly with the size of the supercell, in particular for deep models. For a low-symmetry silicate, the supercell predicts a dynamical instability that the model does not have. Quantities that depend on derivatives of the dispersion, such as the group velocities and the Grüneisen parameter at low temperature, are considerably more affected than the frequencies themselves. When both approaches are used to obtain the same force constants, their computational cost is comparable for crystals with symmetry.

title: Recall-Oriented Precise Binary-to-Source Function Matching
abstract: Binary-to-source function matching supports software composition analysis by identifying reused third-party code, but existing embedding-based approaches restrict subsequent refinement to initially retrieved candidates. When the correct source function is absent from this set, selecting or filtering the available candidates cannot recover the match. Inlining further complicates the retrieval by combining multiple source functions into one binary function. In this paper, we propose BScout to improve matching precision and uncover additional matches. BScout uses the positional information of existing matches to supplement candidates for unresolved binary functions, extending the search beyond the initial candidate set, and adopts composition-aware training to address the inlined composition matching. Large language models are adopted to select and review matches, while positional information also helps filter inconsistent results. Experiments show that BScout is effective in binary-to-source function matching. BScout achieves overall higher precision, recall and F1 scores than BinaryAI and SBridge with acceptable analysis costs. Particularly, on large stripped binaries, BScout outperforms the competitors with a precision increment of 32% and approximately 2.9 times the recall.

title: Uniform-Price Mechanism Design for Automated Market Makers
abstract: Automated market makers (AMMs) are central to decentralized exchanges, but their reserve curves make mechanism design different from classical double auctions. We study a batch double auction with buyers, sellers, and a liquidity-nondecreasing AMM: post-trade reserves must have weakly larger product than the initial reserves. Each user has two-dimensional private information: a unit value and a demand or supply quantity. User trades clear at one uniform price subject to AMM feasibility. The objective is user-side trading volume, benchmarked against the optimal feasible individually rational (IR) uniform-price allocation. We give a randomized uniform-price mechanism based on binary quantity buckets. It randomly chooses one of three clearing modes: peer-to-peer matching, AMM sales to buyers, and seller sales to the AMM. Every deterministic realization of the mechanism is ex-post feasible and satisfies IR and weak quantity incentive compatibility: conditional on any quantity report, truthful unit-value reporting is dominant whenever it gives a non-negative utility, no unit-value deviation gives a positive utility if the truthful one doesn't, and users cannot benefit by under-reporting the quantity together with their truthful unit value. Let $V^\ast$ be the optimal feasible IR uniform-price volume without incentive constraints, and let $γ=\bar q/\underline q$, where $\bar q$ and $\underline q$ are the quantity-domain bounds. For $γ\ge1$, the mechanism achieves an expected trading volume of $ Ω(1/(1+\logγ)^2)V^\ast - O(\bar q). $ We also show that full incentive compatibility over the two-dimensional type space forces a worst-case approximation ratio of $O(1/γ)$ at every prescribed initial reserve ratio, even when both AMM reserves are scaled by an arbitrarily large common factor and the optimal volume $V^\ast$ is arbitrarily large relative to $\bar q$.

title: Reinforcement Learning Based Multi-Terrain Adaptive Whole-Body Control for a Quadruped Manipulator
abstract: Legged robots equipped with manipulators offer promising capabilities for loco-manipulation tasks in unstructured environments. However, achieving task-consistent end-effector behavior during locomotion remains challenging due to terrain-induced disturbances and the strong coupling between locomotion and manipulation, particularly for small-scale quadruped platforms. A reinforcement-learning based whole-body control framework is proposed for quadruped loco-manipulation on complex terrain. The proposed framework combines a hybrid task representation with task-prioritized whole-body learning to coordinate locomotion and manipulation while preserving task-consistent end-effector behavior. A lightweight quadruped manipulator platform is further developed to validate the proposed framework on a small-scale quadruped system. Real-world experiments demonstrate successful deployment on complex terrains such as slopes up to 30 degrees, stairs, and deformable terrain. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying learned whole-body control policy for quadruped loco-manipulation in real-world environments and highlight the importance of task-consistent whole-body coordination for terrain-adaptive loco-manipulation.

title: A compact, dual-colour chirped-pulse laser system for field-deployable coherent Rayleigh-Brillouin scattering diagnostics
abstract: Single-shot coherent Rayleigh-Brillouin scattering (CRBS) requires dual colour, frequency, and pulse duration agile laser systems, currently available only in laboratory layouts. In this work, we present a compact, portable, and robust next generation laser system that meets all of these requirements. Key features include an integrated master-slave seed laser design for stable frequency chirping, fiber-coupled acousto-optic modulator (AOM) gated pulse shaping for long-term thermal stability, and customized amplification stages in a rugged, portable enclosure which simplifiy the alignment and maintenance process. The system in this implementation can deliver up to $450$~mJ per arm, chirp rates up to $\sim22$~MHz$/$ns, and arbitrary temporal profiles within $\sim25$~ns to $\sim1$~$μ$s. This laser system is validated by measuring the neutral number density of an atmospheric plasma jet, and a two-dimensional temperature map is constructed, demonstrating lab-grade diagnostics for field deployment.

title: Reason-guided Human Reward Modeling for Preference-based Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies optimized for task rewards may produce behaviors that are efficient but misaligned with human expectations, safety preferences, or intent. This paper presents a reason-guided preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) framework that learns a human reward model from trajectory-level feedback. In addition to preference labels, the framework incorporates reason tags explaining why a behavior is preferred, enabling the learned reward to capture both human choices and their underlying rationale. Compared with preference-only reward learning, the reason-guided formulation provides additional supervision for learning human-aligned rewards and improves the interpretability of the resulting policy. The learned human reward is combined with the environment reward during policy optimization, allowing the agent to improve task performance while producing more interpretable, human- aligned, and preference-sensitive behavior

title: Embodiment-Aware Planning for Heterogeneous Bimanual Manipulation
abstract: Many manipulation tasks that are effortless for dexterous human hands remain challenging for robotic systems equipped with simple, task-specialized grippers. Industrial platforms commonly rely on end-effectors such as suction cups or parallel-jaw grippers, yet no single mode can reliably satisfy the diverse constraints encountered across different phases of complex manipulation tasks, including pickup, reorientation, insertion, and constrained placement. In this work, we investigate whether complementary simple grippers within a heterogeneous bimanual setup can collectively realize tasks that exceed the capability of any individual gripper alone. Given a single human demonstration specifying the desired object motion, we formulate embodiment-aware execution as a finite-horizon optimization over arm-trajectory assignments. At each segment, the planner determines whether single-arm manipulation or a coordinated dual arm handover is required, jointly reasoning over heterogeneous grasp feasibility, motion constraints, manipulability, and cross-gripper compatibility. Exploiting this formulation, we compute globally consistent assignments with explicit switching regularization. Experiments on a dual Franka FR3 platform equipped with suction and parallel-jaw grippers demonstrate improved feasibility and reliability in tasks that are infeasible under single-gripper execution.

title: Closed geodesics on compact semi-Riemannian manifolds
abstract: We study the existence of closed geodesics on compact quotients of Lie groups endowed with left-invariant pseudo-Riemannian metrics. We construct a compact, geodesically complete pseudo-Riemannian manifold that admits no closed geodesics. We also establish the existence of closed geodesics in several settings, with particular focus on the Lorentzian case.

title: Visibility Sets, Empty Pentagons, and Sufficient Conditions for Hexagons
abstract: Given a set $S$ of $n$ points in general position in the plane, we define the $C$-set $C(p,q)$ of an oriented edge $(p,q)$ as the set of extreme points of the visibility set $V(p,q)$ facing $(p,q)$. Since every point of $V(p,q)$ that is not in $C(p,q)$ gives rise to an empty convex pentagon having $(p,q)$ as a boundary edge, it is natural to study the properties of $C$-sets in order to bound the number of empty convex pentagons of $S$. We prove tight bounds on the intersection size and union complexity of $C$-sets sharing an endpoint. We also consider the problem of bounding the number of empty pentagons and hexagons in terms of the number of interior and boundary points of $S$. While the hexagon bound is weak, it offers a potential step toward a superlinear lower bound. On the other hand, the two-parameter bound for pentagons, combined with the structural results on $C$-sets, yields a simple proof of an $Ω(n^{3/2})$ bound for the number of pentagons. While this is a significant improvement over previously published bounds, a recent preprint \cite{Astudillo2026} attains a better bound using completely different methods. Thus, the primary contribution of this paper lies in the structural results about $C$-sets and the two-parameter bounds for empty pentagons and hexagons.

title: SkillBrowser: Selective Skill Exposure for Scalable Skill-Using Agents
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skills to extend their capabilities in complex tasks. However, scalable skill use requires Selective Skill Exposure (SSE): providing relevant procedural content when needed while avoiding unnecessary exposure that may disrupt reasoning. Existing paradigms fall short in complementary ways. Progressive disclosure exposes metadata for a growing skill library, introducing context pollution; retrieval limits catalog exposure, but static retrieval from the initial task query may be misaligned with capability needs that emerge during reasoning and may still inject unnecessary skills. We propose SkillBrowser, a Meta-Skill-managed framework that enables an agent to identify current capability needs, formulate targeted queries, and selectively load skills on demand. Across six SRA-Bench subsets and five LLMs, SkillBrowser improves aggregate accuracy over static retrieval and LLM-based selection, including multi-step tool use, and mitigates accuracy degradation on already-solvable instances. Benefits remain model- and task-dependent, with under-invocation of useful skills and additional latency as key limitations. These results demonstrate the viability of Meta-Skill-managed SSE for scalable skill repositories.

title: Beyond Latent Personalization: Integrating HRV-Conditioned Personalization via LLM for Interpretable Stress Detection
abstract: Stress detection based on heart rate variability (HRV) has received increasing attention. However, existing personalized approaches integrate personal attributes with HRV through latent representations, limiting the interpretability of their interactions. In this work, we propose an LLM-enhanced personalized stress detection framework that integrates HRV features and personal attributes through LLM-based semantic interpretation. The proposed framework achieves a 29.9% relative MCC improvement over the strongest baseline on TILES-2018 while providing human-readable descriptions of individual physiological responses. The results highlight the potential of LLM-based semantic interpretation for achieving both effective and interpretable personalized stress detection.

title: Magnetic order in epitaxial (La2/3Sr1/3MnO3)3/(BaTiO3)3 trilayer heterostructures
abstract: The realization of artificial magnetic structures with high epitaxial quality and elevated critical temperatures remains a key challenge for spintronics. Here, we report the fabrication and characterization of epitaxial (La2/3Sr1/3MnO3)3/(BaTiO3)3 trilayer heterostructures grown by layer-by-layer laser ablation. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy, magnetization measurements, and neutron diffraction confirm their exceptional crystalline order and the absence of structural defects. Neutron diffraction reveals no antiferromagnetic at non-zero wavevector Bragg peaks, ruling out most antiferromagnetic configurations with a non zero wave vector Q. Magnetic hysteresis loops instead evidence a ferromagnetic order with a remanent moment of about 0.5 Bohr magneton per Mn atom at room temperature, persisting either in-plane or out-of-plane depending on the applied field. Our findings highlight neutron diffraction as a powerful tool for elucidating the magnetic structure of complex thin films and suggest that weak interlayer coupling through BaTiO3 leads to ferromagnetism with a high critical temperature (about 600 K).

title: Heterogeneity among and competition between life stages together extend the stability boundary of complex ecological communities
abstract: Classical models of pairwise species interactions consistently predict that large, complex communities are inherently unstable, yet the observed persistence of diverse communities highlights a central contradiction in theoretical ecology. While foundational frameworks often model species as homogeneous populations, one theoretical resolution lies in including internal species structure. In this work, we incorporate explicit demographic stage structure into a generalized Lotka-Volterra framework to evaluate how ontogenetic changes throughout the life cycle of a species can affect whole-community stability. We show that stage-dependence of inter-specific interactions can significantly expand the stable parameter space for a species network. Furthermore, this enhanced stability requires strong competition between life stages of a species. Our study illustrates that stage structure with population heterogeneity expands classical stability criteria, providing a mathematical foundation for understanding how ontogeny modifies the classically derived complexity boundaries for local asymptotic stability.

title: LiveSync: Iterative Self-Training for Lip-Sync Generation
abstract: Audio-driven lip synchronization aims to match target speech through localized mouth and jaw articulation while preserving subject identity, head pose, and surrounding facial context. Naturally recorded videos provide synchronized reconstruction targets but rarely offer pairs that are matched in identity and pose yet differ primarily in speech-related articulation. Mask-based training enables reconstruction from these videos, but random-reference inputs differ from the aligned self-reference used at inference. We present LiveSync, an iterative self-training framework in which a single mask-based model generates pseudo pairs and is refined for deployment. The model is first trained on a curated real-video corpus augmented with externally generated clips covering under-represented visual conditions. A frozen checkpoint then uses independently sampled audio to generate mouth-edited references from real-video frames, copying pixels outside the edit mask from each source frame. After confidence filtering, these references are paired with aligned masked inputs and original real-frame targets. The retained pseudo pairs are mixed with real training data to refine the same model from its current weights, updating training supervision without adding inference stages. Although we instantiate the framework with a single-pass GAN-based model, the self-training strategy could in principle also be adapted to diffusion-based models. Experimental results show that LiveSync achieves leading synchronization performance on HDTF and competitive performance compared with the baselines on the AIGC-LipSync subset, while maintaining low inference latency.

title: An Interactive GraphRAG Workspace for Reifying, Auditing, and Steering Conversational AI Memories
abstract: Conversational Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely employed in software engineering for code generation, debugging, and architectural design. However, as developers engage in multi-session development tasks, technical knowledge becomes siloed in isolated, linear chat histories. Reusing context across sessions leads to three critical challenges: (1) flat-vector retrieval fails to traverse multi-hop relational dependencies between distant architectural decisions; (2) temporal drift in software packages and APIs results in silent context poisoning when reusing aged dialogue logs; and (3) raw conversation concatenation induces prompt bloat and attention degradation.
