title: Critical limits of generating functions for face-constrained labelled planar maps
abstract: We study connected planar maps with a fixed number of numbered faces, whose vertices carry integer labels such that the minimum label along the boundary of each face is one. Each face has its own positive weight, and an edge shared by two faces receives the geometric mean of their weights. For any fixed number $k\ge3$ of faces, we prove that the suitably rescaled generating function converges locally uniformly as the face weights approach the critical value $1/12$, possibly at different positive rates. The limit is a finite, continuous sum of integrals over cubic schemes. Each scheme edge carries a Green kernel for a singular differential operator on the positive half-line, and each face contributes one insertion of the derivative of the tree scaling profile. The main difficulty is obtaining uniform estimates for small vertex labels, where the minimum-label constraints of different faces can interact. A positive corner-marking expansion reduces this problem to establishing uniform bounds on the contributions of marked configurations, both for small and large vertex labels. These estimates prove integrability of the surviving diagrams and show that coincident marks and noncubic schemes contribute only lower-order terms.

title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. To address this gap, we introduce TREK, a suite of three components: TREKTRACE is a plug-and-play framework that attributes failures to specific stages of retrieval and reasoning. We apply it to TREKBENCH-WILD, a meta-benchmark of real-world questions that require complex reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge. Surprisingly, the main bottleneck is post-retrieval reasoning rather than retrieval: frontier models are often misled by conflicting evidence even after retrieving all the information needed to answer. To study this bottleneck, we build TREKBENCH-CTRL, a controlled benchmark with distractors spanning temporality, relevance, and trustworthiness, and show that benchmarks dominated by outdated distractors substantially underestimate task difficulty. Together, TREK provides a testbed for diagnosing and improving reasoning over rapidly evolving knowledge.

title: The Bellaterra graphs are Ramanujan
abstract: The Bellaterra automaton gives three involutions of every set of binary words of a fixed length. We identify their Schreier graph at level $n$ with a cubic arithmetic graph over $\Q(\sqrt{17})$, and prove that every nonconstant adjacency eigenvalue satisfies the Ramanujan bound. In particular, this proves Malyshev-Pak's Conjecture that the Bellaterra graphs form a family of two-sided expanders.

title: Where Groups Split: A Probe Prior for Nonzero Within-Group Variance in RL Post-Training
abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a prompt only when the rewards in the sampled group disagree. With a binary verifier, a group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has within-group variance zero and a zero advantage. Uniform sampling continues to spend rollouts on prompts that are unanimous now and stay unanimous as training goes on. Pass rate is a weak forecast of that future. Two prompts at the same pass rate can move apart: one into the range where a finite group splits, and one toward a ceiling where the group becomes unanimous again. Aperture estimates the later pass rate from a short probe. A small subset of the pool is trained with the same recipe, every prompt is scored on the base model and on the probe model, and the two pass rates are plugged into the probability that a group of the training size is all wrong or split. The resulting weight is a static prior. It can be used alone or multiplied by an online scheduler, and the GRPO update is left as it is. On mathematical and logical reasoning with 1.7B and 4B models, the prior improves greedy accuracy over uniform GRPO and raises the fraction of groups with a nonzero advantage. The same prior still helps when it is combined with dynamic sampling or with selective rollouts.

title: MPIG: Multi-angle Polarization Image Generation from a Single Polarization Observation
abstract: Polarization imaging provides informative cues for material analysis, scene understanding, and visual perception. However, acquiring complete polarization observations typically requires specialized hardware and multi-angle measurements, thereby increasing system complexity and limiting practical deployment. In this work, we address the problem of predicting the missing $45^\circ$, $90^\circ$, and $135^\circ$ polarization views from a single $0^\circ$ observation by leveraging a learned scene prior. To this end, we propose MPIG (Multi-angle Polarization Image Generation), a Swin Transformer-based framework that couples cross-angle feature interaction with residual decoding to predict angle-dependent intensity variations while preserving shared scene structure. Specifically, measured Stokes differences and polarization-strength-aware supervision guide the recovery of polarization modulation, orientation, and magnitude, while low-rank factorization further reduces the decoding cost. We also construct HighPol, a large-scale real-world polarization dataset comprising 5,474 groups of high-resolution four-angle polarization images collected from diverse indoor and outdoor scenes. Experimental results demonstrate improved image and polarization accuracy, achieving 29.729 dB PSNR, 0.9505 SSIM, and $21.514^\circ$ AoLP MAngE while requiring 85.86 M parameters and 1.126 T FLOPs. Furthermore, downstream validation on glass and semantic-segmentation tasks suggests that the generated polarization images can preserve task-relevant information, demonstrating the effectiveness of MPIG and the practical utility of predicted polarization observations for downstream vision applications.

title: Observability of wave equations with time- and space-dependent potentials: a counterexample under GCC and a positive criterion on the disk
abstract: We show that the geometric control condition (GCC) for the free wave equation does not guarantee internal observability in the presence of a smooth time-dependent potential. On a bounded connected domain with analytic boundary, we construct a nonempty open observation set such that the pair satisfies GCC and the free Dirichlet wave is observable, and a smooth $2π$-periodic potential for which there exists a nonzero smooth Dirichlet wave that vanishes on the observed cylinder for all time. The wave is the unique mild solution in the space $X_Ω=L^2(Ω)\times H^{-1}(Ω)$ on every finite interval, so no finite observation horizon yields an observability inequality for this fixed potential. The construction starts from a real-valued local counterexample to unique continuation across a noncharacteristic hyperplane; this local statement is of independent interest, since earlier constructions for the wave operator use complex-valued waves and potentials. The global counterexample is obtained by joining flat oscillatory solutions along the edges of a polygonal observation set, repairing their sum at the vertices without changing its zero set, and then using a spatial transition to a common time-independent pair near the boundary. For comparison, on the unit disk we show that an observation region containing a central disk and a neighborhood of an embedded cross-cut yields observability for every weak wave at sufficiently large observation time, with constants uniform over bounded measurable potentials; the proof uses a cut, logarithmic polar coordinates, and a Carleman weight whose favorable flux is confined to the observed artificial boundary.

title: Mode coupling theory analysis of water dynamics detected by dielectric spectroscopy
abstract: Mode-coupling theory (MCT), one of the most prominent models of the glass transition, also makes various specific predictions for the molecular dynamics in the liquid state of matter. They can be best experimentally tested by evaluating susceptibility spectra covering a broad frequency range. In the present work, we clarify whether the most recent broadband dielectric-spectroscopy results on water, whose glass transition is highly disputed, are compatible with MCT. The so-called fast beta process, expected within this theory, should be detectable at low temperatures only, inaccessible in water due to its inevitable crystallization upon cooling. Therefore, we also investigate data on aqueous LiCl solutions, which can be easily supercooled. We find that all the available broadband dielectric data on these solutions and pure water are well consistent with MCT. Notably, this includes the expected interrelation of the critical temperature dependence of the alpha relaxation to its often-neglected non-Debye spectral shape. Moreover, the available data on the fast beta process, detected in a 14.8 mol% LiCl solution, are also well consistent with the theory. We find a smooth development of the derived MCT parameters with salt concentration which supports the validity of the critical temperature Tc = 222 K and system parameter lambda = 0.55 deduced here for pure water. We also compare the current dielectric relaxation-time results to those determined by other experimental methods and address the question whether information on the controversial fragile-to-strong transition of water can be obtained from such data. Finally, we discuss the significance of the dominant dielectric relaxation process of water for the glass transition as described by MCT, especially considering scenarios questioning its association with the alpha relaxation.

title: Failure of disjoint additivity under magnetic Gauss constraints
abstract: Under local magnetic Gauss constraints, vertex-disjoint regions can have commuting physical observable algebras that do not generate all observables on their union. We construct such counterexamples for every finite non-Abelian group on regular square tori, retaining the full magnetic physical space and original supports inside a fixed contractible disk. A peripheral projector selects inputs on which a joint transition preserves the constraints, while its loop factor alone fails the universal test over physical exterior completions. For a specified support family around a fixed eight-edge square loop, additivity fails if and only if the group is non-Abelian and each inner face is covered by at least one of its two prescribed peripheral edges. Leaving a face uncovered restores full additivity. For the same loop, additivity also holds with any region at vertex-set graph distance at least two. These results refute a recent group-double additivity proposition.

title: Follow the Mixed Groups: Ridge-Tracking Gaussian Sampling for Zero-Variance Web Rollouts
abstract: Group relative policy optimization learns from a question only when the sampled responses disagree. A group that is entirely correct or entirely incorrect has zero reward variance and a zero advantage. On the Web, that group has already spent its searches and page fetches. Gaussian curricula aim the next batch at pass rates where a finite group can still mix. A Gaussian on the latest empirical rate treats every all-fail history as the same point, and a center stepped by the average signed change of those rates is pushed by prompts already stuck at 0 or 1. RIDGE keeps the Gaussian curriculum and changes the coordinate, the center, and the width. Each prompt carries a Beta posterior. The sampling weight is the marginal of a Gaussian target under a Gaussian approximation of that posterior, divided by a prediction of tool-call cost. The center and the width are an exponential smooth of the posterior means of groups that just came back mixed. All-correct and all-incorrect groups refresh the posterior and do not move the center. The GRPO update itself is unchanged. On two math backbones and a retrieval-augmented question answerer, RIDGE raises average accuracy by 3.4 and 2.9 points over GRPO and average exact match by 3.7 points, at 29.6\% fewer math rollouts and 32.7\% fewer tool calls than dynamic sampling.

title: A gentle introduction to approximating high-dimensional integrals with lattice rules and a maybe-not-so-gentle introduction to the relevant function spaces for QMC integration
abstract: These lecture notes give both a practical and theoretical introduction to high-dimensional integration with lattice rules. We introduce lattice points and rules in combination with accompanying Julia code. Next we introduce the typical function spaces used in the literature. We compare classical Sobolev spaces with Sobolev spaces of dominating mixed smoothness. We derive lower bounds and show that the curse of dimensionality is unavoidable for these unweighted function spaces. Next we switch to weighted periodic spaces and derive a constructive upper bound using the component-by-component construction for the generating vector of a lattice rule. We pick periodic spaces because they are a perfect match with lattice rules. The upper bound shows that under suitable conditions on the weights we obtain dimension-independent worst-case error bounds. We then use embedding constants to transfer these bounds to some common norms for these periodic spaces.

title: $2$-adic Representations of Elliptic Curves over $\mathbb{Q}_2$
abstract: We provide a complete classification of the rational $2$-adic Tate modules $V_2(E)$ of elliptic curves $E/\mathbb{Q}_2$ with potentially good reduction. The classification is given in terms of the filtered $(φ,\mathrm{Gal})$-modules associated to $V_2(E)$ via Fontaine's functor $D_{pcris}^{*}$.

title: CoRe-WM: Conditioned Response-State World Modeling for Longitudinal Treatment-Response Prediction in Breast DCE-MRI
abstract: Pathologic complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a key prognostic indicator in aggressive breast cancer, yet existing prediction approaches either rely on pretreatment imaging alone, missing the patient's evolving response, or optimize multi-visit classifiers under direct outcome supervision, coupling representation learning with the clinical endpoint. We formulate longitudinal pCR prediction as a world-modeling problem and propose Conditioned Response-state World Modeling (CoRe-WM), which learns a latent state-transition model that predicts the next imaging state from the observed sequence. The transition function is conditioned on patient clinical profile and assigned therapy through additive shift and feature-wise modulation, enabling patient- and treatment-specific dynamics. A Factorized Response State pathway further decouples treatment-response dynamics from imaging appearance by encoding the structural prior that response manifests primarily in lesion morphology. After pretraining, all parameters are frozen and a linear readout predicts pCR at each clinical decision point. We evaluate CoRe-WM on I-SPY2 under five-fold cross-validation and assess cross-cohort transfer on I-SPY1. CoRe-WM achieves the highest discrimination among all evaluated methods at every prospective decision point, and demonstrates robust cross-cohort transfer. Ablation studies identify patient-profile conditioning and the factorized response pathway as the principal contributors. These results establish world-model-based representation learning as a promising framework for outcome prediction in oncology and beyond.

title: Can Quantum Entanglement Increase the Capacity of a Classical Relay Channel?
abstract: We show positive and negative results on classical relay channels with entanglement assistance, revealing a sharp contrast between strictly causal and causal relay encoding. First, we consider van der Meulen's setting of a unit-delay relay, with strictly causal encoding. We show that the standard cutset upper bound continues to hold with entanglement assistance, and deduce that entanglement does not increase the capacity for several classes of relay channels. Second, we consider a zero-delay relay, where the encoding is causal. We present an example in which entanglement enables rates that exceed the cutset upper bound by at least 12.5%. Namely, entanglement shared between the source and relay significantly increases the capacity of a classical zero-delay relay channel.

title: A Distribution-Free Separation Between Learned and Fixed Features
abstract: The success of neural networks is largely attributed to their ability to learn useful representations from training data. However, known results that prove a computational advantage of learned features over fixed ones are restricted to specific input distributions. We settle the COLT open question of Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026) by showing that this advantage can persist in the distribution-free setting. We construct a family of hypothesis classes that can be efficiently learned by a natural gradient-based algorithm on a two-layer ReLU network, but cannot be represented by linear predictors over any fixed feature map with polynomial dimension (and runtime). Specifically, for any sufficiently small error and any sufficiently large runtime budget R (depending on the error), there exists a hypothesis class that the neural network learns under any input distribution to the desired expected classification error in time at most R, while the dimension complexity (governing the dimension needed by linear predictors) is superpolynomial in R.

title: Construction of crystal-based light sources with LWFA electron beams
abstract: We discuss a possibility to construct a crystal-based light source (CLS) of gamma-rays using electron beams produce by Laser Wake Field Acceleration (LWFA). This state-of-the-art acceleration technique is capable of producing few-GeV, ultra-short (fs) electron beams. In the case studies presented, we demonstrate the feasibility of novel gamma-ray CLSs based on exposing single crystals to electron beams available at the ELI-ELBA. The results of rigorous numerical simulations are presented to characterise the radiation emitted emitted by 1 and 4 GeV electrons incident on a 200-micron-thick single silicon crystal along the (110) plane. The simulations were performed using the current divergence as well as a smaller value that is believed to be a realistic to achieve in the near future. We demonstrate that it is feasible to achieve a photon yield of $10^6-10^7$ photons/s in the photon energy range from 5 to 50 MeV. Looking further ahead, we also performed a similar analysis for a 4-GeV positron beam incident on much thicker targets, up to 2 mm oriented silicon crystal. In this case, the photon yield can be increased by an order of magnitude.

title: The Calderón Problem for Quasilinear Currents
abstract: We study the Calderón problem for smooth quasilinear current laws on a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\geq3$. Under the stated structural assumptions and analyticity conditions, the interior current law is determined by local Dirichlet-to-Neumann maps, up to a partial-boundary-fixing diffeomorphism and a Hall-effect-type invisible current. The two obstructions come from the linearized inverse problem, which is solved by combining boundary determination for magnetic Schrödinger operators with analytic continuation in solution coordinates. Higher-order linearization and a boundary argument involving products of three solution gradients then determine the remaining Taylor coefficients.

title: Subexponential Algorithms for Total Search Problems in the Dense Pigeonhole Regime
abstract: The class $\mathsf{PPP}$ captures fundamental total search problems, for which a solution is guaranteed to exist by the pigeonhole principle and the main challenge is to find it. We ask whether problems in this class admit significantly faster algorithms in the \emph{dense regime}. More concretly, we study \emph{binary collision Short Integer Solution} (SIS): given a matrix $A\in\mathbb{Z}_q^{n\times m}$ with $m>n\log q$, the goal is to find distinct $\underline{\mathbf{x}},\underline{\mathbf{y}}\in\{0,1\}^m$ with $A\underline{\mathbf{x}}=A\underline{\mathbf{y}}\pmod q$. Brute-force enumeration can be used to find a collision in $q^{\mathcal{O}(n)} \operatorname{poly}(|I|)$ time, and no significantly faster algorithm for that problem is known. We present an algorithm running in time $q^{o(n)}\cdot\operatorname{poly}(|I|)$ whenever the density parameter $δ:= m/(n\log q)$ is $ω(1)$.\footnote{All logarithms are in base $2$, and $|I|$ is the binary input length.} Building on reductions of Sotiraki et al.~(FOCS~2018), we obtain corresponding algorithms for dense variants of weak constrained SIS, Equal Vector Sums, Minkowski, and Blichfeldt. Our algorithm adapts techniques of Bhati et al.~(FOCS~2026), who gave a subexponential algorithm for Equal Sums in the dense regime and proved a tight conditional lower bound. Their conditional lower bound easily transfers to SIS and shows that the running time of our algorithms is essentially optimal.

title: A noncommutative weak $L_1$-estimate for rough singular integrals
abstract: In this paper, we establish a noncommutative version of Andreas Seeger's weak type $(1,1)$ estimate for singular integral operators with kernels satisfying angular $L\log L$ integrability and an averaged radial Dini condition. The strategy for obtaining the sharp integrability condition involves not only some new estimates of the off-diagonal good and bad functions in Parcet's noncommutative Calderón-Zygmund decomposition but also certain essential modifications of Seeger's kernel decomposition and estimates.

title: Edge Deployable Lightweight Framework for Real-Time Driver Safety System with Integrated Lane Departure and Traffic Sign Recognition
abstract: Lane departure and traffic-sign negligence are leading contributors to road accidents, particularly in regions with non-standardized signage and limited annotated data. Existing Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) solutions are often developed as disjointed submodules, are rarely validated for real-time operation, and struggle to balance accuracy with low-latency inference for embedded deployment. We address these gaps with a unified, edge-deployable ADAS framework that simultaneously performs lane-departure warning (LDW) and traffic-sign detection and recognition (TSD/TSR), and validate the proposed system on automotive-class devices. Our framework combines a lightweight, lane-segmentation-driven LDW, which includes a drivable-area fallback for degraded markings, with a two-stage TSD/TSR pipeline consisting of efficient sign localization followed by fine-grained classification, designed to preserve accuracy at embedded latency. To support region-specific deployment under data scarcity, we curate a 35-class local traffic-sign dataset and introduce a generalized augmentation and balancing profile, expanding the corpus from 359 images to 8,750 samples. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, the integrated system sustains 15 FPS end to end (32 FPS for LDW and 18 FPS for TSD/TSR). The TSD/TSR branch achieves 97.4 mAP for detection and 95.6% validation accuracy (93.1% on a local real-world set) while maintaining an approximately 13.9 M parameter footprint. Relative to recent methods that target a single task or report results only on desktop-class GPUs, our approach delivers both LDW and TSD/TSR with real-time performance on edge hardware, providing a practical pathway to low-cost, field-ready ADAS in resource-constrained settings.

title: Formally Verified Autoresearch for Analyzing the Expressivity of Multi-Head Attention
abstract: Multi-head attention is a central component of the transformer architecture, yet how its expressivity depends on the number of heads remains poorly understood. We study a one-layer, attention-only transformer with additive positional embeddings and define the head complexity $H^\ast(f)$ of a Boolean function $f$ as the minimum number of attention heads required to represent it. We derive an exact linear-fractional normal form for head complexity, prove a general threshold-degree lower bound, and give an explicit ten-bit function for which this bound is strict. For symmetric Boolean functions, we independently show that head complexity equals the number of times the function changes value between consecutive Hamming-weight levels, even when positional embeddings are allowed. This agrees with the concurrent characterization of Hsu and Xu (arXiv:2608.04243) in a model without positional embeddings. The symmetric lower bound combines our general threshold-degree bound with the classical result of Aspnes et al. (1994). These results were discovered and formalized by a frontier model through conjecture generation, theorem proving, and machine verification, while human researchers asked the high-level questions and reviewed the generated theorems. We make the Lean formalization and research traces publicly available to support agent-assisted theorem proving and formal verification in mechanistic interpretability. This work provides a proof of concept for using the capabilities of frontier models, grounded by formal verification, to develop an understanding of transformer architectures.

title: CASE: Complementary Articulation-Aware Speech Encoder to Enhance Speech-Driven 3D Facial Animation
abstract: General-purpose self-supervised speech encoders provide strong acoustic representations, but their pretraining objectives are not explicitly aligned with the visible articulatory dynamics required by speech-driven 3D facial animation. We propose CASE (Complementary Articulation-aware Speech Encoder), a complementary speech encoder adapted by contrastively aligning short speech clips with continuous 3D lip-mesh VQ-VAE latents. After adaptation, the geometry branch is removed, and the audio-only CASE representation is fused with the baseline SSL speech representation through residual cross-attention, while retaining the motion-decoder architecture and objective. Across four VOCASET baselines, CASE reduces mean lip vertex error by 2.8-6.0%, and mean full-face vertex error decreases in every system. Under the same fusion protocol, CASE yields lower mean LVE than the unadapted AV-SE stream on all four generators, with model-dependent margins. Because adaptation uses Korean speech-geometry pairs and evaluation uses English VOCASET, the result is consistent with cross-language downstream transfer under a shared English-pretrained audio-visual prior.

title: UnexpectedParrots: Iterating Behavioral Experiment Design with In-Silico Simulations
abstract: Running behavioral experiments is expensive, slow, and prone to design flaws, often detectable after collecting data. We introduce UnexpectedParrots to iteratively refine behavioral study designs before a researcher recruits costly human participants. UnexpectedParrots relies on reasoning traces in addition to responses from LLM participants to uncover diagnostic critiques of structural errors and missed opportunities in existing study designs. When evaluated against a human-pilot or a no-simulation design-only baseline, UnexpectedParrots adds most value, producing unique, high-quality critiques. In a moderated user study with 12 proficient researchers, we find UnexpectedParrots useful, time-saving, and thought-provoking. Critiques provided by UnexpectedParrots often converge on issues researchers identify only during independent human pilots or additional formative interviews, even when the fidelity of the simulated populations remains questionable. Our users deem UnexpectedParrots useful not only as a tool to conduct early pilot studies and identify errors but also as an ideation tool to expand one's research horizon.

title: TOMORI: A Tool-Orchestrated Mixing Operator for REAPER Interaction
abstract: Code-based agents can operate creative software, but mixing requests often describe an intended sound without specifying the edits needed to achieve it. We present TOMORI, a code-based mixing-agent harness for native digital audio workstation (DAW) control. Custom plugins provide REAPER project inspection, optional audio measurement, and execution of model-generated Lua code. All observations return as text; delivery includes an editable project and rendered audio. TOMORI-BENCH pairs 110 human-reviewed reference edits with three instruction forms and evaluates native DAW execution end to end through operation structure, parameter precision, and rendered-audio outcomes. Across 990 cases from three primary models, explicit instructions yield high reference agreement, while abstract requests reduce project agreement and audio improvement. Paired ablations show that the full workflow improves explicit execution over a single submission. Prompted audio measurement succeeds in all 28 selected abstract cases but yields no clear overall improvement on the reference-based metrics and increases tool calls. These results expose the gap between executable DAW control and precise realization of perceptual mixing goals.

title: MCSplat: Multi-View Photometric and Geometric Consistent Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for Driving Scenes
abstract: Driving-scene reconstruction via feed-forward Gaussian splatting from sparse multi-view images remains challenging due to two factors. First, cross-camera photometric inconsistency, caused by variations in exposure, ISP, and illumination, can be incorrectly absorbed into Gaussian geometry. Second, unreliable local geometric supervision arises from normal-based constraints near depth discontinuities. To address these issues, we present \textbf{MCSplat}, a multi-view consistent feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for driving scenes. MCSplat constructs a canonical appearance space from depth-guided multi-camera correspondences to decouple geometry learning from camera-specific appearance. A multi-scale Bilateral Grid Transformer restores raw camera appearance from canonical renderings, enabling photometric supervision without contaminating Gaussian geometry. To improve local geometric reliability, we estimate Fisher-information-based uncertainty from photometric sensitivity and use it to adaptively weight surface-oriented self-supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction quality and generalization across driving datasets. Geometry-oriented evaluations further reveal enhanced cross-view depth consistency and local surface-normal agreement, while qualitative results show fewer geometric artifacts and more coherent structures across overlapping views.

title: Equivalent Non-linear Shift Register Transformations and Espresso
abstract: The stream cipher Espresso was designed by E. Dubrova and M. Hell as a hardware-efficient candidate for 5G security. It has two components - a 256-bit binary non-linear feedback shift register (NFSR), with 14 feedback taps, and a 20-variable non-linear output function. However, the security of Espresso with regard to several standard cryptanalytic attacks are estimated using an alternate NFSR, which has only two feedback taps. The above analysis is based on the claim that this alternate NFSR is obtained using a transformation algorithm which preserves the output sequence of the original NFSR. This issue has become all the more significant in the light of recent results on hardware performance evaluations, which assume that the stated equivalence holds. This article presents the first successful attempt in settling the above question of Espresso NFSR equivalence. We arrive at our main result by a careful analysis of existing transformation methods relevant to the question. In doing so, we first identify and correct a critical flaw in the proof of a foundational result of E. Dubrova. Next, in the context of Espresso equivalence, we analyze and unify the transformation framework of Dubrova and the one proposed by Yao and Parampalli. Based on our analysis, we have succeeded in transforming the LFSR in an Espresso-equivalent design reported by Yao and Parampalli to the Espresso alternate NFSR. Further, we have obtained a corresponding non-linear output function which achieves output-equivalence with the LFSR design, and hence, with Espresso.

title: On Pearl Blockchain's Proof of Useful Work: Systematization and Flexibility
abstract: We revisit the proof-of-useful-work (PoUW) scheme in Pearl blockchain's white paper (Pearl Research Team), giving a systematic sensitivity characterization as an alternative to its Jackpot policy, along with efficient algorithm for verifying the sensitivity condition. Beyond its independent interest, our characterization yields a more flexible PoUW scheme that eenables miner autonomy: each miner can independently choose its noise magnitude to tailor the trade-off between computational accuracy and mining efficiency to its own needs.

title: The Dynamical Bead Model
abstract: We construct an infinite-dimensional diffusion on the space of interlaced particle configurations on Z x R, a process we call the dynamical bead model. The process (self-)interacts through instantaneous reflection and preserves the bead measures of [C. Boutillier, Ann. Probab., 2009]. Through the height function correspondence, our process is equivalent to a reversible interface in (2+1) dimensions. We provide compelling evidence that at large space-time scales the interface exhibits diffusive behaviour, as we compute exactly its diffusivity matrix and show it is non-degenerate and independent of time.

title: Predicted Class Correction: Conformal Thresholds for Classes with No Calibration Data
abstract: Class-conditional conformal prediction calibrates a separate score threshold for every class and therefore requires labelled calibration examples of every class. In long-tailed deployments these are exactly what is missing: rare classes are left with few or no held-out examples, and existing methods are either undefined for them or fall back to the shared marginal threshold. We ask whether the per-class correction can instead be predicted from descriptors of the class that require no labels at all. We propose Predicted Class Correction (PCC), which regresses the offset between the per-class and the marginal conformal quantile on geometric descriptors of the classifier head, shrinks the prediction by a scalar selected on the labelled classes, and refits a single marginal offset. The descriptors depend only on the model's weights, so a class with zero calibration examples still receives its own threshold, and since only one scalar is calibrated, split conformal's marginal guarantee is retained. On ImageNet, PCC improves worst-class coverage on such classes by 0.058 [0.006, 0.110] at matched average set size, 42% of an oracle that sees the test labels. Of eight baselines on the same splits, six change the statistic by exactly zero and the best reaches 0.016 with an interval containing zero, so PCC is the only one distinguishable from no improvement; the gain persists with only 100 labelled classes out of 1000. A second finding concerns evaluation: worst-class coverage becomes unmeasurable before it becomes unachievable. Below roughly 35 test examples per class no improvement can be shown even for an oracle, so a null result there reflects the evaluation set, not the method. Restricting evaluation above this depth recovers a significant improvement on Pl@ntNet-300K, where the effect had appeared absent.

title: Real-time quantum simulation of hadron production in deep inelastic scattering
abstract: We develop a quantum simulation framework for meson production in deep inelastic scattering based on light-front QCD Hamiltonian formalism. A quark-antiquark dipole, prepared either as a single-momentum state or as the $q\bar q$ component of a virtual photon, is evolved in real time through the color field of a nuclear target via Trotterized unitary evolution. We consider both proton and gold nuclear targets, each characterized by their respective saturation scale. From the evolved state we extract the transverse momentum broadening, the total and elastic cross sections, and the $J/ψ$ production rate by projecting onto the $J/ψ$ light-front wavefunction. We then extract the nuclear modification factor $R_A$ at different photon virtuality $Q^2$ and analyze nuclear modification effect. Results of classical simulations show good agreement with analytical eikonal predictions across a broad range of parameters. For the single-momentum dipole, quantum simulation is demonstrated on a quantum circuit emulator with a smaller lattice size, and results are consistent with the classical benchmark. This work establishes a first-principles, amplitude-level pathway toward computing exclusive hadron production in deep inelastic scattering, directly relevant to the physics program of the Electron-Ion Collider.

title: Probing and Mitigating Hallucinations in Speech-augmented Language Models for Automatic Speech Recognition via Small Language Models
abstract: The widespread success of large language models in natural language processing has spurred the development of speech-augmented language models (SLMs) to extend their reasoning capabilities from textual inputs to spoken ones. Despite impressive performance, SLMs remain susceptible to hallucinations, posing challenges in practical utility. To this end, we first probe hallucinations in SLMs for automatic speech recognition (ASR) via the lens of causal mediation and behavioral analysis. To mitigate fabricated ASR hypotheses, we propose AudioSLM, a compact yet effective ASR framework built upon a small language model, which leverages alignment cues and cross-attention layers to synergistically bolster acoustic modeling and cross-modal interactions. Experiments on LibriSpeech reveal that hallucinations arise from multi-head self-attention modules with an excessive attention bias towards textual tokens. AudioSLM considerably eases ASR hallucinations and outperforms some LLM-based ASR models.

title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. Automatic speech recognition supplies a transcript and utterance interval. TED queries audio-free windows with the transcript for Temporal Alignment and Forecasting, or answer candidates for Cross-Modal Temporal Binding, then aggregates evidence relative to that interval. Across four frozen AV-LLMs on SVHalluc, Temporal Forecasting accuracy rises from 29.3-33.7% under full-video questioning to 79.3-82.2% with TED. Query replacement reduces recovery; the observed anchor remains beneficial when temporal-region availability is held fixed. Physical-isolation and timing-shortcut controls test alternative explanations. The findings distinguish locally recoverable evidence from successful full-video decisions, motivating explicit separation of narration content, utterance timing, and time-indexed visual evidence.

title: Large deviations for the largest eigenvalue of a polynomial in Gaussian matrices
abstract: In this article, we prove that the spectrum, the norm, and the largest eigenvalue of a self-adjoint polynomial $P$ in $k$ independent matrices from the GOE satisfy a large deviation principle.

title: Entropy hypocoercivity and query complexity for the bouncy particle sampler
abstract: We study convergence in relative entropy of the bouncy particle sampler with Gaussian velocity refreshment, for a target $e^{-U}$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with $U$ $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth, and condition number $κ=L/m$. For initial laws with bounded density relative to equilibrium, we show that the relative entropy decays exponentially up to an arbitrary additive error $δ$, with a rate that depends only logarithmically on the density bound and on $δ$. From a Gaussian cold start and with a suitably chosen refreshment rate, the relative entropy falls below $δ$ after time $\widetilde O(\sqrt{d/m})$. Combined with exact simulation by windowed thinning, this gives an expected gradient-query complexity of $\widetilde O(d\sqrtκ)$, improving the $\widetilde O(d^2\sqrtκ)$ bound based on $L^2$ hypocoercivity.

title: A coupling normal form for reversible center-center Hamiltonians with application to the restricted three-body problem
abstract: Near a reversible center-center equilibrium, the Birkhoff normal form does not describe the families bifurcating from the continued tori, which resonant normal forms capture through a reduced system.With a reflection symmetry, we develop a coupling normal form in which the bifurcating families also appear as tori of action normal forms. Along a selected coupling direction, the first harmonic in the angle difference is absorbed into an action-dependent counterterm. We prove that the coupled recursion determines unique counterterm coefficients, a formal action normal form, and an exact counterterm factorization. The factorization gives a recovery constraint, whose trivial factor corresponds to the Birkhoff normal form. At every finite order, a symmetric pair of bifurcating branches leaves the trivial branch at a critical curve, carrying approximately invariant tori and circles with residual estimates. In the spatial circular restricted three-body problem, these give approximate halo orbits and quasi-halo tori.

title: CHSM8: A Chess Transformer that Follows Natural-Language Style Prompts
abstract: We present CHSM8, a 210M-parameter chess transformer that plays moves conditioned on a free-text description of a playing style, e.g. "go for the Sicilian Defense", "solid, safe, risk-free chess" or "You are Magnus Carlsen in his prime". The model is pretrained without search on 1.07B filtered Lichess games, using a factorized move representation and legal-move masking. It reaches 1837 Elo against a strength-limited Stockfish and, in 1,000-game matches, beat every other public model we tested that was likewise trained without preference tuning, rewards or search, including one with 13 times as many parameters. We then fine-tune it to follow text on a synthetic dataset: Gemma-4-31B describes the playing style of 3M game sides, a 1B Gemma-3 model distilled from the 2.4M of those descriptions that contradict nothing on the board labels the rest, and every one of 30M selected game sides gets five descriptions. Supervised fine-tuning attaches a frozen text encoder through gated cross-attention, and direct preference optimization (DPO) uses the same moves under a mismatched description as the rejected sample. After DPO, style adherence rises on every prompt we test (for example, queens traded early 53% -> 67%, pawn moves 29% -> 32% of all moves, queenside castling 97.3% -> 99.7%), and strength without a prompt stays within noise of SFT (1792 vs. 1797 Elo). Design choices at every stage were made by fixed-budget automated search loops on top of standard architectures and training recipes. We document the full pipeline and the decisions behind it, report the ablations that failed, and evaluate the models across many style prompts and kinds of games, with 1,000 games per setting. The work is fully open source and reproducible: weights, datasets with all training labels, prompts, configurations, inference code and playable demos are public and free to build on.

title: Studying proof data with proof theory: the case of AI-generated mathematics
abstract: I present a method for analyzing large collections of formally verified mathematical proofs (e.g. OpenAI's) grounded in some historical and philosophical musings on mathematics in the age of AI. Many of the quantities involved, such as the size of a proof term or the number of redundant steps, are already computed by work on improving automated provers, where they serve as targets. My aim is to turn them into measurements of proofs themselves: compared against a reference library and against each proof's own cut-free form, checked against theorems they must obey, and controlled for how the proofs were compiled. With these instruments, I measure how (much) machine-generated mathematics diverges from human mathematics, and find that AI-written formal proofs realize far less of the logical compression available to them than human mathematicians do (31% against 73% in mathlib, and 55% against 86% on proofs that call no automation). These figures are broadly in line with reports from those who build provers and proof-improvement tools that AI-written proofs are often longer than they need to be.

title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
abstract: Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe interaction bottleneck. Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a small set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.

title: CD-OPD: Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Teacher takeover in on-policy distillation (OPD) can produce incorrect responses even when the student and teacher independently answer the same problem correctly, a failure we quantify using Collaboration Failure Rate (CFR). To address it, we propose Contextual Digest for On-Policy Distillation (CD-OPD). CD-OPD structures the earlier context of teacher guidance through a teacher-generated dependency graph, curating the required problem conditions and preceding reasoning as node summaries alongside the unchanged guidance in a Contextual Digest before student continuation. We further develop online meta-reweighting, which compares Digest segment gradients with a task gradient from independent student responses to improve student-only performance, favoring updates predicted to reduce task loss. Across eight benchmarks, CD-OPD improves average accuracy by 1.32--7.05 percentage points over representative existing OPD methods. It also reduces CFR by 27.4\%--56.4\% relative to existing takeover-based OPD methods.

title: Operator-Mismatch Contrastive Learning for World-Relative Trajectory Coherence
abstract: World models are increasingly judged by how well they rank plausible futures, yet plausibility alone is the wrong target. The same scene can evolve under many latent rules, and a future that is smooth and physically valid under one rule can be incoherent under the rule actually in force. We formalize the resulting failure, operator-blindness, and show that it is systematically hidden by standard evaluation: a scorer can attain near-perfect generic ranking while separating current-world from other-world futures no better than chance. We introduce Operator-Mismatch Contrastive (OMC) learning, whose semantic hard negatives are valid-but-wrong-operator trajectories, and a matching protocol that measures world-relative coherence directly. On a controlled synthetic benchmark with in- and out-of-distribution operator parameters, across two trajectory-scoring backbones, and on feature-level external validation with CoPhy ballsCF, OMC raises operator-sensitive scoring far above a chance baseline that nonetheless achieves 0.99 generic top-1. We prove that the wrong-operator negative is necessary both for the protocol to detect the failure and for the objective to fix it, and position OMC as an auxiliary coherence signal (a trajectory-coherence scorer, not a generative model, planner, or control agent) that can be attached to existing world-model representations.

title: Improved algorithms for computing the matrix logarithm based on the double-exponential formula
abstract: Tatsuoka et al. proposed an efficient algorithm for computing the matrix logarithm using the double-exponential (DE) formula. Its discretization error decreases exponentially as the number of quadrature nodes grows, and its nested grids allow previously computed values to be reused when the mesh is refined. They also reported that their approach is more robust than Gauss--Legendre quadrature for ill-conditioned matrices. We propose two algorithms based on the DE formula. The first adaptively refines the mesh while reusing previously computed values and requires no matrix norm computations. The second uses a rigorous error bound to select the number of quadrature nodes a priori. Numerical experiments show that both methods attain lower errors than Tatsuoka et al.'s method at comparable elapsed times over the tested ranges.

title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
abstract: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. Our contribution includes two resources in English and Modern Standard Arabic: a culturally grounded preference dataset for training and evaluation, and a multiple-choice benchmark designed to assess culturally aligned behavior across nations. All test data are validated by native speakers to ensure authenticity. To optimize cultural alignment, we experiment with post-training methods across multilingual and Arabic-centric language models, evaluating performance on both generation tasks and our cultural multiple-choice benchmark. By releasing an evaluation benchmark, we provide a foundation for systematically studying and improving culturally aligned behavior in language models.

title: Isotropy of symplectic involutions and motivic equivalence for groups of type $\sf{C}$
abstract: We extend to arbitrary characteristic a theorem due to Karpenko and Tignol on the isotropy of symplectic involutions after generic index reduction; as a consequence, we also prove the existence of critical varieties for semi-simple algebraic groups of type $\sf C$ over arbitrary base fields. The latter result relies on a characteristic-free argument, which involves the computation of the mod $2$ Tate trace of the variety of isotropic ideals of reduced dimension $2$ for a symplectic involution.

title: Bulk universality of scaling limits for the almost Hermitian Coulomb gas
abstract: Inspired by the recent approach to edge universality of Cronvall and Wennman, we prove several local universality results for scaling limits in the bulk in the almost Hermitian regime, as well as associated results relating to reproducing kernel spaces of the Fock type.

title: Mixed Tate Chabauty--Kim beyond the polylog quotient
abstract: We develop an algorithmic approach to mixed Tate Chabauty--Kim theory for the full unipotent fundamental group of $\mathbb{P}^1 \smallsetminus \{0,1,\infty\}$, beyond the polylogarithmic quotient used in previous work. The key step is computing the cocycle evaluation map in the presence of a nontrivial motivic Galois action, using relations among motivic multiple zeta values. This yields explicit Kim functions involving multiple polylogarithms, as well as an algorithm for solving the $S$-unit equation whose halting is implied by certain natural conjectures.

title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments
abstract: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. GreenNIDS connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a reusable analysis dataset. Model implementations write a common set of outputs, which are ingested into a run-level table with companion tables for model configuration, feature importance, and training history. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.

title: The inviscid limit of 2D Navier-Stokes near a self-similar vortex collapse
abstract: We study the inviscid limit of the two-dimensional Navier--Stokes equations with initial vorticity given by three point vortices whose inviscid trajectories collapse self-similarly at $t=1$. For every fixed $0<γ<1$, we prove that the solution is approximated by a superposition of Lamb--Oseen vortices centered at the point-vortex positions, with an $L^1$ error of order $O(ν^{1-γ})$, uniformly for $0<t\le T_ν=1-ν^γ$. We use coordinates adapted to the self-similar collapse and study a long-time inviscid limit problem on the interval $0<s\leγ\log(1/ν)$, with a time-dependent rescaled diffusion coefficient $η(s)$ that tends to zero as $s\to\infty$.

title: Non-abelian LVM manifolds}
abstract: We extend the tangency construction of López de Medrano, Verjovsky and Meersseman from diagonal abelian actions to non-abelian Samelson groups. For these groups the tangency locus is a moment-map zero set: the commutator term in the leafwise Hessian vanishes there, and under an admissibility hypothesis, Kempf--Ness convexity gives a global transversal whose projectivization is a compact complex manifold. The construction includes compact rotation groups and groups with non-closed central rotations. In the latter setting we construct explicit families of complex dimension $2m-3$, $m\geq5$, which are $4$-connected and admit no symplectic form. Their meromorphic function fields are rational of transcendence degree $m-2$, although every holomorphic map to a projective space is constant. We compute their connected automorphism groups and show that they admit no maximal torus action. They are Hopf-surface bundles over compact complex quotients of stable Grassmannian loci; these bases give related examples already in complex dimension five. The families demonstrate that the non-abelian tangency construction reaches beyond compact complex manifolds with maximal torus actions.

title: Painting Change Map as guidance for generating painting processes
abstract: Digital art generation has undergone a massive paradigm shift, moving from static image synthesis to dynamic video generation that can mimic the human painting process. While existing models can synthesize visually stunning time-lapses of paintings being created or "unpainted," they largely treat the creative process as a black box. Current conditioning mechanisms are either too rigid, relying on static geometric cues like Canny edges or depth maps, or too holistic, utilizing simple scalar progress variables that offer no localized control. Consequently, users lack the agency to steer how a painting evolves over time. In this work, we argue that true control over the video generation of artwork requires a joint understanding of two fundamental dimensions: where an artist acts, and when those actions take place. To achieve this, we introduce the Painting Change Map, a novel spatio-temporal control mechanism that explicitly tracks normalized structural changes across a 1,000-timestep continuum, a resolution sufficient to capture fine-grained stroke-level changes while remaining computationally tractable. By mapping localized visual differences into an encoded RGB space, our representation enables fine-grained guidance for both the forward painting and reverse unpainting processes. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. We outperform existing control baselines and achieve competitive or superior results compared to state-of-the-art painting methods. Furthermore, under oracle conditions, our method surpasses all baselines by a significant margin. Code is available at https://github.com/Markus-Pobitzer/painting-change-map.

title: Multi-site Learning for Forecasting Day-Ahead Wind-Power Production for Onshore Wind Farms in Great Britain with Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Accurate day-ahead wind-power production forecasting is increasingly important for energy system operations, market activity and balancing Great Britain's grid as wind generation grows. In this study, we train multi-site deep neural networks (DNNs) using pooled historical production and reanalysis weather data from 88 onshore wind Balancing Mechanism Units (BMUs). Forecasts are produced at 09:00 UK time for the following midnight-to-midnight delivery day, matching NESO's operational day-ahead forecasting schedule. We use reanalysis weather as future covariates during training and numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts during inference, extending training beyond the available historical NWP archive. Our multi-site recurrent neural network outperforms site-specific RNNs and a multi-site XGBoost model, while processing the full future-weather trajectory for the forecast horizon further improves accuracy relative to hour-aligned approaches. Our best model, an RNN with a bidirectional weather encoder (BiRNN) for NWP trajectory processing, reduces MW mean absolute error and root mean squared error relative to NESO by 17.94% and 12.51%, respectively, across 638,246 matched BMU-hour observations under conditions approximating unconstrained wind farm operations. In 40 leave-one-out trials, the BiRNN achieves lower MAE than NESO at 32 excluded sites, indicating transferable forecasting ability despite reduced accuracy when sites are omitted from training. Our capacity-estimation, data-cleaning and reanalysis-based training approach provides a basis for scaling NWP-aware multi-site forecasting to additional wind farms, longer production histories, and increased forecast accuracy beyond that seen in this study.

title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
abstract: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.

title: SEAL: Towards Persistent Tool Poisoning Attack against LLM Agents via Prefix-Eliciting Trigger
abstract: Tool poisoning has emerged as a critical security threat to LLM agents, where adversaries embed malicious instructions in tool descriptions or external resources that enter the agent's context, allowing adversaries to manipulate agent's tool selection process. However, existing tool poisoning attacks primarily rely on an idealized assumption that the attacks task effect within a single interaction round. We show that their effectiveness degrades sharply in realistic multi-round agentic settings. We further reveal that this degradation stems from the fact that agents do not consistently surface attack-relevant signals in their reasoning as the planning context evolves, thereby weakening the attack's influence across rounds. To investigate whether tool poisoning remains a practical threat in such realistic settings, we propose SEAL, a two-stage method for persistent tool poisoning. Specifically, SEAL first performs Prefix-Eliciting Trigger Optimization (PETO) to optimize context-specific triggers that elicit attack-relevant reasoning prefixes, improving effectiveness within individual contexts. It then applies Local-to-Universal Trigger Aggregation (L2U) to combine these local triggers into a single universal trigger, improving generalization across different contexts and execution rounds. Extensive experiments across seven representative multi-round scenarios and different models demonstrate the attack effectiveness of SEAL, its transferability across target models, and its resistance to potential defenses.

title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data
abstract: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.

title: Mining the Self-Rewriting System: A Vision for Data Mining on AI-Native Infrastructure
abstract: Classical data mining treats data as generated outside the learner. Emerging AI-native infrastructure invalidates this assumption: as agents observe system state, act, update retrieval stores and models, and promote new artifacts into the serving path, their own decisions reshape the future logs, traces, corpora, and evaluation records used for later training and release. We call this new research object a self-rewriting system and the resulting system-induced distribution shift endogenous drift. Our central, falsifiable claim is that cross-surface causes are not identifiable in general from marginal per-surface monitoring: different coupled failures can produce the same individual signals while differing in their joint behavior, requiring joint analysis for reliable attribution. This agenda comprises four foundational research problems: fusing heterogeneous drift signals into calibrated gating and attribution (C1); mining agent traces whose activity alphabet evolves (C2); maintaining knowledge fabrics through online reindexing, faithfulness, and compression decisions (C3); and safely promoting concurrent learning streams through one shared evaluation gate (C4). These remain fragmented across concept drift, performative prediction, process mining, streaming retrieval-augmented generation, and MLOps, without a unified data-mining agenda. We outline public benchmarks and evaluation criteria, using AI-native telecom only as a motivating exemplar with analogues in finance, software CI/CD, and clinical decision support.

title: A dual variational principle for the Moser-Trudinger inequality: existence, uniqueness and stability of extremals
abstract: For $p>1$, with $p'=p/(p-1)$, we prove the sharp dual inequality $$ \int_0^1-\log\left(1-\frac{\left|\int_0^xf(y) dy\right|^{p'}}{x}\right) dx\leq\mathsf{K}_p, \qquad \|f\|_{L^p(0,1)}\leq1, $$ where $\mathsf{K}_p$ is the logarithm of the optimal value in Moser's one-dimensional formulation of the Moser-Trudinger inequality. The dual functional follows from the Gibbs variational principle, monotone transport and the Legendre transform. Its supremum is attained, giving a dual proof of the existence theorems of Carleson-Chang (1986) and Hudson-Leckband (2002); the classical concentration threshold is realized by equality cases in Hoelder's inequality. For $p=2$ we prove, with rigorous computer-assisted estimates, that the nonnegative dual maximizer is unique and nondegenerate. Hence the extremal of the Moser-Trudinger inequality on a disk $D$ is unique up to sign, confirming conjectures of Adimurthi-Karthik-Giacomoni (2016) and of Chen-Lu-Xue-Zhu (2026). The positive extremal $u_*$ is nondegenerate, and, writing $\mathcal{M}_D(u)=|D|^{-1}\int_De^{4πu^2} dx$, we obtain $$ \mathcal{M}_D(u_*)-\mathcal{M}_D(u) \geq c \min_{\pm}\|\nabla(u\mp u_*)\|_{L^2(D)}^2 $$ for all $u\in H_0^1(D)$ with $\|\nabla u\|_{L^2(D)}\leq1$. Here $c>0$, and the exponent two is optimal, giving a quantitative stability theorem of Bianchi-Egnell type.

title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining, we introduce TILDE (Teacher-In-the-Loop Distillation from EFMs), which synergizes on-policy distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

title: Simulating Infant Senses with Age-Tuned Networks
abstract: What a newborn sees, hears and feels, and how this changes month by month, has been measured sense by sense, with different methods and in different units. We bring these measurements together for the first two years of life and ask whether small neural networks tuned to a given age can turn them into a quick, inspectable simulation of sensory perception. Each sense's immaturity is written as a fixed, age-indexed filter on the input, and a small prediction network learns behind it over the first year. The filters alone reproduce the order in which the senses mature, by construction. The networks add what filters cannot: in vision they extract far less than their input allows at early stages (at the newborn stage a toy's position cannot be read out, $R^2 = 0.00$, against 0.57 for a network trained directly on the same input), and a critical period and perceptual narrowing emerge without being built in; in hearing they track what their input allows. The same filters drive the Baby Senses Lab, a free website that shows a user's own images and sounds as a baby of a chosen age might sense them. It is a research and teaching tool, not a diagnostic test.

title: Generalized quaternion groups of order $4p$ are $4$-BCI-groups
abstract: For a finite group $G$ and a subset $S\subseteq G$, the bi-Cayley graph $\operatorname{BCay}(G,S)$ has vertex set $G\times\{0,1\}$ and edges $\{(x,0),(sx,1)\}$ for $x\in G$ and $s\in S$. The group $G$ is called an $m$-BCI-group if, for all subsets $S,T\subseteq G$ with $|S|\leq m$, the isomorphism $\operatorname{BCay}(G,S)\cong\operatorname{BCay}(G,T)$ implies that $T=gS^α$ for some $g\in G$ and $α\in\operatorname{Aut} G$. We prove that, for every prime $p$, the generalized quaternion group $Q_{4p}$ is a $4$-BCI-group. For $p\geq5$, the proof uses regular coverings and voltage assignments: we pass to quotient graphs modulo the Sylow $p$-subgroup and lift isomorphisms between them.

title: Oriented Zoll families of minimal hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{CP}^n$ and $\mathbb{HP}^n$
abstract: Let $M$ be either $\mathbb{CP}^n$ or $\mathbb{HP}^n$. We prove that the family $\overline{\mathcal{F}}=\{Σ_σ\}_{σ\in M}$ of minimal geodesic spheres in $M$ characterizes the Fubini-Study metric $\overline{g}$, that is, $\overline{g}$ is the only metric that makes these real hypersurfaces minimal. This result is related to the recent theory of Zoll families of minimal hypersurfaces $(M,g,\mathcal{F}=\{Σ_σ\})\in\mathcal{Z}$. It is conjectured that the only Zoll metric in $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is $\overline{g}$. We present evidence that suggests a similar rigidity of $(\mathbb{CP}^n,\overline{g},\overline{\mathcal{F}})$ in this context of minimal hypersurfaces. Namely, we show that a direct adaptation of Guillemin's Theorem for conformal deformations of Zoll metrics in $\mathbb{S}^2$ is not possible for $(\mathbb{CP}^n,\overline{g},\overline{\mathcal{F}})$, when $p=2n-1$ is a prime number.

title: The Corners of Ramanujan: Partial- and False-Theta Companions to Third-Order Mock Theta Functions
abstract: Most of the traditional third-order mock theta functions occur naturally as specialized values of partition-rank generating functions. The same finite rank kernels also occur in the ordinary and odd unimodal-rank series studied previously in the literature. We organize a parallel collection of corner series by retaining these kernels and replacing their quadratic core weights by linear peak weights. Their root-of-unity specializations are governed by partial and false theta identities recorded in Ramanujan's Lost Notebook; in one exceptional case the corner companion is itself a mock theta function. The classical rank series and Ramanujan identities are used as inputs. Our new results include exact two- and three-color partition identities with sparse theta discrepancies and an oriented three-dimensional corner with a distinct tower. In both color cases, positive decompositions separate the colored companion into copies of the relevant odd-corner series and a corresponding decorated even-corner series. Thus both sparse discrepancies become signed differences between natural corner families. Burson's boxed modular involution provides a common rank-refined model for the two corrections, whose surviving fixed points produce the exceptional quadratic sequences. For the side rank of the three-dimensional corners we obtain an exact formula at $z=-1$, a strict parity bias, quartic and cubic root-of-unity rank-difference identities, and exact equidistribution modulo $3$ on the progression $6n+5$. The cubic identity also gives exact congruence formulas on the progressions $6n+2$ and $6n+3$. We further classify the associated binary triangular support modulo every integer and derive general congruence families.

title: Inequalities for Higher-Order Logarithmic Differences of Boros--Moll Coefficients
abstract: Let $d_i(m)$ denote the coefficient of $x^i$ in the Boros--Moll polynomial $P_m(x)$. We prove that the sequence $\{d_{i-1}(m)d_{i+1}(m)/d_i(m)^2\}_{i=1}^{m-1}$ is strictly log-concave for every $m\ge4$, settling a conjecture of Chen and Gu. For every $m\ge 3$, we show that the consecutive ratios $d_i(m)/d_{i-1}(m)$ form a strictly log-convex sequence for $1\le i\le\lfloor m/2\rfloor+1$ and a strictly log-concave sequence for $\lfloor m/2\rfloor\le i\le m$, as conjectured by Zhao. For each fixed $i\ge 1$, we establish $(-1)^{r-1}Δ_m^r\log d_i(m)>0$ for $r\ge 2$ and $m\ge i$, where $Δ_m$ denotes the forward difference with respect to $m$. For $i=0$, we obtain the opposite inequalities. We thereby prove a conjecture of Jiang and Wang and two further conjectures of Zhao. For every integer $i\ge 0$, we prove strict infinite log-monotonicity of the sequence $\{d_i(m-1)d_i(m+1)/(\binom{m}{i+1}d_i(m)^2)\}_{m\ge i+1}$, strengthening another conjecture of Zhao. We further show that every positive real power of the binomially normalized ratio sequence is a Hausdorff moment sequence with a strictly totally positive Hankel matrix. We also obtain asymptotic formulas for forward differences of arbitrary fixed order, resolving a conjecture of Jiang and Wang. For integers $i\ge 1$, we prove that the sequence $\{2^n d_i(i)/d_i(i+n)\}_{n\ge 0}$ is an infinitely divisible Hausdorff moment sequence and that the Hankel matrix $[1/d_i(i+j+k)^τ]_{j,k\ge 0}$ is strictly totally positive for every $τ>0$. For the integral interpolation, we show that the Hausdorff moment property of the normalized reciprocals holds precisely when the positive real coefficient index is at least $1/4$.

title: Design and synthesis of laser inscribed flexible Bragg gratings containing silicon oxynitride-doped silicon thin film for authentication applications with the insights from X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy and Quantum Mechanical Calculations
abstract: Silicon-on-insulator is mostly the main driving material system for the field of silicon photonics, including PICs, due to high index contrast and compatibility with current semiconductor manufacturing processes [1]. A recent example is silicon oxynitride-doped silicon [2] discovered recently by our group, offering to set a new position for the fields of silicon photonics with a precise control of refractive index from 2.1 to 2.5 together with the photosensitivity property at different wavelengths. In this study, we demonstrate that the synthesis of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon can be performed on a flexible substrate for the fabrication of Bragg gratings (BG) at low temperatures below 100 degrees Celsius that are emerging for advanced applications. Their use in preserving ultra-fast lasers inscribed micro-information has been demonstrated numerically and experimentally due to its multispectral reflection behaviour from the ultraviolet (UV) to the near-infrared (NIR) regions. The unique structural characteristics of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon were studied at the Si L, O K and N K edges using soft X-ray absorption studies. The quantum mechanical calculations provide the potential formation mechanism of SiON-doped Si, whereas the crystal structure prediction for bulk Si3N4-xOx was conducted using the particle swarm optimization method in combination with density functional theory (DFT).

title: Dependence of the acoustic propulsion of nano- and microcones on their orientation and aspect ratio
abstract: Recent research revealed the orientation-dependent propulsion of a cone-shaped colloidal particle that is exposed to a planar traveling ultrasound wave. Here, we extend the previous research by considering nano- and microcones with different aspect ratios and studying how the propulsion of a particle depends on its orientation and aspect ratio. We also study how the orientation-averaged propulsion of a cone-shaped particle, which corresponds to an isotropic ultrasound field, depends on its aspect ratio and identify an aspect ratio of 1/2 where the orientation-averaged propulsion is particularly strong. To make our simulation results easier reusable for follow-up research, we provide a corresponding simple analytic representation.

title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). Outcome-supervised reinforcement learning derives verifiable outcome rewards from final answers but uniformly assigns each rollout's outcome-level advantage to all policy-generated tokens, creating a trajectory-to-operation mismatch since KG operations within a rollout can have varying effects on the search process and final answer.
