NPE's training objective, log-likelihood, favors posterior approximations that assign arbitrarily high density to the training points, and typical families of amortized conditional density estimators (e.g., normalizing flows, Gaussian encoders) are flexible enough to oblige. The resulting policy of extreme overconfidence translates poorly to held-out data. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. To avoid this trade-off, we propose Cross-Fitting NPE (CF-NPE), which uses sample splitting to separate conditional-mean estimation from the estimation of the posterior's higher moments. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.

title: CAVA: Complementary-Label-Aware Data Valuation
abstract: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains a classifier from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. Such labels are cheap to collect from crowdworkers or vision-language models (VLMs), making them attractive for large-scale annotation. However, both sources can mistakenly assign the true class as the complementary label. Such annotation errors are particularly harmful in CLL because the model is explicitly trained to suppress the correct answer. Optimal transport (OT) data valuation identifies harmful samples by comparing training data with a clean validation set, but transferring it directly to CLL creates a semantic mismatch: label $c$ means not class $c$ in the training but class $c$ in the validation. We show that this makes the OT label groups noisy mixtures whose behavior depends on the noise rate. The transferred score is informative only at sufficiently high noise, becomes uninformative at the crossover rate $1/M$ for $M$ classes, and reverses below it, where practical CLL annotation typically operates. We propose CAVA, which introduces a complementary label cost and a label margin that isolates the contribution of each complementary label to the transport potential. The margin keeps a consistent direction across noise rates, detects diagonal noise with a parameter-free threshold of closed-form precision, and allows detected samples to be recycled as ordinary-label supervision. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, CAVA separates diagonal noise almost perfectly where directly transferred OT valuation performs worse than random. With only a fraction of the clean validation data, it also improves every CLL objective we evaluate, showing that OT-based valuation becomes reliable once the semantics of complementary supervision are modeled explicitly.

title: Large-Level Limit of Doubled Chern-Simons Theory Part I: Regular Sector, Boundaries and Interfaces
abstract: We study three-dimensional $BF$ theory as the large-level limit of the doubled Chern--Simons theory $G_k\times G_{-k}$ for simply connected, compact, simple $G$, a limit that connects the symmetry topological field theories of finite and continuous symmetries. Lines whose two highest weights grow linearly with $k$ at fixed difference become $BF$ lines, with magnetic flux set by their average and electric charge equal to their difference. Representing level-$k$ torus states as normalized flux--charge wave packets, we prove that every fixed modular transformation of any fixed normalizable state with regular flux converges in the strong-$*$ topology to its $BF$ counterpart. The Dehn twist gives each line exactly its Aharonov--Bohm phase at every level, while $S$ converges to a Fourier transform exchanging flux and charge, without escaping to singular holonomies or large charges. States that approach singular fluxes at large $k$ are not covered. The natural boundary 2d theory is speculated to be a decompactified boson in the abelian case $G=U(1)$, and $\dim G$ non-compact free scalars for general $G$. For $SU(2)$, we discuss the gapped interfaces between adjacent levels, which must shift some flux or charge by a finite amount. In the $k\rightarrow\infty$ limit the interface is conjectured to be the $c=1$ Runkel--Watts theory.

title: Phase-sensitive quantum-state texture during thermalization of a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Heisenberg dimer
abstract: We investigate quantum-state texture during the thermal relaxation of an anisotropic spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg dimer subject to a longitudinal magnetic field and a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction. Starting from local transverse and longitudinal couplings to a bosonic bath, we construct a global weak-coupling Lindblad equation, identify its transition channels, and discuss the applicability and limitations of the secular approximation. The Gibbs state is obtained explicitly in the local spin basis, revealing that the DM coupling controls both the modulus and phase of the single-excitation coherence by modifying the energy splitting and rotating the chiral phase. For heating and cooling protocols, we compare rugosity, fidelity-based texture, and trace-distance texture with coherence, vector spin chirality, and purity. The relaxation dynamics separates population thermalization from the decay and precession of deliberately prepared energy-basis coherence. Their combined contribution to local coherence produces DM-dependent texture overshoots and, during cooling, damped oscillations and sign changes of the coherence quadratures. These transients differ from the evolution of coherence magnitude and purity, while trace-distance texture weights them differently from the overlap-based quantifiers. Calculations at reduced dissipation preserve the texture maxima within the secular model. The results identify a phase-sensitive diagnostic of relaxation.

title: The sum-product conjecture holds for fixed-field lattice product constructions
abstract: We study fixed-field analogues of the lattice product construction recently used by Bloom, Sawin, Schildkraut, and Zhelezov to disprove the sum-product conjecture over the real numbers. These sets are of the form $A_n = P_nG_n \subset F$, where $F$ is a fixed number field, $P_n$ can be rescaled to a set of algebraic integers whose conjugates are polynomially bounded in $|P_n \setminus \{0\}|$, and $G_n$ occupies a positive proportion of a bounded box of scale $Y_n$ in a fixed positive-rank multiplicative lattice. We prove that these fixed-field constructions satisfy the sum-product conjecture, $\max\{|A_n+A_n|, |A_nA_n|\} \ge |A_n|^{2-o(1)}$ as $|A_n| \to \infty$, with no restriction on the relative growth of the two factors. More strongly, any fixed power saving in the product set forces an asymptotically maximal sumset: there exists $C > 0$ such that, for each fixed $δ\in (0,1]$, if $|A_nA_n| \le |A_n|^{2-δ}$ for all sufficiently large $n$, then $Y_n \to \infty$ and $|A_n+A_n|/|A_n|^2 = 1/2 + O_δ((\log Y_n)^C/Y_n)$. In particular, the additive-box times unit-box construction of Bloom, Sawin, Schildkraut, and Zhelezov cannot produce sum-product counterexamples in any fixed totally real number field, at any relative scales. The proof combines a bound for factorizations of algebraic integers with a more general maximal-sumset theorem for coefficient sets whose nonzero-element ratios have small Weil height. The latter controls multiplication fibers and combines a lattice strip estimate with logarithmic separation derived from the theorems of Yu and Matveev.

title: A two-dimensional subspace of $\ell_\infty^3$ has a unique operator space structure if and only if it is isometric to $\ell_\infty^2$
abstract: We show that a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\ell_\infty^3$ carries a unique operator space structure if and only if it is isometric to $\ell_\infty^2$; the ``if'' half is the Andô's theorem. For each of the remaining spaces we exhibit an explicit non-normal $Y \in \mathcal{M}_2$, with $(I,Y)$ an extreme point of the associated matrix ball, for which the induced linear map is contractive but not completely contractive. Since every two-dimensional subspace of $\ell_\infty^3$ has the $2$-summing property, the $2$-summing property does not imply uniqueness of the operator space structure for two dimensional complex Banach spaces.

title: Optical imaging in dual-phase xenon time projection chambers for neutrinoless double beta decay searches
abstract: Dual-phase xenon time projection chambers (TPCs) are the leading technology for WIMP dark matter searches and have also demonstrated competitive sensitivities to neutrinoless double beta decays (0$νββ$) of \ce{^{136}Xe}. However, the large energy disparity between these two signals requires different detector optimizations. In particular, 0$νββ$\ searches in liquid xenon desire efficient rejection of closely located multiscatters of background gamma rays near the 0$νββ$\ energy, a capability achieved only in the vertical dimension in existing dual-phase xenon TPCs. We propose a highly customized, wide-angle optical system that can be conveniently integrated into large xenon TPCs and provide mm-scale transverse position resolution for MeV signals by imaging gas electroluminescence light. This approach preserves a TPC's low-energy sensitivity and optimizes a single experiment for both dark matter and 0$νββ$\ searches. This paper discusses the design, simulated performance, and implications of the imaging system for future liquid xenon-based 0$νββ$\ searches.

title: CheckDistill: Adaptive Checklist Distillation for Efficient Distributional Reward Modeling in Image Editing
abstract: Reinforcement learning for instruction-guided image editing requires reward models that provide reliable, accurate, and efficient feedback. Direct scalar prediction compresses multidimensional editing preferences, whereas generative evaluators can expose their judgment through explicit reasoning. However, broad scoring criteria do not specify all instance-dependent editing and preservation constraints, and generating long reasoning trajectories is costly for online optimization. We introduce CheckDistill, a pointwise reward modeling framework that internalizes instruction-adaptive checklists. We decompose each editing condition into atomic, independently verifiable requirements and construct four-dimensional scoring labels together with structured verification evidence. After supervised score initialization, a privileged teacher conditions on checklists, item-level judgments, and dimension-level rationales to supervise the student's own scoring trajectories. A reliability-weighted on-policy self-distillation objective adjusts supervision at score tokens according to agreement between the teacher's expected scores and reference labels, while retaining candidate probability weights in a truncated token support. The deployed student directly predicts four score distributions without checklist inputs or explicit reasoning and aggregates their expectations into a scalar reward. CheckDistill achieves aggregate accuracies of 72.30%, 56.67% and 82.90% on MMRB2, MER-Bench and EditReward-Bench, respectively, exceeding the compared open-source baselines on all three metrics.

title: System Identification for Nonlinear Stochastic State-Space Models Using Ensemble Kalman Inversion with Application to Lithium-Ion Batteries
abstract: Nonlinear state-space system identification has attracted decades of interest, yet remains challenging because of the interplay among unknown parameters, nonlinear dynamics, and latent state variables. Its difficulty increases dramatically when the state and parameter dimensions increase. To address this challenge, we develop an ensemble Kalman inversion (EnKI)-based approach. This approach leverages EnKI to perform maximum a posteriori parameter estimation through successive local Gaussian approximations, enabling an iterative and incremental search for unknown parameters. The search combines Monte Carlo sampling with Kalman-type updates to evolve an ensemble of parameter samples, thereby offering empirical stability and the ability to handle strongly nonlinear models. The EnKI search is coupled with state estimation conditioned on the latest parameter estimates. This enables parameter identification along with latent state recovery. To improve scalability for large datasets, we further develop a cascaded EnKI (CasEnKI) method, which assimilates subdatasets sequentially to accelerate computation. We validate the proposed methods using a lithium-ion battery model with ten state variables and 18 unknown parameters. Simulation results show that the EnKI approach offers high identification accuracy and empirical stability in parameter search. Further, experimental results illustrate the computational efficiency and scalability of the CasEnKI method for large battery datasets.

title: Polar Switch: Fast Muon Orthogonalization with Polynomial Circuits
abstract: Muon, a 2024-born optimizer for language models, differs from the 2015-born spectral gradient descent mainly in its fast, GPU-friendly Newton--Schulz polynomial for orthogonalizing the gradient matrix. Accordingly, a line of research proposes faster polynomial iterations for gradient orthogonalization, such as Polar Express and Gram Newton--Schulz, both built on quintic polynomials. In this paper, we introduce Polar Switch, a new approach to polynomial gradient orthogonalization. Using simple polynomial circuits, Polar Switch reaches a given high polynomial degree at a lower FLOP cost than quintic iterations. We define a circuit as a short sequence of symmetric matrix products on a few square buffers, and circuits with $k$ products form a restricted family of odd polynomials of degree up to $2^{k+1}+1$. We choose the sequence of products in each circuit, their coefficients, and how the circuits are composed by numerically minimizing a worst-case bound on the polar approximation error. This minimization is subject to a FLOP budget that accounts for symmetric matrix multiplication kernels and a rounding constraint for numerical stability in half precision. Our two recommended Polar Switch methods have 15.5--18.7\% lower runtime than Polar Express on square matrices and 8.6--16.2\% lower runtime than Gram Newton--Schulz on rectangular matrices with aspect ratios 3.25, 3.5, and 8, with comparable approximation accuracy. In pretraining Modded-NanoGPT \#91, Qwen3-0.6B, and Gemma 3-1B, Polar Switch reaches final validation losses similar to those of established orthogonalization methods. Across the more than 14 million matrices that each of the two recommended methods orthogonalized in these runs, the estimated output spectral norms never exceed the designed bounds by more than 3\%, demonstrating their numerical stability.

title: FOMTools: Development and AI-Assisted Code Generation for First-Order Methods
abstract: We present FOMTools, an open-source Python package for developing, analyzing, and deploying first-order algorithms for parametric linear and convex quadratic optimization. The user specifies an iteration in Python, with syntax close to its mathematical description. The package represents the iteration as a computation graph of affine and piecewise affine operations. To analyze worst-case performance, FOMTools formulates a mixed-integer verification problem that maximizes a convergence residual over a specified set of problem instances and initial iterates. For probabilistic performance analysis, a batched GPU simulator collects algorithm trajectories and computes statistical bounds on the probability of exceeding a specified convergence tolerance. From the same algorithm description, FOMTools generates specialized solver code for embedded hardware, multicore CPUs, and GPUs. The package first generates the numerical data, factorizations, and matrix-vector routines without any agent. A coding agent then translates the iteration into C or CUDA code and iteratively optimizes the implementation. After each phase, the package runs the generated code on sampled inputs and compares it with a reference execution. FOMTools also serves as a CVXPYgen backend, generating and optimizing solvers for parametric CVXPY problems. We demonstrate FOMTools on sparse coding, network optimization, optimal control, and portfolio rebalancing. The verification bounds reveal worst-case behavior that sampling misses. The generated solvers run up to two orders of magnitude faster than NumPy implementations, and they outperform hand-written GPU code and the OSQP solvers generated by CVXPYgen.

title: Finite convexification by Minkowski summation
abstract: Let $A\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a nonempty compact set and let $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a nonempty compact convex set. We study the problem of when there exists $λ>0$ such that the Minkowski sum $A+λK$ is convex. First, we show that this finite convexification is equivalent to a uniform covering condition on the exposed sets of $A$ and $K$. We then show that another characterization is possible in terms of the covering radii of the iterated exposed sets after translating each exposed face of $K$ so that its relative centroid is $0$. In the case of convex polytopes, we show that it suffices to check the exposed sets in the first level of the iteration. We also study several special cases, such as strictly convex convexifiers, lower-dimensional convexifiers, strongly isomorphic polytopes, and the planar case.

title: A boundary integral method for computing electron repulsion integrals in heterogeneous dielectric environments
abstract: We present a boundary integral method for evaluating electron repulsion integrals (ERIs) in dielectric environments of piecewise constant permittivity. This generalizes conventional bare-Coulomb ERIs by incorporating screening from structured dielectric surroundings, such as the substrates and/or encapsulating layers present in modern two-dimensional-material devices. We formulate the problem as a second-kind boundary integral equation for the induced surface charge on the dielectric interfaces, and discretize it with a Nyström method on adaptively refined panels. The incident potential generated by each smooth orbital source density is evaluated by a Fourier truncated-kernel method in or near to its source box, and by fast multipole method (FMM) accelerated quadrature farther away. The linear system is solved by a Krylov iteration also accelerated by the FMM. We focus on cuboidal device geometries, and retain efficiency at high aspect ratios via close-to-touching panel quadratures. We further develop a distributed pipeline that computes the full ERI tensor, comprising thousands of orbital pairs, embedded in a single dielectric geometry. We demonstrate the method on an effective three-layer graphene slab over a Si/SiO$_2$ heterojunction, focusing on the central graphene layer represented by $198$ $p_z$-like orbitals, retaining the $2613^2$ non-negligible entries of the $198^4$-sized ERI tensor. The model is resolved on $1.3$ million surface unknowns, achieving a relative error of $0.004\%$, at a cost of $22$ node-hours.

title: Probability-Weighting Functions for Normal Tempered-Stable Laws: Orthogonal Channels and Information-Theoretic Indices
abstract: A probability-weighting function (PWF) maps objective probabilities into decision weights. We construct PWFs from changes in the distribution of returns rather than from a parametric family: with prior and posterior return distributions $F_{prior}$ and $F_{post}$, the PWF is $w(p) = F_{post}(F_{prior}^{-1}(p))$. Both distributions are normal tempered-stable (NTS), and the posterior differs from the prior along one of three channels, each isolated with the variance held fixed: scale, skewness and tail thickness. Around a symmetric benchmark with excess kurtosis 3, a 40% change in scale moves cumulative probabilities by up to 7 to 8 percentage points, a skewness of $\pm 0.5$ by 2 percentage points, and a change of $\pm 0.3$ in the tail index by about 2 percentage points. The three channels leave distinct signatures: the deviation $w(p) - p$ changes sign once, twice and three times, respectively. Three information-theoretic indices (a Fisher-normalized logit shift, a signed Jensen-Shannon divergence and a log-odds elasticity) summarize the distortions and avoid the endpoint singularity of the classical ratio $(w(p)-p)/[p(1-p)]$. Applied to NTS parameters calibrated to S&P 500 ETF daily returns over 2015-2025, the same channels produce distortions of 2 to 7 percentage points. Code that reproduces every figure and number in the paper is provided.

title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

title: Gradient descent reaches arbitrary accuracy in a fixed number of large steps on multiclass logistic regression
abstract: We show that gradient descent (GD) with step size $η$ can achieve $\varepsilon$ optimality gap on the multiclass logistic regression loss in a number of iterations $T$ that is independent of $\varepsilon$. To do so, the step size $η$ must be chosen large enough as a function of $\varepsilon$ (and properties of the linearly separable dataset), while $T$ is a constant that only depends on the data. The relevant properties of the data include the number of points and their margin (for $T$), and one additional quantity (for $η$) that turns out to be necessary in dimension $d \geq 3$. The proofs build on the known fact that, as $η\to \infty$, suitably rescaled GD becomes the perceptron algorithm, and the latter finds a perfect classifier in $T$ iterations. A similar claim was shown for two classes in dimension $d = 2$ using other proof techniques. This result adds to previous works that showed GD on the logistic regression loss can be accelerated by taking large step sizes. Those provoke a wild, oscillatory initial phase, followed by a stable phase. We provide results of this (qualitatively different) nature, too.

title: Trajectory Replay: Continuous-Time Mixture Transport for Lifelong Generative Models
abstract: Adapting pre-trained continuous-time generative models to sequentially incoming data without forgetting earlier tasks is a central challenge in lifelong learning. A leading strategy, generative replay, uses a generative model trained on historical tasks to augment its own continual update with synthetic samples from experience. However, it requires full trajectory simulations at every training step, which accumulate discretization errors and can degrade the replayed historical distribution. Here, we propose trajectory replay, which bypasses sample generation by training an updated velocity field to match both a frozen historical velocity along its trajectories and the incoming task's velocity field, weighted by a stability-plasticity coefficient. Through the lens of continuous-time transport, we show the resulting optimum averages the two task velocities by their respective densities and generates the mixture of their probability paths. Combined with mean velocity distillation, trajectory replay accesses historical trajectories using only a few network evaluations per continual update. Empirically, it outperforms generative replay and distillation baselines on class-incremental image generation. In two biological case studies, trajectory replay extends generative perturbation models to new contexts and experimental batches across two data modalities while preserving treatment-effect prediction.

title: Analytic results for the two-loop renormalization constants of Feynman gauge QED
abstract: The two-loop renormalization constants $Z_m$ and $Z_1\!=\!Z_2$ of Feynman gauge quantum electrodynamics (QED) in the on-shell scheme are computed using dimensional regularization. Analytic results are obtained for these constants. In addition, analytic expressions are obtained for their expansion coefficients in the dimensional regularization parameter $ε$ from order $1/ε^2$ through order $ε^5$. The high-order expansion coefficients will be needed for future multiloop calculations in QED and will provide a useful check for multiloop calculations in QCD.

title: Beyond Omni: A Unified MLLM for Embodied Sensory Understanding
abstract: Recent embodied systems increasingly build on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for their pretrained understanding and reasoning capabilities, but their perception of the physical world remains largely limited to basic modalities such as vision and audio. However, broadening MLLMs to more diverse sensory modalities from the physical environment is challenging: their representations are often weakly connected to the MLLM and vary substantially in structure and statistics, while their interpretation still requires shared high-level understanding and reasoning. We therefore propose Unisense, a unified embodied MLLM framework that supports diverse physical sensory modalities within a shared multimodal architecture. Unisense follows a two-stage training process: (i) aligning sensory representations with language to establish a language-accessible interface; and (ii) tuning modality-specific experts within the shared LLM to provide specialized processing for different sensory modalities. To support broad sensory learning, we curate Unisense-1M, a large-scale embodied sensory training corpus comprising 1M samples across 8 sensory modalities. We further evaluate Unisense on 12 benchmarks spanning depth, point cloud, IMU, tactile, thermal, radar, motion, and smell understanding. Across these heterogeneous sensing tasks, Unisense achieves strong performance and outperforms both generalist and specialized models on most benchmarks, demonstrating the potential of pretrained MLLMs as unified models for embodied sensory understanding.

title: An Efficient Open-Source Framework for Thermohygromechanical Phase-Field Simulation of Drying Damage Refractory Castables
abstract: The water removal from refractory castables is a complex process involving heat and mass transport and thermohygromechanical stresses. In order to reduce the risk of explosive spalling by improving the heat-up curves, numerical models are critical to predict the castable behavior during drying. However, most of the existing models either neglect the thermomechanical stresses or consider them as an \textit{a posteriori} assessment of the likelihood of failure. The present work proposes an open-source thermohygromechanical phase-field model to simulate the drying of refractory castables and predict the occurrence of explosive spalling. The model is based on an adaptive two-scale time-stepping strategy that allows for a significant reduction of the computational cost associated with the simulation. The model was validated against literature results and qualitative comparisons with experimental data were carried out to assess its ability to predict the failure behavior of partially saturated porous media during heating. The numerical simulations were also applied to investigate the impact of different heating methods on the risk of failure during drying. It was found that even at the significantly lower heating rates typical of refractory castable drying - compared to the fire accidents that motivate most thermomechanical studies on concrete structures - thermomechanical stresses still play a significant role in the explosive spalling, a finding well established for concrete under fire but novel for refractory castables. As a consequence, it was also concluded that the use of heterogeneous heating methods can increase the likelihood of explosive spalling. Ultimately, feasible solutions to increase the drying efficiency and safety that are compatible with the industrial setting were proposed and a free, open-source implementation of the model is provided.

title: A General Master Equation for Two Accelerated Detectors: Stationary States and Entanglement
abstract: We derive a general Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan master equation for two co-located, uniformly accelerated two-level detectors weakly coupled to scalar fields in the Minkowski vacuum, retaining coherent and dissipative contributions for arbitrary orientations, field masses, and spacetime dimensions. For equal orientations, we determine stationary states and their entanglement for two couplings to massless fields in four dimensions: symmetric coupling yields acceleration-dependent concurrence, whereas rotating-wave coupling gives acceleration-independent concurrence.

title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.

title: A McLennan formula for equiaccessible steady states
abstract: Near equilibrium, the Boltzmann distribution is corrected by the transient irreversible entropy flux, a result known as the McLennan formula. By expanding around equiaccessible steady states instead, we derive an analogue that can hold arbitrarily far from equilibrium. At zeroth order, steady-state occupation is determined solely by local escape rates, yielding a strong form of the active-matter principle of "low rattling." The first-order correction measures the impact of traffic imbalances on the accessibility of each state, marking the onset of nonlocal determinants of relative occupation.

title: Fourth moments of prime exponential sums and exceptional sets for sums and differences of primes
abstract: We prove a square root bound for the exceptional sets in the binary Goldbach and prime difference problems under quasi Riemann Hypothesis. If every nontrivial zero of every primitive Dirichlet $L$-function has real part at most a fixed $1/2\leqΘ<11/12$, then $E_+(N)\ll_ΘN^{1/2}(\log N)^{100}$ and $E_-(N)\ll_ΘN^{1/2}(\log N)^{100}$. Here $E_+(N)$ counts the even integers greater than $2$ and at most $N$ that are not sums of two primes, and $E_-(N)$ counts the positive even integers at most $N$ that are not differences of two primes. The common analytic estimate is a fourth moment bound of the minor arcs for a smoothed prime exponential sum.

title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.

title: AI Misconception and Adoption Among Indonesian K-12 Teachers
abstract: Indonesia's fragmented geography and uneven infrastructure pose persistent challenges for adopting new educational technologies. While national initiatives aim to mainstream AI in K-12 schools by 2025, policy readiness does not automatically mean teachers are ready for the classroom. This study surveys Indonesian K-12 teachers to examine: (1) their understanding of AI, (2) how they and their students use AI, and (3) their views on the acceptability of AI in learning activities. Through semi-automated thematic analysis, we identify common misconceptions and use cases. Our findings reveal a notable mismatch: while teachers find AI use in education acceptable and support it for the sake of efficiency, they remain fully aware of the risks to learning depth and academic honesty. We also find that this high level of acceptance is currently coupled with a poor understanding of how AI actually works.

title: Tactile In-Hand Object Rotation: A Comparative Study of Hand Morphology in Simulation and Hardware
abstract: Continuous in-hand rotation requires coordinated contact maintenance and renewal, linking manipulation performance to both hand geometry and tactile feedback. We investigate these relationships through rotational progress, finger participation, and fingertip loading on two versions of the low-cost LEAP Hand with anthropomorphic and symmetric finger arrangements. Both hands are integrated with TacTip vision-based tactile sensors and use a shared reinforcement learning framework. Simulation evaluates full tactile, binary touch, and proprioception-only observations on 12 unseen objects; hardware experiments evaluate full tactile policies on ten objects under multiple hand orientations. In simulation, full tactile observations increase mean normalized rotation per episode over proprioception alone by 94.8% for the anthropomorphic hand and 66.9% for the symmetric hand, with longer mean episode durations and lower mean total fingertip loads. Hardware contact measurements reveal more differentiated finger participation in the anthropomorphic hand, while cumulative loading is more evenly distributed across the symmetric hand's fingers. Overall, the symmetric hand achieves a 32.0% higher mean rotation count and a 25.8% higher aggregate rotation rate, together with longer manipulation duration. Additional hardware force recordings show a 19.9% lower mean total fingertip load for this layout. These findings relate finger arrangement to contact organization and load sharing, and show that richer tactile information supports greater task progress at lower mean loading in both simulated embodiments.

title: An Inverse Problem for the Moore Gibson Thompson Equation: Injectivity and Stability
abstract: We study an inverse problem for the variable coefficient Moore Gibson Thompson (MGT) equation in a bounded domain, where the objective is to recover an unknown initial acceleration from boundary measurements of the acoustic field. We establish both injectivity and stability of the associated measurement operator. Injectivity is established through a unique continuation property by applying a theorem of Tataru for analytically principally normal operators. The argument relies on a factorization of the third order operator into wave type components, combined with Carleman estimates and propagation techniques in the spirit of Tataru. Stability is derived through a microlocal analysis of the forward operator, based on the construction of geometric optics approximate solutions and the identification of an elliptic pseudodifferential operator arising from microlocal back propagation of the data. These results connect the MGT inverse problem with the classical theory of hyperbolic inverse problems, such as photoacoustic tomography, while highlighting new features induced by the third order dynamics and damping.

title: Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism with non-invertible symmetry
abstract: We formulate the Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism in the framework of non-invertible symmetries obtained by $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauging of $\mathbb{Z}_N$ or $U(1)$. While the non-invertible selection rules can constrain the texture-zero structure of fermion mass matrices, they do not by themselves determine the magnitudes of the allowed couplings. Introducing a flavon field allows the fusion rules to fix the leading powers of the small parameter $\varepsilon=\langle S\rangle/Λ$, thereby determining both the texture zeros and the orders of magnitude of the nonzero entries up to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ coefficients. We have constructed explicit quark and lepton models and study their predictions for the fermion mass and mixing hierarchies through analytical estimates and numerical analysis. In particular, a benchmark model with nine texture zeros in the quark sector can well accommodate the quark masses and mixing parameters with non-Hermitian Yukawa matrices. Its lepton sector admits a minimal type-I seesaw realization with normal neutrino mass ordering and one massless neutrino. These results provide a common symmetry framework for fermion mass hierarchies and texture zeros.

title: DexOAK: Object-Aware Kinematic Retargeting
abstract: We introduce DexOAK, a learning-based object-aware kinematic retargeting framework for generating contact-consistent robot hand references from human motion-capture data. DexOAK first minimizes an interaction-graph Laplacian objective over a joint hand-object graph, so the robot reproduces the demonstrated object-relative interaction geometry rather than the human hand pose alone. These per-frame solutions form seed retargeted references, from which a feed-forward network conditioned on human keypoints and object point clouds learns the retargeting function. Object-aware finetuning then refines the network under contact, non-penetration, and self-collision losses that position the fingers on the demonstrated contacts and reduce artifacts destabilizing physics-based refinement. Once trained, the network transfers to unseen data by inference alone, without per-frame optimization. DexOAK references improve dynamic retargeting over the state-of-the-art across bimanual tasks with rigid and articulated objects. On the Inspire hand, success rises from 39.5% to 48.4% on OakInk-v2, and ADD-AUC rises from 62.7% to 77.9% on ARCTIC. Ablations trace the gains to object-aware kinematic retargeting and the amortized network refined with contact losses. Trained on OakInk-v2, it transfers to ARCTIC zero-shot and nears in-domain performance after fine-tuning. On hardware, 46/56 open-loop replays succeed across five tasks, enabling dexterous robot data generation from human data. Visualizations and interactive results are at: https://fspinola.github.io/dexoak/.

title: Small subgraphs of large minimum degree
abstract: In 1991, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp asked to estimate the smallest $u=u(n,d,s)$ such that every $n$-vertex graph with average degree at least $d$ has a subgraph on at most $u$ vertices with minimum degree at least $s$. We resolve this problem up to polylogarithmic factors for all even values of $s$. More precisely, we prove that every $n$-vertex graph with minimum degree $d\geq s$ has a subgraph on $O_s\left(\max\left\{\frac{n}{d^{s/(s-2)}}(\log n)^{180},\log n\right\}\right)$ vertices with minimum degree at least $s$, whenever $s\ge 4$ is even. This improves a result of Janzer, Sudakov and Tomon, who obtained a similar conclusion for subgraphs of average degree at least $s$. We also prove that for every positive integer $s$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a finite family $\mathcal{H}$ of graphs with minimum degree $s$ such that $\operatorname{ex}(n,\mathcal{H})=O(n^{2-2/s+\varepsilon})$. This is tight and is the first result of similar kind that applies to odd values of $s$ greater than 3.

title: Socle formulas for rigid irreducible components of Lusztig's nilpotent varieties in type $A$
abstract: Let $F$ be a non-archimedean local field. For any irreducible component $C$ of a nilpotent variety of type $A$ let $π(C)$ be the irreducible representation of a general linear group over $F$ attached to it. We show that if the multisegment of $C$ is multiplicity free, $C$ is rigid if and only if $π(C)$ is $\square$-irreducible. In this case, \[ π(C*D)=soc\bigl(π(C)\timesπ(D)\bigr),\qquad π(D*C)=soc\bigl(π(D)\timesπ(C)\bigr) \] for every irreducible component $D$, where $*$ is the binary operation defined by Aizenbud and Lapid, in accordance with a conjecture of Lapid and Mínguez. We also give a computer-assisted example in $A_7$ of a non-simple rigid module $z\ne0$ which does not admit a proper rigid submodule $y\ne0$ such that $Ext_Π^1(z,z/y)=0$, answering negatively a question of Aizenbud and Lapid.

title: HandsOn: A Large-Scale Simulation Benchmark for Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands. We introduce HandsOn, a composable simulation platform and benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation. It supports five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, and approximately 200 rigid, articulated, and deformable assets in randomized scenes. The benchmark pairs 18,000 curated human demonstrations with 66 human-verified tasks: Core-50 supports demonstration-based learning and execution tests, while Transfer-16 evaluates asset and relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task training demonstrations. Qualitative real-robot rollouts illustrate sim-to-real transfer. Across diffusion, vision-language-action, world-action, and prompted VLM-based methods, the best trained multi-task policy achieves 29.1% Core-50 success. Without benchmark finetuning, GPT-6 using move_eef for palm-and-finger control achieves 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials. Trained-policy stage diagnostics expose failures in contact establishment, action coordination, and maintaining achieved goals, with additional sequencing errors in composed tasks. HandsOn provides a shared basis for investigating manipulation generalization and the limits of reliable physical interaction.

title: Spectroscopy as a Probe of Spacetime Foam
abstract: Quantum-gravitational spacetime foam varying in space and in time imprints, respectively, a transverse phase decoherence and an achromatic, stochastic arrival-time jitter on light from distant sources. We show that the jitter modifies the first-order temporal coherence $g^{(1)}(τ)$ and hence the observed spectrum, providing a spectroscopic probe of the temporal variation, complementary to existing imaging-channel constraints on the spatial variation. In the dynamical-foam limit, where the foam decorrelates within the light's coherence time, the spectrum splits into a coherent line core suppressed by $e^{-σ_ϕ^2}$, with $σ_ϕ^2$ the variance of the foam-induced phase jitter, and an incoherent pedestal, yielding a spectral shape-distortion bound on the foam exponent $α$. Three probes follow: the outright survival of broadband flux, the fractional width of a spectral line, and a chromatic deficit across a broadband continuum. Applied to the MeV emission lines of GRB\,221009A we obtain $α\gtrsim 0.63$, a weak, lever-arm-dominated floor. For the broadband CMB the foam induces an $e^{-σ_ϕ^2(ν)}$ deficit ($σ_ϕ^2 \propto ν^2$); a fit to the COBE/FIRAS monopole spectrum reaches $α\gtrsim 0.52$ ($95\%$ CL), and next-generation spectrometers reach only $α\gtrsim 0.54$--$0.55$ (forecast), limited by the foam--temperature degeneracy. The pedestal-independent line-width and CMB bounds are floors below the holographic value $α= 2/3$, consistent with and excluding no part of the imaging window reported for GRB\,221009A; only the conditional TeV survival bound ($α\gtrsim0.74$), which holds only for near-Planck-refresh foam ($τ_{\rm foam}\lesssim4\times10^{-28}$\,s), would exclude it --- and, with it, the window.

title: Exact model reduction by Lie symmetry groups
abstract: We develop a model-reduction technique based on Lie group theory for general engineering models described by a system of algebraic, ordinary, and/or partial differential equations with an arbitrary number of inputs, outputs, and constant parameters. The proposed method reduces the parameter space of these models without changing their external behavior, that is, their input-output maps. We apply this method to phase-field models used for high-fidelity simulations in electrochemistry to accelerate the analysis and design of metal-ion batteries.

title: Meromorphic modular differential equations for the elliptic genus of Calabi--Yau varieties
abstract: We study differential equations -- not necessarily monic -- for Jacobi modular forms. As an application, we derive a second-order differential equation for the elliptic genus of a $K3$ surface involving the logarithmic derivative of the modular invariant $j(τ)$, and we explicitly find a third-order equation with a leading coefficient of weight 12 for the elliptic genus of any four-dimensional Calabi--Yau variety. Furthermore, we propose a simple recursive algorithm for investigating second-order differential equations with leading coefficient $E_4(τ)$ or $E_6(τ)$.

title: X-ray Comptonization in an Accreting Kerr Black Hole System with a Tilted Disc and Thermal Corona; A General-Relativistic Monte Carlo Simulation: I. Model, Radiative Transfer and Spectral-Timing Properties
abstract: Quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the X-ray emission of accreting black hole binaries are commonly attributed to the relativistic Lense--Thirring precession of the inner accretion flow, in which a hot inner flow, tilted with respect to the black hole spin axis, precesses as a solid body while a cooler outer disc remains at its own, different tilt -- a warped, Bardeen--Petterson-type geometry. Testing this picture requires a radiative-transfer model that self-consistently follows photons through such a system: from emission near the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), through Compton scattering in a hot corona, to possible reflection off the misaligned outer disc, all under the full effects of light bending in Kerr spacetime. In this first paper of a two-part series, we present a general-relativistic Monte Carlo (GRMC) radiative-transfer model of a misaligned, warped, two-zone accretion system around a Kerr black hole. We describe the disc--corona geometry, the seed-photon prescription, the photon-transport engine -- including the geodesic integration scheme, the coronal Compton-scattering module and the outer-disc reflection treatment -- and the observer pipeline used to construct energy spectra, photon path-length and arrival-time distributions. We present the resulting energy spectra, light curves and spectral lags as functions of the black hole mass, corona size, outer-disc geometry, reflection albedo, photon-injection radius and observer inclination, and show how gravitational light bending systematically lengthens the path-length and arrival-time distributions of the escaping radiation. This model and its spectral-timing predictions form the foundation for Paper II, which extends the framework to track the full photon polarization state and presents the resulting energy- and precession-phase-resolved polarimetric signatures.

title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

title: $\mathbb{C}$-Motivic Eilenberg-Mac Lane Spectra as $\mathrm{MGL}$-Motivic Thom Spectra and Normed $\mathbb{G}_m$-Hochschild Homology
abstract: We exhibit the $p$-complete $\mathbb{C}$-motivic Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra $\mathrm{M}\mathbb{F}_p$ and $(\mathrm{M}\mathbb{Z})_p^{\wedge}$ as $\mathbb{E_3}$-$\mathrm{MGL}_p^{\wedge}$-motivic Thom spectra over the motivic $\mathbb{G}_m$-loop spaces $Ω_{\mathbb{G}_m}\mathrm{BGL}$ and $Ω_{\mathbb{G}_m}\mathrm{BSL}$, respectively. Furthermore, for $p=2$, we compute the $\mathrm{MGL}_2^{\wedge}$-relative $\mathbb{G}_m$-Hochschild Homology $\mathbb{G}_m \odot^{\mathrm{MGL}_2^{\wedge}} {-}$, recently introduced by Bachmann-Burklund-Dundas-Østvær, of $\mathrm{M}\mathbb{F}_2$ and $(\mathrm{M}\mathbb{Z})_2^{\wedge}$ to be $\mathrm{M}\mathbb{F}_2[\mathrm{BGL}]$ and $(\mathrm{M}\mathbb{Z})_2^{\wedge}[\mathrm{BSL}]$ as $\mathbb{E}_2$-$\mathrm{M}\mathbb{F}_2$-algebras and $\mathbb{E}_2$-$(\mathrm{M}\mathbb{Z})_2^{\wedge}$-algebras, respectively.

title: Tight Inapproximability for Generalized Circuits
abstract: Generalized circuits are a fundamental tool for establishing PPAD-hardness and membership of approximate equilibrium problems. Despite their importance, the complexity of finding approximate solutions has remained unresolved for a wide range of approximation parameters. We settle this question by establishing a tight threshold at $\varepsilon=1/6$. Specifically, we prove that $\varepsilon$-GCircuit is PPAD-complete for every constant $0<\varepsilon<1/6$, even when restricted to four gate types, and polynomial-time solvable for every constant $\varepsilon\ge1/6$. This closes the gap between the previously known hardness bound of $1/10$ and the polynomial-time solvability bound of $1/2$. We further investigate the relaxation in which a fraction $δ$ of the gates may be violated. We establish polynomial-time solvability of $(\varepsilon,δ)$-GCircuit for every constant $\varepsilon>0$ and $δ>1/5$, and of the fan-out-one formulations of $δ$-Pure-Circuit for every constant $δ>1/8$. These results follow from a decomposition theorem for directed graphs of maximum in-degree two and establish that the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture cannot be true for the aforementioned values of $\varepsilon$ and $δ$, unless PPAD = P. To showcase the contribution of our positive results, we apply them to a variety of problems in algorithmic game theory, including public goods games, financial networks, Bayesian, polymatrix, and graphical games, and obtain improved approximation guarantees.

title: Functional Model for Isometric Pairs Satisfying an Automorphic Covariance Relation - I
abstract: We derive a canonical functional model for a pair of isometric operators $(V_1, V_2)$ acting on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ that satisfy the automorphic covariance relation $V_1 V_2 = V_2 φ(V_1)$, where $φ$ is an automorphism of the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$. This extends the classical Bercovici--Douglas--Foias functional model for commuting isometric pairs to a dynamically twisted setting. When both $V_1$ and $V_2$ are pure isometries (shifts), the model simplifies to $(M_z, M_Θ W_φ^*)$ acting on $H^2(\mathcal{F})$, where $W_φ$ is a unitary weighted composition operator on the Hardy space $H^2$ and $Θ\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D}, \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{F}))$ is an operator-valued inner function such that $M_Θ$ is a shift. As an application, we establish a complete unitary classification theorem for automorphically covariant isometric pairs by identifying a complete set of joint unitary invariants. Notably, our results are novel even in the special case of rotation automorphisms ($V_1 V_2 = q V_2 V_1$ with $|q| = 1$).

title: Weights of KZ motives and quantum groups
abstract: The Knizhnik--Zamolodchikov (KZ) connection is defined on the constant bundle determined by $n$ finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ and a nonzero complex parameter $κ$, over the configuration space of $n$ distinct points on the affine line. Work of Schechtman--Varchenko and Looijenga shows that, when $κ$ is rational, the resulting local systems admit natural motivic realizations, called KZ motives. The Kazhdan--Lusztig equivalence identifies the local systems underlying these motivic variations with certain representations of the pure braid group arising from the corresponding Lusztig quantum group at a root of unity. We formulate conjectures relating the weight filtrations of KZ motives to structures in quantum-group representation theory, particularly tilting modules and the Jantzen and Andersen filtrations, and provide evidence for these conjectures. Our methods use a new deformation of the representation ring that records the first moments of the weight filtration, together with Schmid's theorem on limiting mixed Hodge structures and results on the Hodge filtration obtained in earlier joint work with S. Mukhopadhyay.

title: Spherically symmetric solutions with dust and radiation sources in Schouten-Codazzi Gravity
abstract: We examine in this paper exact solutions of Schouten-Codazzi gravity (SCG), a second order metric theory in which a Codazzi tensor is added to the Einstein field equations. We consider two spherically symmetric geometries that describe null radiation and inhomogeneous dust, corresponding to generalized Vaidya and Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi (LTB) spacetimes. The Codazzi tensor has to comply the Codazzi equations, this imposes restrictions on the geometry of spacetime that are determined up to two integration functions that naturally generate an effective ``cosmological constant'' and an additional degree of freedom. We show that for the Vaidya geometry, these Codazzi contributions modify the Misner-Sharp mass, while the LTB models have as an evolution equation a cubic polynomial whose coefficients depend on the Codazzi integration functions. This leads to a broader class of dynamics than those of General Relativity, and allows for an accelerated expansion and ever-expanding models without the introduction of ``dark energy''. Overall, our analysis suggests that Schouten-Codazzi gravity provides an appealing framework for applications in cosmology.

title: Monsoon: Scalable Spontaneous Speech Collection for Low-Resource ASR in 50 Languages
abstract: For most languages, automatic speech recognition (ASR) is limited less by model architecture than by a lack of accurately transcribed spontaneous speech. We present Monsoon, a framework for collecting such data at scale. It elicits unscripted conversations between paired contributors, screens recordings with automated classifiers, corrects transcripts over five levels of human review, and selects segments for lexical and acoustic coverage. It has collected speech in 50 languages; we analyse seven 3,500-hour corpora. At equal volume, its quality stages reduce semantic word error rate (WER) by 10-39% relative to a conventional protocol. Compared with an architecture-matched baseline trained on public corpora, Whisper fine-tuned on Monsoon performs comparably on the baseline's own test sets and reduces semantic WER by 20-44 points on conversational benchmarks. The gains transfer to a second architecture and grow with data volume. We release the framework, its quality-control models, and the fine-tuned models.

title: Topological Sheaves of Irreducibility: A Theoretical Framework for Multi-Agent Task Obstructions
abstract: Multi-agent systems can differ under identical agents and communication budgets when they support different forms of joint interaction. We introduce Topological Sheaves of Irreducibility (TSI), a sheaf-theoretic framework separating task-level compatibility obstructions from system capability. A task is represented by an interaction complex $K$ and a capacity sheaf $\mathcal{F}$; nonzero $H^n(K;\mathcal{F})$ defines a structural signature, while registered interventions test capability. For cocycle data, cochain realization is solvable exactly when the represented cohomology class vanishes. Examples show that the signature is sheaf-relative, and the degree-1 reduction yields cycle-space witnesses and observation requirements. We evaluate two finite one-round models. Across 15,625 degree-1 inputs, an all-agent additive primitive solves decision and repair exactly; the optimal pairwise system reaches 88.80% on decision, one input above the 88.79% majority-class baseline, and 26.63% on repair. On a degree-2 tetrahedral-boundary task over 531,441 inputs, the same-2-skeleton system retains all four three-agent primitives yet matches the pairwise-only optimum throughout the registered separation window, whereas adding the class-filling four-agent primitive makes both tasks exact. Status-preserving robustness checks retain exact performance but are not cost-matched to the class-restoring ablation. Conditional on the registered primitives and cost models, TSI provides task-relative, falsifiable tests of higher-order interaction.

title: The moduli space of quasimorphisms on subshifts and its pressure geometry
abstract: We introduce a metric geometry on the space of positive, linearly growing quasimorphisms on a mixing subshift of finite type. Two such quasimorphisms are identified when their homogenizations agree up to multiplicative scaling. The resulting moduli space carries a natural symmetrised Thurston-type metric, defined from the extremal ratios of their periodic orbit lengths. We prove that this is a genuine metric and determine several global features of the resulting space: it is unbounded, separable, incomplete, and has geodesics that are canonically generated by thermodynamic pressure functions. We then describe the endpoints of these geodesics and develop a boundary theory for our moduli space. We apply this theory to metric structures on right-angled Artin and Coxeter groups. In particular we construct isometric embeddings of geometric moduli spaces into our quasimorphism moduli spaces. As a consequence, Manhattan curves for metrics on these groups are $C^1$, with equality cases characterised by rough similarity of the underlying metrics. This provides insights into Manhattan curves in settings where neither classical thermodynamic formalism for Hölder potentials nor Patterson-Sullivan theory apply. The same construction recovers the corresponding results for hyperbolic groups and places these examples within a common dynamical-geometric framework.

title: Rational T cell repertoire allocation to control the gut microbiota
abstract: The gut microbiota shapes host metabolism, development and immunity, yet how the host regulates its composition in the presence of complex ecological interactions remains poorly understood. Recent experiments that measured T cell reactivity to individual strains in germ-free mice inoculated with a defined microbial community found that T cell recognition across microbial strains is sparse but broad, with a few polyspecific clones recognizing antigens shared across taxonomically diverse strains. Reanalyzing these experiments, we show that these T cell responses are associated with abundance changes of the strains they target. To interpret these findings, we develop a model linking the T cell repertoire to microbial abundances, in which a repertoire is allocated to minimize microbe-driven harm at the cost of maintaining an immune response. The model rationalizes the observed sparsity of gut T cell reactivity and shows that this allocation can emerge from competition between T cells for microbe-derived antigens. Finally, we find that while immune recognition can regulate microbial abundances, ecological interactions between strains may interfere with this mechanism. Together, these results provide a quantitative framework for immune control of gut microbial composition and identify principles governing the organization of T cell repertoires in the gut.

title: V-JEPA Hand: Simple, Accurate and Fast 3D Hand and Camera Trajectory Recovery from Egocentric Videos
abstract: Egocentric video supports diverse applications, including robot learning, augmented reality, and human activity understanding. Recovering metric 3D hand trajectories from such video requires estimating both hand motion and camera egomotion to express the hands in a consistent reference frame. Many existing pipelines recover hand and camera motion in separate stages, combining hand detection, hand reconstruction, camera tracking, and trajectory refinement. We present V-JEPA Hand, a simple feed-forward video model that jointly reconstructs bilateral hand motion and camera motion from egocentric clips. It uses a self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to extract spatio-temporal features from full-frame video and a query-based predictor to decode these features into per-frame hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion. We use the predicted camera motion to express the hand trajectories in a common world frame. The model accepts known focal lengths or predicts them when unavailable. It reconstructs each clip in a single forward pass. We train both components end to end in a single stage on a mixture of diverse pseudo-labelled videos and high-precision 3D annotations. A single model achieves the lowest coverage-aware mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard. It also yields lower world-frame trajectory errors than the compared SLAM-based pipelines. Ablations support the benefits of video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision. V-JEPA Hand achieves a forward-pass throughput of 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000. Project page: https://qft-333.github.io/V-JEPA-Hand-Page/.

title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .

title: RESIN: Multi-Chain Reasoning with Entity-Structured Indexing
abstract: Multi-chain reasoning is a challenging task not only because the multi-chain evidence is dispersed, but also because different parts of reasoning may require distinct, interacting chains of support. Flat retrieval can flood a model with loosely related text, whereas early selection of a single reasoning path can discard evidence that becomes useful only after other facts are considered. We introduce RESIN (Reasoning with Entity Structured Indexing), which uses structure to locate evidence while keeping the original source as the basis for reasoning. RESIN decomposes a question into focused one-hop needs, retrieves a small set of source-grounded units for each hop, and places only this relevant evidence in a compact reasoning buffer. The buffer preserves alternative supports until final composition, making intermediate decisions explicit without forcing a brittle path. On the full HolisQA benchmark, RESIN achieves 82.92 context recall and 76.70 answer relevancy over all questions, with higher reported CR and AR across five domains and higher F1 in four domains than the published baselines. Ablations show that both typed evidence diversity and hop-wise decomposition are essential, supporting a clear conclusion: Precise evidence organization and delayed commitment make multi-chain reasoning effective and auditable. Our code is available at https://github.com/RamonMeng/RESIN.

title: PPT-assisted capacities of bosonic Gaussian channels
abstract: We determine the exact quantum communication and entanglement-distribution capacities of three fundamental bosonic channels, namely thermal loss, thermal amplification and additive Gaussian noise, assisted by operations that completely preserve positive partial transpose (PPT). These operations are more powerful than local operations and classical communication (LOCC), but cannot generate distillable entanglement on their own. For thermal loss, the unconstrained capacity coincides with the Pirandola-Laurenza-Ottaviani-Banchi (PLOB) bound throughout the non-entanglement-breaking regime. The corresponding upper bounds are also attained for thermal amplification and additive noise. We extend these results to energy-constrained communication, establishing exact capacities for all three channels at every prescribed mean input energy. Our results solve a class of bosonic capacity problems under PPT assistance and establish exact benchmarks for determining whether the same communication rates can be achieved via LOCC alone.

title: High-Accuracy Propagation-Assisted Local Decoding for Fast Transversal Clifford Circuits
abstract: We benchmark the Iterative Redecode Scheme (IRS) on fast transversal Clifford circuits, achieving high-accuracy correlated decoding using local memory-style detectors and decoders. On a deep random Clifford benchmark, IRS yields approximately $4\times$ lower logical failure rates than the ghost protocol at $d=11$ with matched buffers, and $15\times$ lower rates than logical observable matching (LOM). In three-block GHZ preparation, IRS achieves $2\times$ lower logical error rates than reliable logical Pauli-product decoding with matched initialisation, improving to $25\times$ at $d=19$ with $\lceil d/2\rceil$ full initialisation rounds. We place IRS, which builds on Wan et al.'s scheme, within a broader propagation-assisted local (PAL) framework, where local decoders exchange messages rather than decoding a global hypergraph. IRS alternates local minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) on memory-equivalent detector error models (DEMs) with Pauli-frame propagation and detector updates across transversal CNOT layers, seeking local error estimates consistent with the global detector record. Prior-informed DEMs account for probabilities of propagated errors missing from the memory-equivalent model, improving initial decoding and reducing logical error rates. Zero-weight physical Pauli mechanisms enable inference and propagation of initially indeterminate stabilizer outcomes. Error rates saturate after a few iterations even for deep, adversarial alternating-tCNOT circuits, allowing iteration caps with negligible loss of accuracy. We find syndrome-extraction buffers of order $\lfloor d/4\rfloor$ sufficient for distance-dependent error suppression in the demanding regimes studied. The approach extends to other local decoders and CSS codes; for repeated logical $S$ gates, IRS achieves approximately $4$ to $10\times$ lower logical error rates than LOM, depending on initialisation.

title: Correlated decoding loses the surface code's effective distance below threshold
abstract: Correlated decoding improves matching and clustering surface-code decoders by reweighting one decoding subgraph conditioned on the other's correction. We show that standard reweighting can cause correlated decoders to fail on size-$(d-1)/2$ fault configurations that a distance-$d$ code should correct, reducing error suppression deep below threshold. Under circuit-level noise, a single first-pass edge can discount several correlated edges, even though their joint occurrence requires additional independent faults, so the decoder favors an over-discounted correction. Regularizing the reweighting rule restores the nominal distance scaling and a clear correlated-decoding advantage.

title: Fast Hubbard-Thouless Pumping with Local Counterdiabatic Driving
abstract: Counterdiabatic (CD) driving suppresses the excitations of fast protocols by adding an auxiliary Hamiltonian, but in many-body and topological systems the exact CD term is generally non-local and multi-body. We study this obstruction for Thouless pumping in the Rice-Mele model, first without and then with interactions. For noninteracting fermions, the exact CD term of the pump is non-local, but the variational framework of Sels and Polkovnikov yields accurate nearest-neighbor approximations. For the spinful Rice-Mele chain with onsite and nearest-neighbor repulsion, in the regime where the competition of the two interactions stabilizes quantized pumping, this approach fails: the infinite-temperature variational action only penalizes the CD amplitudes, and the resulting two-parameter nearest-neighbor term does not prevent the pump from breaking down when the cycle time is reduced from $50/t$ to $2/t$. We trace the failure to the structure of the exact many-body gauge potential, whose amplitude for each hop depends on the interaction energy that the hop costs. Resolving the nearest-neighbor currents by this energy, and fixing the coefficients with a ground-state-weighted action, gives a local ansatz with 14 coefficients that keeps the interacting pump quantized for cycle times $T=2/t$ and $T=1/t$, with an accuracy per site that does not degrade between rings of 8 and 12 sites.

title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
abstract: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model's consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain.

title: Low-mass and High-sSFR H$α$ Emitters at $z \sim 2$ in the ZFOURGE-COSMOS Field
abstract: We present a near-infrared spectroscopic follow-up study of seven H$α$ emitter candidates at $z\sim2$ in the ZFOURGE-COSMOS field, selected via the $K_{\rm s}$-band flux excess method. Spectra obtained with Subaru/SWIMS confirm strong H$α$ emission line at $z=2.06-2.49$ for all the targets. Three galaxies are low-mass systems ($\log(M_\star/M_\odot) < 9$) with high specific SFRs, while four are high-mass systems ($\log(M_\star/M_\odot) > 10$) on the star-forming main sequence. The low-mass galaxies show consistent H$α$ flux measurements between the $K_{\rm s}$-band flux excess method and the spectroscopy, whereas the high-mass galaxies show higher H$α$ flux inferred from the $K_{\rm s}$-band flux excess than the spectroscopic measurement which may be attributed to their extended star formation distributions. The low-mass galaxies exhibit extreme [O III] $\lambda5007$ emission with high rest-frame equivalent widths ($\mathrm{EW}_{\mathrm{rest}}$) ranging from 480 to 1064 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$. They are characterized by high [O III]/H$β$ ratios ($>4$) and weak [O II] and [N II] emission lines, indicating high ionization parameters and low metallicity. The line ratios are comparable to those of star-forming galaxies at $z \gtrsim 6$ and their local analogs. JWST/NIRCam imaging reveals a clear mass-dependent color gradient: the low-mass galaxies present positive F115W-F277W radial gradients with blue cores, while the high-mass galaxies exhibit negative gradients with red cores. These results suggest distinct assembly pathways for low- and high-mass galaxies during the cosmic noon epoch.

title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books
abstract: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. We study market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning on prediction markets, specifically Polymarket, whose thin order books pose distinct challenges. Three challenges underpin this research: adverse selection may cause a policy trained on real data to stop quoting; the consequences of a quote can arrive many steps after the action; and prediction-market L2 data does not identify individual orders needed for simulation. We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.

title: Training with ML-labeled Data via Stochastic First- and Zeroth-Order Optimization
abstract: Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.

title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials
abstract: Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material's internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions.
